q: 61 years old complaining of bloody nipple discharge , examination of right breast normal , what is the next step?

Ductography is a second-line test, considered when mammogram and ultrasound are negative and the discharge persists; it is not the first step. | D. CT has no role in evaluating nipple discharge; it is used for staging established cancer.

q: 45-year-old woman with bloody nipple discharge alone . Did mammogram and this is the finding: Heterogeneously dense breast tissue with microcalcification . What is the next step?

The compiler explains that suspicious microcalcification on mammogram should really go to biopsy, but biopsy and ultrasound are not offered; ductogram and MRI share the same indication (bloody discharge with a negative mammogram), so among the listed choices MRI is

Observation is unsafe with pathologic (bloody) nipple discharge and a mammographic abnormality.

q: 32 year old patient was undergoing elective thyroidectomy . What preop antibiotic should be given?

Prophylaxis, when indicated, is a single dose (redosed only for long surgery or major blood loss); a routine second dose adds no benefit.

q: A 50-year-old man is 6 days post-uneventful subtotal colectomy and ileocolic anastomosis when he develops sudden-onset shortness of breath and one episode of hemoptysis . q: Following a head-on motor vehicle collision, a 21-year-old unrestrained passenger presents to ER with dyspnea and respiratory distress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Air in the wrong places after chest trauma. Pneumomediastinum + cervical/subcutaneous emphysema + pneumothorax: tracheobronchial injury Persistent air leak or failed lung re-expansion after chest tube: suspect bronchial
r: In blunt high-energy trauma, the triad of subcutaneous/cervical emphysema , pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax points to a tracheobronchial injury : air escaping from a torn airway tracks into the mediastinum and neck. A pneumothorax alone explains decreased breath sounds, but not the extensive medi
x: A. Tension pneumothorax causes hypotension, raised JVP and tracheal shift away from the affected side; it does not explain pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema. | B. Open pneumothorax requires a chest wall defect (sucking chest wound), which is not described. | D. Pulmonary contusion produces hypoxia and patchy alveolar opacities developing over hours, not free air in the mediastinum and neck.

q: Day 5 post sigmoidectomy , no mention of the surgical site , fever only 38.5 Next most important initial step ?
k: Postoperative fever by timing (5 Ws). Day 1 to 2: atelectasis (wind) Day 3: UTI (water), also pneumonia Day 5: wound infection; days 5 to 7 anastomotic leak/abscess Day 7 and beyond: DVT/PE, deep collection (CT abdomen)
r: Fever on postoperative day 5 after sigmoidectomy falls in the window when surgical site infection and anastomotic leak/intra-abdominal collection become likely. The most important initial step is to examine the surgical site (wound and abdomen), because it is the commonest source at this time and is
x: B. Reviewing drugs (drug fever) is considered after the wound and other infectious sources are excluded, in an otherwise asymptomatic patient.

q: Patient with haemoroid that reduce spontaneously Hg = 8 What is the definitive ttt ?
k: Hemorrhoid ladder: conservative, then office procedure, then surgery; complications or failure jump to surgery. Grade I to II: fiber, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths Grade III (manually reducible): rubber band ligati
r: The lead-in asks for the definitive treatment, and the patient has symptomatic bleeding hemorrhoids with Hb 8 , i.e. anemia from chronic blood loss. Significant anemia is a complication that moves hemorrhoids past the conservative and office-procedure steps of the ladder, and hemorrhoidectomy is the
x: A. Observation: acceptable only for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic hemorrhoids; a patient bleeding enough to drop the Hb to 8 cannot be observed. | B. Band ligation: the outpatient choice for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids with uncomplicated bleeding, but it has higher recurrence and is not the definitive answer when bleeding has caused significant anemia.

q: Pt. For appendectomy (Uncomplicated) , the question was about when to give Abx. ?
k: Antibiotics in appendicitis depend on the operative finding: Uncomplicated: single preoperative prophylactic dose, stop after surgery Complicated (perforation, abscess, peritonitis): continue a short therapeutic course a
r: For uncomplicated appendicitis, antibiotics are prophylactic: a single dose given before incision covers the operation, and once a non-perforated appendix is removed there is no residual infection to treat. Postoperative courses add no benefit in infection rates and increase resistance, side effects
x: A. 1 dose preoperative, 3 days postoperative: a short therapeutic course is used for complicated (perforated or gangrenous) appendicitis, not uncomplicated disease. | B. 1 dose preoperative, 5 days postoperative: unnecessary in uncomplicated cases; a postoperative course is reserved for perforation, abscess or peritonitis. | C. 1 dose preoperative, 7 days postoperative: too long even for most complicated cases after adequate source control.

q: A 70-year-old women p7+1 with chronic constipation presented to Emergency Room with abdominal distension and vomiting. Examination revealed abdomen is distended, tympanic, with round tender nonreducible swelling in the right groin bellow and lateral to pubic tubercle (see report). X-ray abdomen: Distended small bowel with multiple fluid levels . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Groin swelling: locate it relative to the pubic tubercle. Above and medial: inguinal hernia (direct or indirect) Below and lateral: femoral hernia Femoral: more common in women, highest strangulation risk, always repair
r: An elderly multiparous woman with chronic constipation has a tender, irreducible groin swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle , plus small bowel distension with multiple fluid levels. That position marks the femoral canal, so this is an obstructed femoral hernia; the narrow rigid femoral r
kw: bellow and lateral to pubic tubercle
x: B. Direct inguinal hernia: emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle through Hesselbach triangle, typically in older men, and rarely strangulates because its neck is wide. | C. Metastatic lymph node: a firm, non-reducible node does not cause small bowel obstruction with fluid levels; the obstruction picture points to a hernia. | D. Indirect inguinal hernia: passes through the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle, often extendin

q: A 72 year old man otherwise healthy came complaining of left inginal hernia reducible with moderate pain What's the most appropriate management
k: Inguinal hernia management: Symptomatic, fit patient: elective tension-free mesh repair (open Lichtenstein) Recurrent after open repair or bilateral: laparoscopic mesh repair Minimal symptoms or unfit: watchful waiting i
r: A healthy 72-year-old with a symptomatic (moderate pain) primary unilateral reducible inguinal hernia should have elective repair. The standard is a tension-free mesh repair (for example Lichtenstein), which has the lowest recurrence; age alone is not a reason to avoid surgery in a fit patient.
x: A. Bassini ("bandini") repair: a tissue repair that sutures structures under tension; it has higher recurrence and is now reserved for situations where mesh cannot be used, such as a contaminated field. | C. Do nothing: watchful waiting is acceptable only for minimally symptomatic hernias or patients unfit for surgery; this patient has pain and is otherwise healthy. | D. Not recalled: cannot be assessed.

q: 65-year-old man is scheduled for colon surgery. He has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus , both well-controlled with medications. He is physically active and walks to the mosque daily without limitations . What is his ASA physical status classification?
k: ASA physical status: I: healthy II: mild, controlled systemic disease III: severe systemic disease, functional limitation IV: severe disease that is a constant threat to life V: moribund, not expected to survive without
r: He has hypertension and diabetes, but both are well-controlled and he has no functional limitation (walks daily without difficulty). Systemic disease that is mild and controlled, without functional limitation, is ASA II.
x: A. ASA I: a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; his hypertension and diabetes exclude it. | C. ASA III: severe systemic disease with functional limitation, such as poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, morbid obesity or COPD limiting activity. | D. ASA IV: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, such as recent MI or decompensated heart failure.

q: During excision of a back lipoma under local lidocaine, the surgeon suspects an excessive dose . Earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity ? (p. 37)
k: Lidocaine toxicity progression: Early: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness Then: visual disturbance, muscle twitching, confusion Then: seizures, coma, respiratory depression Late: bradycardia, hypotens
r: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity starts with CNS excitation at the lowest blood levels, before cardiovascular effects. The earliest symptoms are perioral numbness, metallic taste, lightheadedness and tinnitus ; with rising levels the patient progresses to muscle twitching, seizures, CNS depression
x: A. Skin rash: suggests an allergic reaction, which is rare with amide anesthetics like lidocaine and is not a sign of toxicity. | B. Bradycardia: a late cardiovascular sign (with hypotension, arrhythmia and arrest) at high plasma levels. | C. Seizures: occur after the early warning symptoms, as levels rise further; a late CNS sign.

q: A male patient after MVA a head injury associated with a temporal bone fracture . He initially experiences a period of unresponsive interval but arusable but later becomes unconscious again while in the hospital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Lucid interval + temporal fracture = extradural. Extradural: middle meningeal artery, biconvex, does not cross sutures Subdural: bridging veins, crescent, crosses sutures, elderly/alcoholics Signs of herniation: ipsilate
r: Temporal bone fracture after trauma with a lucid interval (initially rousable, then deteriorating in hospital) is the classic extradural (epidural) haematoma. The fracture tears the middle meningeal artery , and arterial bleeding expands quickly to cause secondary loss of consciousness; CT shows a b
x: A. Subdural haematoma comes from torn bridging veins, typically in the elderly or alcoholics after deceleration injury, with gradual decline and a crescent shaped collection; it is not classically tied to temporal fracture and lucid interval.

q: A patient presents to the emergency department after sustaining a stab wound to the right side of the chest. On examination, the trachea is deviated to the left , breath sounds are absent on the right side , and the neck veins are distended . What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Chest trauma: read the neck veins and percussion. Tension pneumothorax: hyperresonant, absent breath sounds, trachea away, raised JVP, hypotension Massive haemothorax: dull, absent breath sounds, flat neck veins, shock C
r: Penetrating right chest trauma with absent right breath sounds , trachea deviated to the left (away from the injury) and distended neck veins is tension pneumothorax. A one way valve traps air, shifts the mediastinum and kinks the great veins, so venous return falls and the JVP rises. It is a clinic
kw: trachea is deviated to the left
breath sounds are absent on the right side
x: A. A simple haemothorax causes dullness and reduced breath sounds but is usually too small to shift the trachea or raise the JVP. | B. Massive haemothorax (over 1500 mL) gives dullness and shock, but the neck veins are typically flat from blood loss; distended veins favour tension. | C. Simple pneumothorax reduces breath sounds without mediastinal shift, raised JVP or haemodynamic compromise.

q: at screening clinic mamgram show dense breast , posative family history of cancer , BARCA posative
o: do a biopsy guided by ultrasound
k: High risk breast screening = MRI. Indications: BRCA1/2 carrier, lifetime risk about 20% or more, chest irradiation at young age, strong family history BRCA carriers: annual MRI from about 25 to 30, add mammogram from 30
r: A BRCA positive woman with dense breasts is high risk, and dense tissue lowers mammogram sensitivity because it masks tumours. High risk women are screened with annual breast MRI (in addition to mammography), which is the most sensitive test in this group. With no focal lesion seen, MRI is the next
x: B. Repeating the mammogram adds nothing; the limitation is the dense tissue itself, which will mask lesions again. | C. Ultrasound guided biopsy needs a target lesion; there is no focal abnormality to biopsy here.

q: Pt with mets have bowle incontenance , MRI show cord compression . despite medical management what appropriate next step
k: Malignant cord compression is an emergency. Red flags: back pain in cancer, leg weakness, sensory level, sphincter dysfunction Investigation: urgent whole spine MRI Immediate: high dose dexamethasone Definitive: surgical
r: Metastatic spinal cord compression with bowel incontinence (autonomic involvement) that is progressing despite medical management (high dose steroids) needs urgent surgical decompression to save neurological function. Surgery followed by radiotherapy gives better outcomes than radiotherapy alone in
x: B. Dexamethasone is started at once to reduce cord oedema, but escalating steroids does not relieve mechanical compression when deficits keep worsening.

q: Teenage with testicular torsion after detorsion what is appropriate next step ?
k: Testicular torsion: time is testis. Sudden severe scrotal pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex Strong clinical suspicion: straight to surgery (salvage best within about 6 hours) Manual detorsion
r: Manual detorsion is only a temporising manoeuvre; the testis can twist again because the underlying bell clapper anomaly persists. The next step is surgical exploration with orchidopexy , and because the anomaly is usually bilateral the contralateral testis is fixed too (bilateral orchidopexy, as ke
x: A. Doppler ultrasound is used only when the diagnosis is uncertain and must never delay surgery; after detorsion the diagnosis is already made and fixation is still required.

q: breast lump which type of biopsy .
k: Breast lump: triple assessment = exam + imaging + core biopsy. Age under 30: ultrasound first; 30 or older: mammogram ± ultrasound BI-RADS 4/5: core needle biopsy Simple cyst: aspirate (FNA) ADH or discordant core: wire
r: Tissue diagnosis of a suspicious ("hard") breast lump is made by core needle biopsy , the biopsy step of triple assessment after clinical exam and imaging. A core gives tissue architecture, so it distinguishes invasive from in situ cancer and allows grading and receptor testing (ER, PR, HER2) before
x: B. Excisional biopsy removes the whole lump as a diagnostic first step; it is reserved for discordant or nondiagnostic core results or atypia (e.g. ADH needing wire localization excision), not as the first biopsy. | C. Incisional biopsy (removing part of the mass surgically) is open surgery and has been replaced by core needle biopsy; it is rarely needed in breast work-up. | D. FNA gives cytology only, with no architecture, so it cannot separate in situ from invasive disease and has more false n

q: case presentation: mostly likely Choledocholithiasis and asked about initial management :
k: Suspected CBD stone, by probability: High (stone seen on US, bilirubin > 4 with dilated CBD, cholangitis): ERCP Intermediate (abnormal LFTs or dilated CBD alone): MRCP or EUS Low: lap cholecystectomy ± intraoperative cho
r: When choledocholithiasis is likely (ultrasound showing a dilated common bile duct or stone with cholestatic labs: raised bilirubin and ALP), the next step is ERCP , which both confirms the stone and removes it (sphincterotomy and extraction). It decompresses the duct before definitive cholecystectom
x: B. MRCP is diagnostic only; it is used when the probability of a CBD stone is intermediate (e.g. raised LFTs but normal duct size), not when the stone is already likely. | C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder but leaves the duct stone; it follows ERCP (ideally in the same admission).

q: A 45-year-old woman presented with postprandial right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and emesis for few days that became persistent for the last 20 hours (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 87 /min, Temperature 37.2 °C. WBC 11 (normal 4.5-10.5 x 109/L), Direct bilirubin 9.5 (1.5-6.5 mol/L), Total bilirubin 18.5 (3.5-16.5 mol/L), Alkaline phosphatase 463 (39-117 IU/L). Ultrasound: Cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall thickening, and a common bile duct of 12 mm . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Biliary picture by clues: Biliary colic: brief pain, normal labs: elective lap chole Cholecystitis: fever, raised WBC, Murphy sign, normal bilirubin: lap chole within 72 hours Choledocholithiasis: raised bilirubin/ALP, d
r: The key clues are raised direct bilirubin and ALP 463 (cholestasis) plus gallstones with a CBD of 12 mm on ultrasound: this recall's key reads that as choledocholithiasis needing duct clearance, so the answer is ERCP , followed by cholecystectomy. She is afebrile (37.2) and stable, so it is not seve
x: B. MRCP only images the duct; it is chosen when the probability of a stone is intermediate, whereas a 12 mm duct with cholestatic labs already justifies therapeutic ERCP. | C. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is right for acute cholecystitis or biliary colic without duct obstruction; here the CBD stone must be cleared first. | D. Conservative treatment leaves an obstructing stone that risks cholangitis and pancreatitis.

q: Patient present to the clinic with request of sick leave he has backpain felt when awaking from sleep. Yesterday he was playing football and had no injuries or trauma . PE there was localized tenderness and no limitation of movement in flexion?
o: Give him sick leave for 3 days …
Give analgesia and avoid (long or bed) rest
k: Acute mechanical low back pain: Reassure, stay active, avoid bed rest First line: NSAIDs or paracetamol; topical NSAIDs; heat No imaging in the first 6 weeks without red flags Red flags: age > 50, cancer history, fever,
r: This is acute non specific (mechanical) low back pain: pain after football without trauma, localized tenderness , normal range of movement and no red flags. Management is reassurance, simple analgesia (NSAIDs or paracetamol, topical agents) and staying active; bed rest is avoided because it slows re
x: A. Urgent MRI is only for red flags: cauda equina features (saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention), progressive neurological deficit, suspected cancer, infection or fracture. | B. Sick leave for rest encourages inactivity; patients with simple back pain should keep up normal activities, with work modified if needed, rather than resting. | D. Not recalled; it cannot beat analgesia with advice to stay active in uncomplicated back pain.

q: 38 M brought by ambulance following an MVA. He has abdominal distention with signs of hemorrhage (echmosis i think) and a suspected pelvic fracture . He is orientated and appears in distress and pain. Vitals: BP 60/40 , HR 120 , RR 20 with O2 sat 92%, temp a febrile. Whats the nect appropriate step in management
k: Hemorrhagic shock in trauma: stop the bleeding and restore volume. Class III: HR 120-140, low BP, confused or anxious Class IV: HR >140, very low BP, lethargic Two large bore IV lines, warm crystalloid bolus, early blood
r: BP 60/40, HR 120 after an MVA with abdominal distension, ecchymosis and a suspected pelvic fracture is class III to IV hemorrhagic shock. He is oriented and talking, so the airway is protected, and the immediate life threat is circulatory collapse; the next step is IV access with a warmed crystalloi
x: A. Exploratory laparoscopy: never for an unstable trauma patient; unstable abdominal trauma needs resuscitation and laparotomy (or angioembolization for pelvic bleeding), not laparoscopy. | C. IV morphine: analgesia matters, but opioids worsen hypotension in profound shock and do not treat the life threat; give it in small titrated doses after resuscitation starts. | D. Supplemental O2: is given to every trauma patient in the primary survey and is reasonable with SpO2 92%, but it does not revers

q: 30 smth male Post MVA in ER with increase WOB and dullness percussion over R lung base . GCS9 . Whats next appropriate management
k: Chest trauma: percussion note chooses the procedure. Dull + reduced breath sounds: hemothorax: chest tube Hyperresonant + hypotension + raised JVP: tension pneumothorax: needle then chest tube Simple pneumothorax: chest
r: After an MVA, dullness on percussion over the right lung base with increased work of breathing indicates a traumatic hemothorax. The treatment is a large bore chest tube, which drains the blood, re expands the lung and lets you measure the output. GCS 9 is above the ≤8 intubation threshold, so the a
kw: dullness percussion over R lung base
x: B. Intubation: right for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, or refractory hypoxia; at GCS 9 with a cause that a chest tube fixes, it is not the next step. | C. Supplemental O2: given to all trauma patients but does not treat the cause of respiratory compromise; the blood still needs draining. | D. Needle decompression: for tension pneumothorax with hyperresonance, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension; dullness means fluid, not air.

q: Pretty much the Q stem was asking when should we surgically intervene for chest tube for a hemothorax
k: Hemothorax: thoracotomy when the bleeding is massive or ongoing. Initial chest tube output >1500 ml Ongoing output 200 ml/hr for 2 to 4 hours Persistent hemodynamic instability or ongoing transfusion need Otherwise chest
r: After a chest tube for hemothorax, surgical intervention (thoracotomy) is indicated by an initial drainage of more than 1500 ml or by ongoing bleeding of about 200 ml per hour over 2 to 4 hours, or persistent instability or need for transfusion. Of the listed options, ongoing drainage of 200 ml/hr i
x: A. Immediate 500 ml output: well below the 1500 ml immediate drainage threshold; most hemothoraces stop with a chest tube alone. | C. Concurrent hemo and pneumothorax: a hemopneumothorax is managed with a chest tube; its presence alone is not an indication for surgery. | D. (forgot): recalled as irrelevant; judge any option against the 1500 ml immediate or 200 ml/hr ongoing rules.

q: 44 YO woman presenting to post op clinic following an appendectomy for appendicitis ( no mention of any surgical complications ) (also don't remember exactly when it was i.e exactly what day post op ) . She complains of fould discharge from the wound . She is febrile 38.8 . inspection of the wound revels erythema with purulent discharge . How to manage
o: wound opening and either exploration or wash out (not sure which one)
k: Postoperative wound problems: Seroma: clear fluid, no inflammation: observe or aspirate Wound abscess or SSI with pus: open the wound, drain, wash out Cellulitis without collection: antibiotics Deep intra abdominal colle
r: After an appendectomy, foul purulent discharge , wound erythema and fever 38.8 indicate a surgical site infection with a wound abscess. The cornerstone of treatment is opening the wound (removing sutures or staples), draining the pus, exploring and washing it out, then leaving it to heal by secondar
x: A. Conservative: right for a seroma (clear fluid, no inflammation, afebrile); pus and fever need drainage. | B. PO antibiotics: right for mild superficial cellulitis without collection; antibiotics alone cannot clear an abscess. | D. (don't remember): recalled as irrelevant.

q: present with head trauma . On examination, bilateral periorbital raccoon eye Which type of intubation is most appropriate?
k: Basal skull fracture: nothing through the nose. Signs: raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea, hemotympanum Avoid nasotracheal tube and nasogastric tube (use orogastric) Facial or maxillofacial trauma: oro
r: Bilateral periorbital (raccoon) eyes after head trauma indicate a fracture of the anterior skull base. Nasal routes are contraindicated because a tube can pass through the cribriform plate into the cranium, so the airway is secured by orotracheal intubation (with in-line cervical stabilization).
x: A. Nasotracheal intubation: contraindicated in suspected basal skull or midface fracture (risk of intracranial tube placement, CSF leak, infection). | C. Cricothyrotomy: the surgical airway when oral intubation fails or is impossible, for example massive maxillofacial injury with the mouth full of blood. | D. Tracheostomy: a planned, slower procedure for prolonged ventilation or laryngeal injury, not the emergency airway in trauma.

q: 52 year old male medically free came to the clinic complaining of red urine for 2 days associated with right flank pain , no dysuria no fever no other symptoms On examination: right flank tenderness and palpable rectal prostate ( written like this) Urine culture : negative Urine analysis: + erythrocyte Nitrate: absent WBC: absent What is the most appropriate next investigation :
k: Hematuria: pain decides the first test. Painful hematuria with flank pain: non-contrast CT-KUB (stone) Painless visible hematuria, older or smoker: CT urography plus cystoscopy With fever, dysuria, pyuria: urine culture
r: Red urine with right flank pain and tenderness , no fever or dysuria, a negative culture and no nitrites or WBC is painful hematuria without infection, most likely a ureteric stone. Non-contrast CT-KUB is the investigation of choice for suspected urolithiasis.
x: A. Urine cytology: adjunct for suspected urothelial cancer (painless hematuria, smoker); low sensitivity and not first line with flank pain. | C. Retrograde urethrogram: for suspected urethral injury after pelvic trauma (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate); no trauma here. | D. Cystoscopy: evaluates the bladder in painless visible hematuria over 40 to exclude bladder cancer; not the first test for flank pain.

q: A boy presents with periumbilical pain that shifted to the right iliac fossa , accompanied by vomiting. Physical examination reveals tenderness, and labs show leukocytosis . What is the most appropriate step to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Order abdominal US or CT scan
k: Appendicitis: clinical diagnosis, imaging to confirm when needed. Classic: migratory pain, anorexia, vomiting, RIF tenderness, fever, leukocytosis Children and pregnancy: ultrasound first Adults, obese, equivocal ultraso
r: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with vomiting , local tenderness and leukocytosis is suspected acute appendicitis. The lead-in asks how to confirm the diagnosis, which is imaging: ultrasound first in children (no radiation), CT if ultrasound is inconclusive or in adults.
x: B. Give IV fluids and observe: fluids, analgesia and NPO are supportive and active observation suits an equivocal low-risk picture, but it does not confirm the diagnosis. | C. Discharge and reassess after 48h: unsafe with a high-probability picture; risk of perforation. | D. High fiber diet and laxative: management of constipation; laxatives are contraindicated in suspected appendicitis.

q: An old patient came with subdural hematoma with signs of lateralization imaging revealed 13 mm shifting . His GCS 7/15 then was intubated and resuscitated, what to do next?
k: Acute SDH: evacuate if mass effect is significant. Surgery: thickness over 10 mm or midline shift over 5 mm regardless of GCS Also: GCS drop of 2 or more, asymmetric or fixed pupils, ICP over 20 ICP bridges: head up 30 d
r: An acute subdural hematoma with lateralizing signs , a 13 mm midline shift and GCS 7 meets criteria for surgical evacuation (shift over 5 mm or thickness over 10 mm, or GCS ≤8 with deterioration). The airway is secured and he is resuscitated, so the next step is urgent craniotomy to relieve the mass
x: A. IV mannitol: a temporizing measure for raised ICP or impending herniation while arranging surgery; it does not remove the clot. | B. Elevate head of bed: a simple supportive ICP measure, not definitive for a large hematoma with shift. | C. Hyperventilate: brief rescue for signs of herniation only; prolonged use causes cerebral ischemia.

q: Patient prepared for left adrenal adenoctomy what should be given postoperative
o: High dose glucocorticoid and gradual tapering
k: Steroid cover depends on what the tumour secreted. Cortisol-secreting (Cushing): stress dose hydrocortisone, then slow taper Bilateral adrenalectomy: lifelong glucocorticoid plus fludrocortisone Aldosteronoma: no steroid
r: The keyed scenario is a cortisol-secreting adenoma : its autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH and atrophies the contralateral adrenal, so after unilateral adrenalectomy the patient is cortisol deficient. Give a stress (high) dose of glucocorticoid perioperatively, then taper gradually over months as
x: A. Lifelong glucocorticoid: needed after bilateral adrenalectomy; after unilateral surgery the other gland recovers, so steroids are tapered off. | B. Initiate fludrocortisone: the contralateral gland's zona glomerulosa is controlled by renin-angiotensin, not ACTH, so mineralocorticoid replacement is not routinely needed after unilateral surgery. | D. Nothing: right for a non-functioning adenoma or an aldosteronoma, where the axis is not suppressed; risky after removing a cortisol-secreting tumo

q: A 25-year-old male with bilateral breast enlargement since the age of 18 , he's uncomfortable and reluctant to swim or exercise at the gym PE revealed grade 4 gynecomastia ,. Most appropriate management?
k: Gynecomastia management ladder. Pubertal: reassure and observe, most regress Find causes: drugs (spironolactone, anabolic steroids), liver disease, hypogonadism, testicular tumour, hyperthyroidism Recent and tender: medi
r: Gynecomastia that has persisted for about 7 years (since 18) is unlikely to regress, because long-standing glandular tissue becomes fibrotic. It is high grade (4) and is causing distress and avoiding activities ( reluctant to swim or exercise ). Surgical excision with bilateral subcutaneous mastecto
x: A. Reassurance: right for pubertal gynecomastia in adolescents, which usually regresses within 1 to 2 years; not for persistent, symptomatic, high-grade disease. | B. Bilateral core needle biopsy: for a unilateral, hard, eccentric or fixed mass, skin or nipple changes suspicious for male breast cancer; bilateral symmetric enlargement does not need biopsy. | D. Endocrine and liver work up: the right step for new-onset adult gynecomastia, rapid growth or features of an underlying cause (testicular

q: Male patient came with epigastric pain, came with history of using NSAIDs , now he is vitally stable , with erect chest x-ray showing AIR UNDER DIAPHRGM . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Free air under the diaphragm = perforated viscus = surgery. Commonest cause: perforated peptic ulcer (NSAIDs, H. pylori) Steps: NPO, IV fluids, NG tube, PPI, antibiotics, then repair Repair: omental (Graham) patch, test
r: Epigastric pain in an NSAID user with air under the diaphragm on erect chest x-ray is a perforated peptic ulcer. Free intraperitoneal air means perforation and peritoneal contamination, so after resuscitation and IV antibiotics the definitive step is surgical exploration and repair (omental patch);
x: A. Gastroduodenoscopy: for upper GI bleeding or ulcer diagnosis; insufflating air into a perforated viscus worsens the leak and it does not close the hole. | C. Laparoscopy: laparoscopic patch repair is an accepted option in stable patients where expertise exists, but the classic exam answer for free air is laparotomy. | D. Observation: non-operative management is only for highly selected sealed perforations; being vitally stable does not remove the need for repair.

q: A patient with comorbidity , with nothing in the question indicating it is uncontrolled , and the question stated that he walks to the mosque 3-4 times daily. What is the ASA classification?
k: ASA physical status: judge control and functional impact, not just the number of diseases. I: healthy II: mild, controlled systemic disease, no limitation III: severe disease with functional limitation IV: constant threa
r: He has a comorbidity but nothing suggests it is uncontrolled, and he walks to the mosque 3 to 4 times daily , showing no functional limitation. Mild, well controlled systemic disease without limitation of activity is ASA II .
kw: nothing in the question indicating it is uncontrolled
x: A. 1: a normal healthy patient with no systemic disease; any comorbidity excludes ASA I. | C. 3: severe systemic disease with functional limitation (poorly controlled diabetes or hypertension, COPD, morbid obesity, MI or stroke more than 3 months ago). | D. 4: severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life (recent MI, ongoing ischaemia, severe valve dysfunction, sepsis).

q: 24 YO Male Patient present with abdominal pain and tenderness right to the umblicus. Diagnosed with appendicitis and taken to the OR and abdominal explored with gridiron incision and found (healthy looking or normal appearing appendix ?) Wbs 17.4 What to do?
o: Insert a draing and close the wound
Perform appendictomy and close the abdominal
k: Normal appendix at surgery for suspected appendicitis. Inspect terminal ileum (Meckel's, Crohn's) Mesenteric lymph nodes Cecum, sigmoid, gallbladder if reachable Female: ovaries and tubes Usually still remove the appendi
r: A normal looking appendix in a patient with real signs (pain, tenderness, WBC 17.4 ) means another cause must be found. The surgeon should explore systematically, starting with the terminal ileum (about 2 feet, 60 cm) for an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum , plus mesenteric nodes, the cecum and the p
x: B. A drain is used for an abscess or contaminated field, not when the pathology has not yet been found. | C. Closing the abdomen leaves the true cause (for example Meckel's diverticulitis, Crohn's, mesenteric adenitis) undiagnosed. | D. Removing the appendix is reasonable to avoid future confusion, but doing it and closing without searching misses the real cause.

q: 65 years man brought to the clinic due to the finding of reducible inguinal hernia , he said it bulge when he coughs and when he stands but it return back when lying back, mild discomfort without significant pain . What is The Most Appropriate Management
k: Hernia management. Inguinal, symptomatic and fit: elective mesh repair Femoral: always repair (high strangulation risk) Irreducible or strangulated: emergency surgery Recurrent or bilateral: laparoscopic repair Infant um
r: A reducible inguinal hernia with a cough impulse that causes mild discomfort is symptomatic. In a fit patient the standard treatment is elective surgical repair (open mesh repair for a primary unilateral hernia), to relieve symptoms and remove the risk of incarceration and strangulation, which rises
x: B. Lifestyle measures (weight loss, stopping smoking, treating cough or constipation) improve surgical outcomes but do not treat the hernia. | C. Avoiding heavy lifting may reduce discomfort but does not cure the hernia or remove the strangulation risk. | D. Watchful waiting is acceptable for men with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic hernias, especially if unfit for surgery, but most cross over to surgery over time; in a fit patient with a symptomatic reducible hernia the standard exam answ

q: Patient with bowel obstruction. Most appropriate investigation?
r: Suspected bowel obstruction: CT abdomen with contrast confirms it, shows the transition point and signs of strangulation; plain X-ray is only a quick screen.

q: Medium age present with pelvic injury followed by mva Ct showed multiple pelvic injury with severe hematoma and hypotensive patient. What’s Next appropriate management after fluid resuscitation?
r: Pelvic fracture + hypotension after fluids = pelvic bleeding: close the pelvis with a pelvic binder first, then angio-embolisation or packing.

q: A patient sustained a high-velocity trauma and is hypotensive despite receiving IV fluids. Xray shows an open-book pelvic fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Unstable pelvic fracture: binder first, then stop the bleeding.
r: Hypotension with an open-book pelvis: binder before any imaging or fixation.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1712).

q: 34 yo woman k/c of RA and have been using NSAIDs for 3 months presented to the ER complaining of severe epigastric pain Amylase: 233 WBC: 14.5 What is the most appropriate next step ?
k: Severe epigastric pain with mildly raised amylase: Pancreatitis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase 3 times or more the upper limit, typical imaging.; Risk of perforation (NSAIDs, steroids, PUD): erect CXR first.; Free air: laparotomy or laparoscopic patch repair.
r: If the stem says the erect CXR is already normal, the answer moves to CT abdomen.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0039).

q: A surgeon is performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. During the procedure, he suspects that an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?
k: LAST progresses CNS first, then cardiovascular.
r: If tinnitus is not among the options, the author picks drowsiness as the next earliest sign.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0090).

q: 14 years old child diagnosed with ADHD, started treatment on methylphenidate 10mg twice daily 4 weeks ago. Now his mother reports loss of appetite, weight loss and difficulty falling asleep. Examination reveals 2kg weight loss, no other symptoms. Labs are unremarkable. Which of the following best explains his symptoms ?
o: Known sides effects of methylphenidate in children
Weight loss due to poor eating habits (paraphrased, but the same idea)
r: Methylphenidate (stimulant) commonly causes loss of appetite, weight loss and insomnia: known side effects, adjust dose/timing.

q: An unstable trauma patient has confirmed multiple liver lacerations. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Individual ligation of the bleeding vessel
k: Solid organ trauma by haemodynamic status.
r: Unstable liver injury = pack; unstable spleen injury = remove.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0671).

q: A 28 year old man presented with a 2 year history of reducible right Inguinal hernia that became painful for 16 hours. It is associated with progressive abdominal distension, and vomiting. Physical examination confirmed a distended abdomen, exaggerated bowel sound, and a tender right inguinal swelling with red discoloration of the overlying skin. Erect abdominal Xra: Multiple air fluid levels. Which of the following is the most likely hernia complication?
k: Hernia complications escalate; choose the most severe state the stem supports.
r: Remove the skin redness and the same stem becomes an obstructed hernia.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0718).
kw: red discoloration of the overlying skin
Erect abdominal Xra: Multiple air fluid levels.

q: 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of blood in her stool. On examination, she has grade III hemorrhoids at the 6 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions, with active bleeding. Vitals and labs: Blood pressure: 126/75 Heart rate: 120 bpm Hemoglobin: 105 g/L I forgot the rest of the CBC What is the most appropriate next management?
k: Hemorrhoids: when to scope first.
r: Visible hemorrhoids plus anemia at 45 or older: colonoscopy before any hemorrhoid treatment; the tachycardia (HR 120) means stabilise first if she is actively bleeding heavily.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9138).

q: A 14-year-old patient presented with a painless neck swelling. Examination confirmed a midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone that moves up and down with swallowing. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Neck lumps by position: Midline, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst; Midline, moves with swallowing only: thyroid nodule/goiter; Midline (often submental), no movement with swallowing or tongue: dermoid
r: Movement with tongue protrusion separates a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid nodule.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-1472).
kw: midline neck swelling below the hyoid bone
moves up and down with swallowing

q: A 50-year-old patient underwent a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. He has developed a large neck swelling associated with stridor and shortness of breath. Blood pressure: 165/90 mmHg, Heart rate: 130/min, Respiratory rate: 24/min, Temperature: 37 °C Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: A neck haematoma with stridor after thyroidectomy is an airway emergency. Open the skin and strap-muscle sutures at the bedside to evacuate the clot and decompress the trachea, then return to theatre for haemostasis.
n: مكرر من القديم (NOV-300).

q: Preschool child with hypermetropia. What you will do?
k: Refractive error → lens type: match the lens to where the image falls.
r: Glasses first, patch second: occlusion is for amblyopia, not for the refractive error itself.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2361).

q: 50 years old male came c/o painless hematuria (literally written) started 3 day ago. What most appropriate INITIAL investigation?
o: KUB (literally written without mentioning xray nor CT)
k: Hematuria: confirm with urinalysis first, then investigate the cause.
r: "Initial" picks urinalysis; if the question asks for the most appropriate or definitive investigation of painless hematuria in an older man, pick cystoscopy plus CT urography.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0169).

q: 26-year-old man complains of pelvic pain after a motorcycle collision. Physical and radiologic examinations confirm a pelvic fracture. Urologic workup reveals a normal urethrogram and extraperitoneal bladder injury. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his bladder injury?
o: Placement of a permanent suprapubic tube
Catheter drainage followed by definitive repair after 2 weeks
Catheter drainage for 2 weeks followed by repeat imaging
k: Pelvic fracture with urinary tract injury: Blood at meatus or high-riding prostate: retrograde urethrogram before any catheter; Urethral injury: suprapubic catheter; Normal urethra, extraperitoneal bladder rupture: urethral catheter drainage about 10 to 14 days, then cystogram
r: Extraperitoneal = catheter and repeat imaging; intraperitoneal = operate.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1662).

q: After appendectomy, a patient’s wound shows moderate erythema and exudate. Which type of dressing is most appropriate?
k: Dressing choice by exudate (the deck's working rule).
r: Read the adjective: moderate exudate = alginate; mild = hydrocolloid.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8790).

q: Surgeon performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. During the procedure, it appears an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?
k: LAST progresses CNS first, then cardiovascular.
r: If tinnitus is not among the options, the author picks drowsiness as the next earliest sign.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0090).

q: A 25-year-old man underwent an open appendectomy for a perforated appendix. He was discharged on the 2nd post- operative day uneventfully. He returned on the 8th post-operative day complaining of pain and redness around the wound site. On examination, there is purulent discharge from the wound site. His abdomen is soft with tender over the wound site. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 110 /min Respiratory rate 18 /min Temperature 38 °C Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: Day 8 after appendectomy with painful red wound = wound abscess: open the wound and drain; antibiotics alone are not enough.

q: A 28 year old female presented following radiation of neck with neck swelling. Ultrasound showed swelling in the left lobe of the thyroid of 3x4cm of papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the best management?
k: Differentiated thyroid cancer: any high-risk feature means total thyroidectomy.
r: Size alone (3x4 cm) might tempt lobectomy, but radiation history flips it to total thyroidectomy.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2534).

q: A 75-year-old man is hospitalized following a surgical procedure. During the postoperative period, he develops episodes of coffee-ground emesis. Blood-stained fluid is also noted in the nasogastric tube (NGT) drainage. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis and identify the source of bleeding?
k: Upper GI bleed (hematemesis, coffee-ground vomit, melena, bloody NGT aspirate): resuscitate, IV PPI, then upper endoscopy.
r: Blood in the NGT puts the source above the ligament of Treitz, so endoscopy, not colonoscopy or imaging, comes first.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3362).
kw: confirm the diagnosis and identify the source of bleeding

q: A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin. On examination, he appears distressed, with marked lower abdominal tenderness and guarding. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
k: Abdominal or groin pain in a boy: always examine the genitalia and hernial orifices first.
r: Missed torsion because the scrotum was never examined is the classic trap; examination always precedes imaging.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3403).
kw: severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin

q: A 55-year-old man with a history of hypertension, currently taking aspirin, presents to the ophthalmology clinic with sudden-onset redness in one eye. He denies eye pain, photophobia, or visual disturbances. On examination, there is a well- demarcated area of bright red discoloration over the sclera. Visual acuity is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Painless red eye, no visual change, on aspirin/HTN = subconjunctival haemorrhage: reassure, resolves in 1-2 weeks.

q: A 28-year-old woman presents with neck swelling and mild neck discomfort. She has no other significant symptoms and no known medical illness. Laboratory investigations are unremarkable except for a markedly elevated serum calcitonin level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Thyroid cancer by cell of origin: follicular cells → papillary, follicular, anaplastic (marker thyroglobulin); C cells → medullary (marker calcitonin, also CEA).
r: Before operating on MTC, exclude pheochromocytoma (MEN 2) to avoid an intraoperative hypertensive crisis.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-3505).

q: A patient presents diagnosed with acute appendicitis. During open appendectomy via a gridiron incision, the surgeon finds a completely normal appendix. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform appendectomy and close the abdomen
Insert an abdominal drain and close
r: Normal appendix at operation: look for other causes, first Meckel's diverticulum (check the last 2 feet of ileum), plus ovaries in women.

q: A man presented with trauma to his chest complains of severe pain in his chest, he has severe tenderness on the chest with multiple bruises, during initial assessment the airways are patent and clear, he is alert and conscious but his chest wall is unstable when he moves or tries to take a deep breath and bruising in his right chest. Air sounds present bilaterally clear. Vital signs normal apart from saturation 86%. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Chest wall trauma with pain, airway and breathing OK: give good IV analgesia (rib fractures) so he can breathe and cough.

q: Female lactating with 6 days history of tender swelling 2x3 cm. On US, deep cystic lesion with thick fluid 3x4 cm. ttt ?
r: Lactational breast abscess (US: deep collection): ultrasound-guided aspiration + antibiotics; incision only if aspiration fails or skin is necrotic.

q: A 60 year old patient known case of prostate cancer presents with an acute urinary retention. Foley catheter insertion failed. What is the next step?
r: Acute retention, urethral catheter failed (prostate cancer): suprapubic catheter.

q: A 70-year-old female presents with a complaint of rectal pain and passing mucus. This exact picture was shown: What is the diagnosis?
k: Protruding anal mass: look at the folds.
r: Concentric rings on the picture = rectal prolapse; radial grooves = hemorrhoids.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0338).

q: A male patient has a thyroid nodule of 2 cm classified as TIRADS 4. Which of the following is an indication for surgery?
o: Increasing 10% in size over the last 6 months
k: Thyroid nodule: TSH, then ultrasound, then FNA, then Bethesda decides.
r: Follicular lesions need histology to see invasion, so Bethesda IV goes to lobectomy, not repeat FNA.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0225).

q: A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain, constipation, and vomiting. What is the most important initial investigation?
r: Woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vomiting: pregnancy test first (ectopic must be excluded).

q: A 27-year-old male motorcyclist was rendered unconscious after being hit by a car. He was rushed to the Emergency Room (ER), where he regained consciousness but exhibited labored breathing. He suffered a penetrating chest wound through a glass, with air bubbling of the wound after being hit with the right wing of the car mirror. His vital signs: BP: 90/59 Oxygen Saturation: 89% What should be the next step in his treatment?
k: Primary survey order: treat each life threat as you find it, A then B then C then D then E.
r: Versions that keep him unconscious or with SpO2 <88% flip to a definitive airway; once he "regained consciousness", go to breathing.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8906).

q: A young man presents with a stab wound to the abdomen. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate investigation?
k: Abdominal trauma: stable = CT; unstable = decide by mechanism.
r: Same stab wound but hypotensive, peritonitic or eviscerated: skip imaging and go to laparotomy.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-4906).

q: A patient after an RTA presents with pelvic instability and hypotension. What is the initial management?
k: Unstable pelvic fracture: binder first, then definitive bleeding control.
r: If transfusion and binder both appear, this exam pattern keys the binder.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0959).

q: A 30-year-old patient presents to the Emergency Department with an 8-hour history of severe upper abdominal pain that is not relieved by oral medications. History confirmed recurrent similar events over the last year that were relieved by antispasmodic and anti-inflammatory drugs. Examination revealed jaundiced patient, with a soft abdomen and marked tenderness in the right hypochondriac region (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 110/min Respiratory rate 18/min Temperature 37.9 °C Test Result Normal Values WBC 16 4.5-10.5 x 10/L Indirect bilirubin 5 3.2-12.1 mol/L Direct bilirubin 15 1.5-6.5 mol/L Total bilirubin 20 3.5-16.5 mol/L Alkaline phosphatase 400 39-117 IU/L Amylase 115 24-151 IU/L Ultrasound: Minimal CBD of 1.1 cm with dilatation of intrahepatic ducts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Charcot triad (fever + jaundice + RUQ pain) on a background of gallstone attacks = ascending cholangitis.

q: Quistion about patient with anal fissure and asking about next step?
r: Anal fissure: first line conservative (fibre, sitz baths) + topical diltiazem 2% or GTN; sphincterotomy only if it fails.

q: 35 years female presented with appendicitis and she scheduled for laparoscopic Appendectomy , she has history of asthma, what is from the following will improve the surgical or patient safety ?
r: Patient safety in surgery = WHO checklist: site marking and equipment check.
n: Option “B” Was “OMIT Pre-Op Abx” Athar: Even If “B” Was “GIVE Pre-Op Abx” , Answer Would Still Be “A” Since It Is The One That Improves Surgical Safety And It’s More Important Than Abx

q: Patient with comunuted distal femur fracture with open 5 cm wound. Bone and tissue is visible whats the initial management ?
o: Iv antibiotic in the first hour
k: Open fracture = bone communicating with the outside through a wound: antibiotics first, then theatre.
r: Wound + fracture (even a 1 cm oozing wound) = open fracture; antibiotics come before the knife.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-1923).
kw: distal femur fracture with open 5 cm wound

q: A 20-year-old female presents after a minor injury to her leg. She complains of severe pain out of proportion. On examination, the leg is swollen, erythematous, and tender, crepitation, also the patient is febrile. What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Necrotizing fasciitis = early surgical debridement saves life; delay raises mortality.
r: Crepitus or pain out of proportion in a soft tissue infection means theatre now, not a scan or antibiotics alone.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-1626).

q: Patient with schizophrenia and a history of presents with abdominal distension. Abdominal CT imaging shows marked colonic dilatation, with the colon measuring approximately 10 cm and no mechanical obstruction shown. The patient is hemodynamically stable, with no evidence of peritonitis or bowel perforation. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Colonoscopic decompression with insertion of a rectal tube
k: Ogilvie syndrome: colon dilated without mechanical cause.
r: Add peritonitis or free air to the same stem and the answer becomes emergency colectomy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2775).

q: A male presents with a history of painless, bright-red rectal bleeding during defecation. 3 and 7 o'clock positions. The patient undergoes injection of a sclerosing agent. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Painless vs painful anal bleeding: Painless bright red bleeding, 3, 7, 11 o'clock: internal hemorrhoids; Sharp pain on defecation plus bleeding, midline: fissure; Acutely painful bluish lump at the verge: thrombosed external hemorrhoid or perianal hematoma
r: "Painless" plus "sclerosing injection" = internal; any pain sends you to fissure, thrombosis or abscess.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9136).

q: A patient has a perianal fistula whose external opening is at 7 o'clock (posterior). What is the most likely location of the internal opening?
r: Goodsall's rule: external opening posterior to the transverse anal line -> internal opening in the posterior midline.

q: post thyroidectomy with respiratory distress and neck swelling, what is the best next step?
r: Post-thyroidectomy neck swelling + respiratory distress = haematoma compressing the airway: open the wound at the bedside immediately.

q: Patient with right iliac fossa pain for 7 days. On examination: palpable mass in the iliac fossa, WBC high, ultrasound shows appendiceal mass with no collection. What to do?
k: Late appendicitis (days of pain, RIF mass): image first, then manage by what is found.
r: Mass without collection = phlegmon = no intervention; mass with collection = abscess = percutaneous drainage.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0245).

q: A 27-year-old male motorcyclist was rendered unconscious after being hit by a car. He was rushed to the Emergency Room (ER), where he regained consciousness but exhibited shallow breathing. He suffered a penetrating chest wound through a glass, with air bubbling of the wound after being hit with the right wing of the car mirror. His vital signs: • BP: 100/70 • Oxygen Saturation: 89% What should be the next step in his treatment?
k: ATLS primary survey: treat each life threat as you find it, in order A → B → C → D → E.
r: If "3 sided occlusive dressing" is among the options for a sucking chest wound, it beats every other choice.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-3241).

q: A young male presents after a motorcycle trauma. On examination ,there is blood at the urethral meatus. Pelvic X-ray reveals an open book pelvic fracture. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. What is the initial investigation?
r: Blood at the meatus with pelvic fracture = urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram before any Foley.

q: 30 years old male with history of RTA 6 years ago that end with splenectomy. He has history of multiple adhesive small bowel obstruction 4 years ago. Now he present with nausea vomiting distension and pain (obstruction symptoms). Abdominal examination showed generalized tenderness with rigidity and guarding. (not sure if there was vital or not but I don’t remember I see it). What is most appropriate next step in management ?
r: ⚠ Adhesive bowel obstruction is usually treated first with NGT, IV fluids, bowel rest; laparotomy if signs of strangulation/peritonitis or failure. Key here = laparotomy.

q: Classical case of mesenteric ischemia with A fib (100% sure). on abdominal examination there was tenderness and rigidity. ( not sure if there was vital or not but I don’t remember I see it) What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Long (does or term something like that) therapeutic anticoagulant
r: Acute mesenteric ischaemia (AF embolus) with peritonism: urgent laparotomy (embolectomy and resection of dead bowel).
n: A. Laprotomy

q: Pt with RTA present to ER they did definitive airway and breathing supporting and put two IV access. on abdominal examination there was abdominal tenderness and rigidity. The vitals was HR more than 100 and Bp was 90/60. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: Trauma with peritonitis (rigid abdomen) and haemodynamic instability: straight to laparotomy, no CT.

q: 68 years old known spinal metastasis present with lower weakness and (bowel or urine incontinence not sure which one), they tried medical therapy and failed( not sure of spilling but that was the meaning 100% sure). What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Surgical decompression or intervention not sure
r: Malignant spinal cord compression failing medical therapy (steroids): surgical decompression (+ radiotherapy).

q: A 27-year-old male motorcyclist was unconscious after being hit by a car. He was rushed to the Emergency Room (ER), where he regained consciousness but exhibited labored breathing. He suffered a penetrating chest wound through a glass, with air bubbling of the wound after being hit with the right wing of the car mirror. His vital signs: - BP: 90/60 - Oxygen Saturation: 89% What should be the next step in his treatment?
k: Primary survey order: treat each life threat as you find it, A then B then C then D then E.
r: Versions that keep him unconscious or with SpO2 <88% flip to a definitive airway; once he "regained consciousness", go to breathing.
n: ⚠ يشبه OCT-8906 لكن جوابه: Initiate assisted ventilation.

q: An orthopedic surgeon has completed a fellowship in spinal surgery and finished the program on time. He is now requesting clinical privileges to perform spinal surgeries in the hospital. What should the hospital do?
o: Grant privileges based on his years of experience.
Approve privileges based solely on completion of the fellowship.
Do not grant privileges until he completes at least 2 years of supervised clinical practice.
Assess competency of his performance after certification.
r: Privileging rests on verified current competence: the certificate (credential) is necessary but not sufficient, so the hospital assesses his performance (e.g., focused evaluation/proctoring) before granting specific privileges.
n: ⚠ يشبه NOV-708 لكن جوابه: Assess the competency of his performance.

q: A young patient sustains severe head trauma resulting in a skull fracture and pupillary dilation. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Elevation of the head of the bed
r: Raised ICP after head injury: first simple measures, head of bed 30 degrees; then mannitol/hypertonic saline; hyperventilation only briefly.

q: 30 year male brought to ER after RTA, there is chest ecctymosis and sternum fracture ECG: Arrhythmia What is the diagnosis?
r: Sternal fracture + new arrhythmia = blunt cardiac (myocardial) contusion: monitor ECG and troponin.

q: An elderly diabetic underwent major upper abdominal surgery 72 hours ago. Temperature: 38 °C Oxygen saturation: 80% Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Post-op fever by day (the W's).
r: Same stem at 24 hours = atelectasis; at 72 hours = pneumonia.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0190).

q: A newborn presents with mucus and bubbling from the mouth and nose during the first feeding. An X-ray shows a coiled orogastric tube in the esophageal pouch. Which of the following is a complication associated with surgical correction of this condition?
k: Rule: after esophageal atresia / TEF repair, GERD is the most common long-term complication.
r: Coiled tube in the upper pouch = esophageal atresia; the most common complication after repair is GERD, and the stricture that follows it.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8561).
kw: bubbling from the mouth and nose
coiled orogastric tube in the esophageal pouch

q: Woman post head injury admitted to ICU for observation. They did NGT and Foley cath for her, after 3 days she was cooperative and talking to the staff except she was febrile T 38.9 C. What to do next?
r: Fever on day 3 in a catheterised ICU patient who is otherwise well: think catheter-associated UTI, check the Foley.

q: 54-year-old male with history of DM and CKD , recently admitted for acute coronary syndrome , presents to clinic for follow-up. He has high creatinine, slightly high cholesterol, low HDL, and high LDL . Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen?
k: Statin benefit groups (adults over 21): Clinical ASCVD (ACS, stroke, PAD): high intensity statin LDL ≥190 mg/dL: high intensity statin Diabetes aged 40 to 75: moderate to high intensity statin High 10 year risk: statin p
r: A recent acute coronary syndrome means clinical ASCVD, which is an indication for high intensity statin therapy regardless of the baseline LDL. His diabetes and CKD add risk and strengthen the indication. Atorvastatin is the standard choice and needs no renal dose adjustment.
kw: recently admitted for acute coronary syndrome
x: B. Niacin raises HDL but has not reduced cardiovascular events when added to statins and causes flushing; it is not used for secondary prevention. | C. Ezetimibe is an add on when LDL stays above target despite a maximally tolerated statin, or in statin intolerance; it is not first line. | D. Doing nothing is wrong: every patient after ACS needs a statin, and his raised LDL makes it even clearer.

q: A patient presents with pneumonia (productive cough, fever and pain; the picture shows a lobar pneumonia). Treatment is started with IV ceftriaxone , azithromycin, paracetamol and tramadol. After one day he is stable and improving, but the platelet count has fallen to about 70 . Which drug should be stopped ?
k: New thrombocytopenia after starting drugs: think drug induced immune thrombocytopenia and stop the culprit. Classic culprits: heparin (HIT), beta lactams such as ceftriaxone and piperacillin, vancomycin, quinine, sulfona
r: The patient is improving on standard CAP therapy, then the platelets fall to about 70 after starting new drugs , which suggests drug induced immune thrombocytopenia. Among the four drugs, ceftriaxone (a beta lactam) is the one classically associated with drug induced immune thrombocytopenia, so it i
kw: platelet count has fallen to about 70
x: A. Paracetamol at normal doses rarely affects platelets; its main toxicity is hepatic in overdose. | B. Tramadol causes nausea, seizures and serotonin syndrome, not thrombocytopenia. | D. Azithromycin's concerns are QT prolongation and GI upset; it is not a typical cause of thrombocytopenia.

q: A patient with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis three times per week develops a pericardial effusion . Blood pressure is 83/60 mmHg and heart sounds are muffled . What is the next step?
k: Uremic pericardial effusion: decide on tamponade first. No tamponade (stable BP): dialysis is initial, next and definitive treatment Tamponade (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds, pulsus paradoxus): pericardiocentes
r: ESRD on dialysis with a pericardial effusion points to a uremic or dialysis associated effusion. The decisive clues are BP 83/60 and muffled heart sounds : hypotension makes this tamponade, not a simple effusion. An unstable tamponade needs immediate pericardiocentesis for rapid stabilization; inten
n: ✔ تحديث الحمراني (16 نوف): Urgent/intensified hemodialysis، الـ B كان typo. Dialysis-associated pericardial effusion تتعالج بالـ dialysis.
x: A. Urgent or intensified dialysis is the right answer for a uremic effusion WITHOUT tamponade (normal BP); a hypotensive patient may not tolerate dialysis and needs drainage first. | C. Furosemide reduces preload, which worsens tamponade (filling depends on preload), and it does little in an anuric ESRD patient. | D. Doing nothing is wrong: hypotension from tamponade can progress to cardiac arrest.

q: A 45-year-old woman known to have end-stage renal disease secondary to type 1 diabetes mellitus came to the clinic for a routine follow-up. She had no complaints but was found to have abnormal blood results (see lab results; the laboratory panel was not captured in the recall). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: CKD mineral bone disease: the kidney cannot activate vitamin D, so phosphate rises, calcium falls and PTH rises. Low Ca, high PTH, low vitamin D in ESRD: calcitriol (active vitamin D) High phosphate: dietary restriction
r: A 45 year old with ESRD from type 1 DM on routine follow up with abnormal labs is the classic picture of secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH and low vitamin D. The failing kidney cannot make active vitamin D, so calcitriol (1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D) is given
x: A. Sevelamer is a phosphate binder; it is right when the main issue is hyperphosphatemia, but it does not correct low active vitamin D or suppress PTH directly. | C. Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic for persistently high PTH with normal or high calcium; it lowers calcium further and is avoided when calcium is low. | D. 25 hydroxy vitamin D (calcidiol) still needs renal 1 alpha hydroxylation, which fails in ESRD; it fits nutritional vitamin D deficiency with normal kidneys.

q: Elderly patient came to hospital with dysuria and UTI symptoms , known to have hypertension, diabetes and COPD, with a previous admission for urosepsis with shock. Now he is agitated and aggressive on the ward. Vitals mostly normal but temperature high and oxygen saturation 92% . What is the most appropriate management?
k: Delirium in the elderly: find and treat the cause, then non drug measures first. Causes: infection (UTI, pneumonia), drugs, hypoxia, retention, constipation, electrolytes Non drug: reorientation, sleep wake cycle, glasse
r: An elderly patient with a UTI who becomes agitated and aggressive on the ward with fever has hyperactive delirium from infection. Treating the cause (antibiotics) is not offered, so the best answer is non pharmacological delirium care, here sleep cycle regulation (day night orientation, lights, mini
x: A. Sedation (antipsychotic or benzodiazepine) is a last resort only when the patient endangers himself or others after non drug measures fail; benzodiazepines worsen delirium and may depress breathing in COPD. | B. Physical restraint increases agitation, injury and delirium duration; it is avoided except briefly in an emergency. | D. Oxygen would be right if SpO2 were below 88% in COPD; at 92% he is on target, and long term oxygen needs two ABGs with chronic hypoxemia when stable.

q: Young man 30 years smoker . Has pulmonary nodule . Risk factor for pulmonary nodule to be malignant *in this patient * Culture send for TB
k: Nodule malignancy risk: size, smoking, age, spiculated margin, upper lobe, growth. ≤4 mm: no follow up (low risk) more than 4 to 8 mm: CT at 3 to 6 months more than 8 mm to 2 cm: PET/CT then biopsy more than 2 cm: surger
r: Of the options, size is the strongest independent predictor of malignancy in a pulmonary nodule, and a lesion over 2 to 3 cm is treated as malignant until proven otherwise (a 'mass'). The mention of a TB culture shows TB is on the differential, and TB also explains apical position and hypercalcemia,
x: A. Older age (over about 40 to 50) raises risk, but this patient is a young man, so age argues against malignancy here. | B. High serum calcium may occur with squamous cell cancer (PTHrP) but also with TB and sarcoidosis granulomas, and it is not part of nodule malignancy risk models; benign calcification patterns in the nodule favour benign disease. | D. Upper lobe location is a recognized cancer risk feature, but apical disease is also classic for reactivation TB, which is being investigated h

q: A 64-year-old man with liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C completed treatment for HCV and now has undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment. He is asymptomatic (see lab results). Which of the following is the most diagnostic ?
o: Triphasic CT scan of the abdomen
k: HCC in cirrhosis: Surveillance: ultrasound every 6 months, with or without AFP, continues after HCV cure Nodule below 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in 3 months Nodule ≥1 cm or rising AFP: multiphasic CT or contrast MRI Arteria
r: This recall's key is triphasic CT because the lead in asks for the most diagnostic test: triphasic (multiphasic) contrast CT shows the arterial enhancement and venous washout that diagnose HCC without biopsy. Even after HCV cure (undetectable RNA at 12 weeks), established cirrhosis keeps the HCC ris
x: A. Contrast MRI is at least as accurate as triphasic CT for diagnosing HCC, but this option is a yearly surveillance schedule, which is not standard; surveillance is ultrasound every 6 months. | B. Liver ultrasound every 6 months (with or without AFP) is the surveillance (screening) test after HCV cure in cirrhosis; it is the answer when the question asks for follow up or screening. | C. AFP alone is not sensitive enough and is not used every 3 months; it is an adjunct to ultrasound every 6 mont

q: 50-52 y/o female patient came to the screening clinic , medically and surgically free, No family history , what to do?
k: Average risk CRC screening starts at 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered). Colonoscopy: every 10 years (gold standard) FIT / high sensitivity FOBT: annually Stool DNA: every 3 years Flexible sigmoidoscopy: every 5 years C
r: A 50 to 52 year old woman with no family history and no risk factors is average risk, so she needs routine colorectal cancer screening. Annual stool testing for blood (FOBT/FIT) is a valid average risk strategy with the correct interval. The other listed options carry the wrong interval for an avera
x: A. Sigmoidoscopy: per the recaller's correction this option was every 10 years, a wrong interval for sigmoidoscopy alone; as printed (every 5 years) it would be a guideline interval, which is why the correction matters. | C. Colonoscopy every 5 years: the average risk interval is every 10 years; 5 years is for higher risk (e.g. first degree relative with CRC, prior adenomas). | D. Option not recalled; no basis to choose it.

q: 20 year old male KC of DM1 and diabetic nephropathy had a tonic colonic seizure lated for 4 minutes after 2 hour EEG show wave ( I can't remember) and tha labs was Na 132 RBG 4
k: First seizure: is it provoked? Check glucose, Na, Ca, Mg, toxins, head imaging Provoked only if the abnormality is severe: Na below about 120, glucose clearly low, marked hypocalcemia Unprovoked + epileptiform EEG: epile
r: The labs are Na 132 and RBG 4 : a sodium of 132 is only mildly low and a glucose of 4 mmol/L is normal, so neither can explain a 4 minute tonic clonic seizure . Provoked metabolic seizures need much more marked derangements, and the EEG showing epileptiform wave discharges points to a primary genera
x: B. Hypoglycemia seizure: right when glucose is clearly low (around 2.5 mmol/L or less, or about 45 mg/dL), common in type 1 diabetics on insulin; a glucose of 4 mmol/L is normal. | C. Hyponatremia: seizures usually occur with severe (Na below about 120) or rapidly falling sodium; 132 is mild and not a seizure cause. | D. Option not recalled (hypocalcemia in the earlier version): Ca 2.1 is only slightly low; hypocalcemic seizures need marked hypocalcemia with tetany signs.

q: A patient with DM, non-compliant with medications, presents with confusion Na 121 HbA1c = 8.something What is the most likely cause?
k: Hyponatremia symptoms track severity and speed. Mild (130 to 134): usually asymptomatic Moderate (125 to 129): nausea, headache, malaise Severe (below 125): confusion, seizures, coma Work-up: serum osmolality, then volum
r: The only value given that is markedly abnormal is Na 121 , and significant hyponatremia causes confusion. HbA1c around 8 shows poor long term control but is not an acute cause of altered mental status, and the other labs were said to be about normal. So the confusion is best explained by hyponatremi
x: A. Hypokalemia: causes muscle weakness, ileus and arrhythmias (flat T waves, U waves), not confusion, and no low potassium was reported. | C. Hypocalcemia: causes tetany, perioral tingling, Chvostek and Trousseau signs and prolonged QT; no low calcium was reported. | D. Hypoglycemia: a classic cause of confusion in diabetics, but on treatment (insulin or sulfonylurea); a patient non compliant with medications with HbA1c 8 is more likely hyperglycemic.

q: A woman with a BMI of 35 kg/m² and a family history of diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic. She is concerned about her risk of developing diabetes. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
o: Follow a diet with reduced carbohydrate intake.
Undergo bariatric surgery because losing weight may be difficult.
Engage in regular physical activity and maintain a healthy diet.
k: Obesity and diabetes prevention. First line: diet + exercise (at least 150 minutes per week of moderate activity) for weight loss Bariatric surgery (classic exam criteria): BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with comorbidity; newer crite
r: She has BMI 35 and a family history of diabetes but no diabetes or other obesity related complication of her own. The first and most effective recommendation for diabetes prevention is lifestyle modification: regular physical activity combined with a healthy diet, aiming for weight loss. Option C co
x: A. Reduced carbohydrate diet: only one part of lifestyle change; diet without regular exercise is less effective than the combined approach. | B. Bariatric surgery: not the first recommendation for diabetes prevention before any lifestyle trial; classic exam criteria are BMI ≥ 40, or ≥ 35 with her own obesity related comorbidity (diabetes, hypertension, OSA), and a family history does not count (newer 2022 surgical society criteria allow BMI ≥ 35 alone, but lifestyle still comes first).

q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of recurrent epigastric pain that resolves spontaneously, associated with nausea but no vomiting and unintentional weight loss . He has no family history of GI malignancy. Examination reveals epigastric tenderness on deep palpation. Labs show anemia with low MCV . What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Dyspepsia + any alarm feature = endoscopy. Unintentional weight loss Iron deficiency anemia or GI bleeding Progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting Palpable mass, new symptoms in older age No alarm features and young:
r: Recurrent epigastric pain in a 55-year-old with unintentional weight loss and iron deficiency (microcytic) anemia has alarm features for upper GI malignancy or a bleeding ulcer. Alarm features mandate direct visualisation and biopsy, so upper GI endoscopy is the next step regardless of family histor
x: B. CT abdomen is used for staging once a cancer is found or for suspected complications; it cannot see mucosa or take biopsies. | C. Test and treat for H. pylori is for young dyspeptic patients without alarm features; with weight loss and anemia it would delay a cancer diagnosis (biopsies at endoscopy can test for H. pylori anyway).

q: A 51-year-old man presents to the ER with vomiting blood . He has a previous history of two gastrointestinal bleeds of unknown site . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step?
k: Upper GI bleed sequence. 1. ABC, two large bore cannulas, fluids or blood 2. Risk score and medical therapy (PPI; terlipressin and antibiotics if variceal suspected) 3. Endoscopy within 24 h (sooner if unstable) 4. Faile
r: Hematemesis with two previous GI bleeds of unknown site needs a diagnosis of the source, and upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic (it can inject, clip, band). The true first action is ABC and resuscitation, but that is not offered, so among these options endoscopy (after stabilisati
kw: two gastrointestinal bleeds of unknown site
x: B. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is a temporary rescue for uncontrolled variceal bleeding when endoscopic therapy fails or is unavailable; the source here is not even known. | C. Laparotomy is reserved for bleeding that endoscopy (and interventional radiology) cannot control, or for perforation. | D. Barium studies cannot treat bleeding, are poor at finding the source and coat the mucosa, making later endoscopy harder.

q: A 20-years-old male patient with sickle cell disease presented to the ED with acute vaso-occlusive crisis. He was managed with IV fluids, morphine and enoxaparin . His thrombocytopenia (80) . Creatinine and urea were normal. What's the cause of his thrombocytopenia?
k: Thrombocytopenia after heparin: think HIT. Timing: typically 5 to 10 days after start (earlier if heparin exposure in the past 100 days) Fall in platelets about 50% or more, rarely below 20 Thrombosis, not bleeding Stop
r: The new drop in platelets ( 80 ) appeared after the patient received enoxaparin , a heparin, and he has normal creatinine and urea . Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction to heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes, causing thrombocytopenia (typically 5 to 10 days after starting) with a
x: A. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion with isolated thrombocytopenia in a well patient (often after a viral illness); a clear drug trigger is present here. | B. HUS needs microangiopathic hemolysis plus acute kidney injury; renal function is normal. | C. TTP presents with hemolysis, fever, neurological signs and severe thrombocytopenia; nothing points to it, and no drug trigger is needed.

q: A 49-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history presents for lung cancer screening. What is the best screening test ?
o: Low-dose CT scan of the chest
k: Lung cancer screening (USPSTF 2021). Who: age 50 to 80 with 20 pack-years or more, current smoker or quit within 15 years How: annual low dose CT Stop: quit 15 years or more, or health limits curative surgery
r: The question asks for the best screening test in a heavy smoker (30 pack-years). Annual low dose CT of the chest is the only lung cancer screening test shown to reduce lung cancer mortality, and it uses a fraction of the radiation of a diagnostic CT.
