r: A young, recently married (sexually active) woman with burning micturition and suprapubic tenderness , no fever or flank pain, has acute uncomplicated cystitis. Oral nitrofurantoin is a first-line agent for uncomplicated lower UTI because it concentrates in the bladder and keeps resistance low.
x: B. Oral fluoroquinolone: effective but reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of resistance and adverse effects. | C. IV gentamicin: parenteral therapy is for severe or complicated infection such as septic pyelonephritis; not needed for simple cystitis. | D. Oral beta-lactam: less effective than first-line agents for cystitis; used when others are unsuitable or in pregnancy (e.g. amoxicillin late in pregnancy).

q: 76-year-old man, known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 meters. He denied any history of syncope, chest pain, or palpitation. Precordium examination revealed a forceful apex beat and a crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids = aortic stenosis. Classic triad: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope Signs: slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, heaving apex Elderly: degenerative calcification;
r: An elderly man with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia), progressive exertional dyspnea , a forceful (heaving) apex from LV pressure overload and a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids has calcific aortic stenosis.
x: A. Mitral stenosis: mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with opening snap, tapping apex; typically rheumatic, not a systolic murmur to the carotids. | C. Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge, louder on inspiration, does not radiate to the carotids; usually congenital in the young. | D. Aortic regurgitation: early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure.

q: An adult woman presents with high fever and urinary symptoms. Her temperature is 39.1 C and the white cell count is high. Urinalysis shows significant pyuria . Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
k: Febrile UTI = pyelonephritis: choose an agent with renal tissue penetration. Systemically unwell or cannot take oral: IV ceftriaxone Mild, tolerating oral: oral fluoroquinolone outpatient Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin: c
r: High fever (39.1 C) , raised white cell count and significant pyuria point to an upper or systemic urinary infection (acute pyelonephritis), not simple cystitis. A systemically unwell patient needs parenteral therapy, and IV ceftriaxone is a standard empiric choice.
x: B. Oral cephalosporin: an option for mild pyelonephritis managed as an outpatient, but a high fever with leukocytosis favours initial IV therapy. | C. Oral nitrofurantoin: does not reach adequate tissue levels in the kidney; only for lower UTI (cystitis). | D. Oral amoxicillin: high E. coli resistance; not a reliable empiric choice for febrile UTI in adults.

q: A young woman with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis is evaluated in the Emergency Department. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit to start ceftriaxone and vancomycin
k: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: outpatient oral therapy if tolerating oral and stable. Options: oral fluoroquinolone, or ceftriaxone Admit if: sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, obstruction, failed outpatient therapy Get urine c
r: A young woman with acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis (no sepsis, obstruction, pregnancy or inability to take oral) can be managed as an outpatient with an oral fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin. Ceftriaxone is also acceptable, but it is not offered alone in the options.
x: B. Clarithromycin: a macrolide for respiratory or atypical infections; no useful activity against E. coli in the urinary tract. | C. Admit and start a carbapenem: reserved for severe or complicated infection, sepsis or known ESBL organisms; overtreatment for an uncomplicated case. | D. Admit for ceftriaxone plus vancomycin: vancomycin covers gram-positives such as MRSA, not the gram-negatives that cause pyelonephritis; admission is unnecessary when uncomplicated.

q: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with cola-coloured urine , a persistent headache and light-headedness for the past day. He had an episode of severe sore throat and fever 4.5 -5 days ago , for which he did not seek medical care. Which of the following laboratory findings would best support the provisional diagnosis?
k: PSGN vs IgA nephropathy: latency and complement. PSGN: 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis (3 to 6 after skin), low C3, raised ASO IgA nephropathy: hematuria within 1 to 2 days of URTI (synpharyngitic), normal C3 Nephritic: h
r: Cola-coloured urine with headache and light-headedness (hypertension and fluid overload) days after a severe sore throat with fever is a nephritic picture keyed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. PSGN activates the alternative complement pathway, so a low C3 (with normal C4) is the laboratory
x: A. High ANA titre: supports lupus nephritis (multisystem features, usually low C3 and C4), not a post-infectious nephritis in a young man. | B. Normal ASO titre: would argue against a recent streptococcal infection; PSGN is supported by a raised ASO (or anti-DNase B). | C. Normal serum creatinine: does not support any diagnosis; PSGN often shows a raised creatinine from reduced GFR.

q: Ptn with non-hodgkin lymphoma and he passed away before going through chemotherapy by 1 week wil he died before his chemotherapy session and he is known case of uncontrolled DM2 for 20 years and HTN. Labs: high uric acid, high potassium What's the cause of his death?
k: Tumor lysis syndrome: release of intracellular contents. High: potassium, phosphate, uric acid; low: calcium (binds phosphate) AKI from uric acid and calcium phosphate deposition High risk: Burkitt and other high-grade l
r: A patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma , a high cell-turnover tumour, who dies before chemotherapy with high uric acid and high potassium (and, per the compiler, raised creatinine) fits spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome. TLS can occur before treatment in bulky, rapidly growing lymphomas, and hyperkalemi
x: A. Drug induced nephropathy: possible with nephrotoxins or chemotherapy, but he had not started chemotherapy and it does not explain hyperuricemia. | C. Undiscovered renal failure: 20 years of diabetes and hypertension can cause CKD, which can raise both potassium and uric acid, but an acute fatal picture just before chemotherapy in a high-turnover lymphoma is best explained by spontaneous TLS, and the stem gives no history of renal impairment. | D. Renal tubular acidosis: type 4 RTA in diabetic

q: Which of the following diagnostic tools is the best option for screening for hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic patients ?
k: HCC surveillance ladder in cirrhosis. Screen: ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months Nodule under 1 cm: repeat ultrasound in 3 months Nodule over 1 cm: triphasic CT or contrast MRI Typical HCC: arterial enhancement with venous
r: HCC screening in cirrhosis is done with abdominal ultrasound every 6 months , with or without AFP. When only one tool is chosen, ultrasound is preferred because it is safe, cheap and detects lesions AFP misses.
x: A. Liver function test: assesses synthetic function and injury; it cannot detect a tumour. | B. Alpha fetoprotein: poor sensitivity alone (many HCCs do not secrete it); used together with ultrasound, not as the single screening test. | D. Triphasic CT: the diagnostic test after ultrasound finds a nodule over 1 cm (arterial enhancement with washout); too costly and radiation-heavy for routine screening.

q: A 28-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of lower back pain associated with morning stiffness for almost 1 hour , as well as joint pain affecting both knees and ankles bilaterally. He denied any history of skin rash or mucosal ulcerations. Clinical examination reveals limited lumbar spine movements, a positive modified Schober test , and active arthritis in both knees bilaterally. He also has tenderness over the Achilles tendon . Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
k: Ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory back pain in a young man. Stiffness improves with activity, worse with rest Signs: reduced Schober, enthesitis (Achilles), uveitis Plain pelvic X-ray: initial test; MRI SI joints: mos
r: A young man with over 3 months of inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness "almost 1 hour"), reduced lumbar movement with a "positive modified Schober test", peripheral arthritis and Achilles enthesitis = axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis). The diagnosis is established by imaging sacr
x: A. HLA-B27 analysis: supportive only; many healthy people are positive and some patients are negative, so it cannot establish the diagnosis. | C. Knee joint aspiration: for an acute effusion to exclude septic or crystal arthritis; it does not diagnose spondyloarthritis. | D. CT scan of sacroiliac joint: shows erosions and structural change but misses early inflammation and gives high radiation; MRI is preferred.

q: A 60-year-old man with liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Room with increasing ascites. He has no history of fever or decreased level of consciousness. His medications include spironolactone 50 mg/day and furosemide 40 mg/day . His physical examination confirms the presence of large ascites (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Cirrhotic ascites ladder. Sodium restriction (under 2 g/day) Spironolactone, add furosemide (ratio 100:40) Large/tense or refractory: large-volume paracentesis + albumin Repeated need: TIPS or liver transplant Fever, pai
r: He already takes spironolactone and furosemide yet presents with "increasing" and "large ascites" (grade 3). Large, tense or diuretic-refractory ascites is treated with large-volume therapeutic paracentesis (with albumin replacement for large volumes), which relieves symptoms quickly; there is no fe
x: A. Intravenous diuretics: no benefit over oral in cirrhosis and raise risk of renal failure and electrolyte disturbance. | C. Increase the dose of furosemide: dose titration (keeping the 100:40 spironolactone:furosemide ratio) suits moderate ascites; large ascites needs paracentesis first. | D. TIPS: for truly refractory ascites needing frequent paracenteses, in selected patients; not the next step.

q: A 38-year-old woman, mother of three, presents with fatigue and weight loss for the last few months. She was unable to breastfeed her last child and her menses did not return after giving birth . She has cold intolerance and loss of appetite. Examination reveals a croaky voice with delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks (see lab results). What is the next step in management?
o: Treat with levothyroxine 50 mcg per day
k: Sheehan syndrome: severe PPH leads to pituitary necrosis. Earliest sign: failure of lactation (prolactin) Amenorrhea (LH/FSH), hypothyroidism (TSH), adrenal insufficiency (ACTH) Labs: low/normal TSH with low free T4, hyp
r: Failure of lactation and no return of menses after delivery suggest Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary infarction), and the cold intolerance, croaky voice and "delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks" show hypothyroidism. The next step is to confirm with thyroid function tests: TSH together
kw: unable to breastfeed her last child
menses did not return after giving birth
delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks
x: A. Give conjugated estrogen: hormone replacement for hypogonadism comes later, after the diagnosis is confirmed and more urgent axes are treated. | C. Correct hyponatremia with hypertonic saline: only for severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma); she is not described this way. | D. Treat with levothyroxine 50 mcg per day: needs a confirmed diagnosis first; in hypopituitarism, cortisol must be replaced BEFORE thyroxine to avoid an adrenal crisis.

q: A 42-year-old homeless man was recently released from prison . He presented to the Emergency Room with a fever, productive cough, weight loss, and night sweats over the past 3 months (see report). Chest X-ray: Left lung apical infiltration . Sputum sample was collected and sent to the lab. Which of the following tests has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Suspected pulmonary TB workup. Risk groups: prisoners, homeless, HIV, contacts, migrants CXR: upper lobe infiltrate or cavity Sputum x3: Ziehl-Neelsen for AFB, NAAT (GeneXpert) for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistan
r: "Homeless", "recently released from prison", 3 months of fever, productive cough, weight loss and night sweats with "left lung apical infiltration" = pulmonary tuberculosis. On the sputum sample, the Ziehl-Neelsen stain detects acid-fast bacilli and is the most useful listed test; culture (or NAAT/G
x: A. Thin blood film: identifies the malaria species (and blood cell morphology); not used on sputum. | B. Congo red stain: detects amyloid (apple-green birefringence under polarised light); not for infection. | C. Thick blood film: the most sensitive test to detect malaria parasites; irrelevant to a chronic cough with apical infiltrate.

q: A 38-year-old woman who is not known to have any medical illness is referred to the clinic because of a chest x-ray that showed prominent hilar structures bilaterally. She is having on- and-off cough but denies any history of shortness of breath, sputum production, chest pain, skin lesions, weight loss, fever, or contact with sick people. She is not a smoker. Examination reveals clear chest bilaterally (see lab results and reports). CT chest: Confirmed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy , otherwise lung parenchyma was clear . CT-guided biopsy: Showed noncaseating granuloma . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Sarcoidosis: treat according to severity, not according to the diagnosis alone. Hilar nodes only, mild symptoms, normal exam: observe Progressive dyspnea, parenchymal infiltrates, crackles: glucocorticoids Noncaseating g
r: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with noncaseating granuloma on biopsy in a young non-smoking woman is sarcoidosis. Her disease is mild: only an "on-and-off cough", a clear chest, and CT shows the lung parenchyma was clear (hilar nodes only, stage I). Stage I sarcoidosis with minimal symptoms usually
x: B. Prednisone: reserved for progressive or symptomatic disease (worsening dyspnea, parenchymal infiltrates, falling lung function) or serious extrapulmonary involvement (eye, heart, nervous system, hypercalcemia); none is present here. | C. Azithromycin: treats atypical pneumonia or chlamydia; there is no fever, sputum or infiltrate, and granulomas are not an infection to cover. | D. Anti-tuberculosis therapy: TB gives caseating granulomas with fever, weight loss or sick contacts, all denied her

q: A 65-year-old man, a heavy smoker, known to have hypertension and COPD on Ventolin, Anoro Ellipta (Umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol) , and lisinopril, presents with worsening shortness of breath for 4 months. There has been no change in his sputum amount or purulence , and he has had no fever, PND, or orthopnea. He was not admitted to the hospital for more than a year. Examination reveals decreased breath sounds without added sounds (see lab results and report). Chest CT 6 months ago: Diffuse emphysematous changes . Which of the following is the best intervention to improve his shortness of breath?
k: COPD: only smoking cessation and long-term oxygen (in hypoxemic patients) improve survival. Persistent dyspnea on LAMA/LABA: check oxygenation, refer to pulmonary rehabilitation Long-term oxygen if resting hypoxemia or c
r: He has severe emphysematous COPD with 4 months of worsening dyspnea but no exacerbation (no change in sputum, no fever, no admission for over a year), and he is already on a LAMA/LABA (Anoro) plus Ventolin. Inhaler therapy is already maximised for his phenotype, so the keyed answer is home oxygen ,
kw: no change in his sputum amount or purulence
x: B. Add LABA: he already takes vilanterol, a LABA, inside Anoro Ellipta; adding a second LABA adds nothing. | C. Volume reduction surgery: for selected patients with upper lobe predominant emphysema after pulmonary rehabilitation; this is diffuse emphysema and he still smokes. | D. Add inhaled corticosteroid: added for frequent exacerbations or high eosinophils; he has had no exacerbation or admission for over a year.

q: A 44-year-old man complains of dyspnea on exertion. Heart auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the base of the heart. The intensity and duration of the murmur increase during inspiration . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Timing and site pick the valve, the respiratory change picks the side. Early diastolic at base: AR or PR Louder on inspiration: right-sided (PR, TR) Louder on expiration: left-sided (AR, MR); leaning forward accentuates
r: An early diastolic murmur at the base comes from a semilunar valve: aortic or pulmonary regurgitation. The decisive clue is that it increases during inspiration : inspiration raises venous return to the right heart, and right-sided murmurs get louder, so this is pulmonary regurgitation.
kw: early diastolic murmur at the base
x: A. Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, louder on expiration; not diastolic. | B. Aortic regurgitation: also an early diastolic murmur at the base, but left-sided, so it is louder in expiration with the patient leaning forward. | C. Tricuspid regurgitation: increases with inspiration but is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, not diastolic at the base.

q: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for a 2-day history of dysuria and urethral discharge . He had recent sexual activity with a new female partner . He is afebrile, and his examination is unremarkable (see report) . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Urethritis in a young man after a new partner = STI until proven otherwise. Chlamydia: azithromycin single dose or doxycycline 7 days Gonorrhea: ceftriaxone IM (plus chlamydia cover if not excluded) Cystitis in a woman:
r: A young sexually active man with dysuria and urethral discharge after a new partner , afebrile, has urethritis; the recall (report) points to Chlamydia trachomatis, the commonest cause of non-gonococcal urethritis. The key treats chlamydia with azithromycin (single dose); doxycycline is the alternat
x: A. Gentamycin: an aminoglycoside used in pyelonephritis or sepsis combinations; not a urethritis treatment. | C. Ceftriaxone: right for gonococcal urethritis (gram-negative intracellular diplococci, purulent discharge), usually with chlamydia cover; alone it misses chlamydia. | D. Nitrofurantoin: for uncomplicated cystitis, mostly in women; it does not treat sexually transmitted urethritis.

q: A 33-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital after a road traffic accident that resulted in multiple fractures and had undergone multiple orthopedic surgical procedures. She has a positive urinary culture for Candida albicans . She denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms . She had an indwelling urinary catheter . Her examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Treat candiduria only if: symptomatic, neutropenic, or undergoing a urologic procedure. Asymptomatic + catheter: remove or change catheter, no antifungal Treatment of choice when needed: fluconazole Candidemia: echinocan
r: This is asymptomatic candiduria in a catheterised inpatient: she "denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms" and the exam is unremarkable. Candida in the urine of a catheterised patient is usually colonisation, so no antifungal is given; the catheter is removed or changed.
kw: positive urinary culture for Candida albicans
denies any history of fever or urinary symptoms
x: A. Fluconazole: first line when candiduria needs treatment: symptomatic, neutropenic, or before a urologic procedure; none applies. | B. Caspofungin: an echinocandin for invasive candidiasis or candidemia; it also concentrates poorly in urine. | C. Amphotericin B: for severe invasive fungal infection or fluconazole-resistant species; far too toxic for colonisation.

q: A 55-year-old man with diabetes mellitus for 10 years was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with severe pneumonia that required intubation and ventilation. He was treated with intravenous antibiotics, and his vital signs, including his blood pressure, were maintained within the normal range. However, last night, he developed hypotension that required two inotrope agents (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Very high transaminases right after shock = ischemic hepatitis. AST/ALT often >1000, LDH high, rapid fall after recovery Risk: hypotension, heart failure, sepsis Viral or toxic (paracetamol) are the other causes of level
r: A previously stable ICU patient developed sudden hypotension needing two inotropes last night; the labs (not shown) would show a sharp rise in liver enzymes. Hypoperfusion of the liver causes ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), with AST and ALT rising quickly, often above 1000, then falling over days
kw: developed hypotension that required two inotrope agents
x: A. Acute cholangitis: fever, RUQ pain and jaundice (Charcot triad) with a cholestatic pattern from biliary obstruction; nothing points to the biliary tree here. | C. Acute viral hepatitis: develops over days to weeks with prodrome and exposure history, not overnight after a hypotensive episode. | D. Drug-induced hepatitis: possible with antibiotics, but the timing tied to the hypotension and inotrope need points to ischemia.

q: A 45-year-old man was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with fever. He required a vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of more than 65 mm Hg . He is receiving adequate IV fluid resuscitation (see lab result). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Sepsis continuum: SIRS, sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock. SIRS: ≥2 of temp <36 or >38, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12 or <4 Sepsis: SIRS + infection Severe sepsis: + organ dysfunction Septic shock: hypotension needing vasopr
r: He has fever (infection) and needs a vasopressor to keep MAP above 65 mm Hg despite adequate IV fluid resuscitation . That is the definition of septic shock: sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors (Sepsis-3 also adds lactate above 2 mmol/L).
x: A. Sepsis: infection with organ dysfunction; it becomes septic shock once vasopressors are needed despite fluids. | B. Septicemia: an old term for bacteria in the blood with systemic illness; it is not a defined stage and does not describe refractory hypotension. | D. SIRS: two or more of temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate or WBC criteria without necessarily an infection or hypotension; the earliest stage.

q: A 70-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 2-hour history of confusion and irritability . He was well until 5 days ago, when he injured his right leg and has been bed-bound since the accident . He is hypertensive and well-controlled on medication. He has no fever (see reports). Chest X-ray: Normal . ECG: Sinus tachycardia . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Immobilization + sudden cardiorespiratory or mental change = think PE. Risks: surgery, trauma, immobility, long travel, malignancy ECG: sinus tachycardia most common; S1Q3T3 and RBBB less common CXR usually normal Diagno
r: He has been bed-bound for 5 days after a leg injury , a major DVT risk, and now has sudden confusion with sinus tachycardia and a normal chest x-ray , without fever. Acute confusion in the elderly can be the presenting sign of hypoxia from pulmonary embolism; sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG f
x: A. Arrhythmia: the ECG shows only sinus tachycardia, which is a response, not a primary arrhythmia like AF or VT. | B. Cerebral infarction: gives focal deficits (weakness, aphasia) rather than isolated confusion and irritability, and does not explain tachycardia after immobilization. | C. Brain hemorrhage: sudden headache, vomiting, focal signs and severe hypertension; his BP is well controlled and there is no head trauma.

q: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was recently diagnosed with hypertension . Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive medication?
k: Diabetes or CKD with hypertension: ACE inhibitor or ARB first. Age <55 or diabetic: ACEi/ARB Age ≥55 or African descent (non-diabetic): calcium channel blocker Pregnancy: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine; ACEi contraind
r: In a patient with type 2 diabetes and new hypertension, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is first line because it lowers intraglomerular pressure and protects against diabetic nephropathy. Ramipril is the ACE inhibitor among the options.
x: A. Hydralazine: a direct vasodilator kept for hypertension in pregnancy (IV) or resistant heart failure combinations, not first line. | B. Amlodipine: first line in non-diabetic patients of African descent or older than 55, or as add-on; no renal protection. | C. Metoprolol: beta blockers are for compelling indications (post MI, heart failure, rate control), not first line in uncomplicated hypertension, and may mask hypoglycemia.

q: A 31-year-old woman known to have rheumatic mitral stenosis recently developed atrial fibrillation , for which she was placed on warfarin therapy. What is the most appropriate target of the international normalized ratio (INR) range?
k: Warfarin targets: most indications 2 to 3, mechanical mitral valve higher. AF (with or without MS), DVT, PE: 2.0 to 3.0 Mechanical aortic valve without risk factors: 2.0 to 3.0 Mechanical mitral valve or extra risk facto
r: She has rheumatic mitral stenosis with atrial fibrillation , a very high embolic risk lesion that needs warfarin whatever her stroke score (DOACs are not used in moderate to severe rheumatic MS). The standard therapeutic INR target for AF, including AF with mitral stenosis, is 2.0 to 3.0 .
x: A. <1.0: this is below a normal untreated INR (about 1.0) and means no anticoagulation at all. | B. 1.0-1.5: a near normal, subtherapeutic INR that gives no protection against thromboembolism. | D. >3.0: higher targets (2.5 to 3.5) are used for some mechanical valves, especially mitral; above 3 in AF mainly raises bleeding risk.

q: An elderly patient with end-stage metastatic cancer receiving palliative care becomes aggressive and confused , and the staff cannot calm her. What is the best drug to give?
k: Delirium: treat the cause, non-drug measures first, then an antipsychotic. Search reversible causes: drugs (opioids), infection, hypercalcemia, retention, hypoxia First-line drug: haloperidol Benzodiazepine first: alcoho
r: An end-stage cancer patient who becomes acutely confused and aggressive has delirium (terminal agitation). When non-drug measures fail, haloperidol is the first-line drug for delirium in palliative care because it controls agitation and psychotic features without worsening confusion.
x: B. Lorazepam: benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and confusion; they are used for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, seizures, or added to an antipsychotic for refractory terminal agitation.

q: Elderly diabetic, black toe , dorsalis absent/not palpable , next or initial management :
k: Diabetic foot: first decide if it is ischemic, infective or neuropathic. Absent pulses, gangrene: ABI first, then duplex or angiography ABI <0.9: PAD; >1.3: non-compressible calcified vessels Probe to bone or deep ulcer:
r: An elderly diabetic with a black toe (dry gangrene) and an absent dorsalis pedis pulse has suspected peripheral arterial disease with critical limb ischemia. The initial bedside test is the ankle brachial index ; arterial calcification in diabetics can falsely raise it, so toe pressures or duplex fo
x: A. Tissue Biopsy: for a chronic non-healing ulcer suspicious of malignant change (Marjolin ulcer), not for ischemic gangrene. | C. MRI: the best imaging for suspected osteomyelitis under a diabetic foot ulcer; the problem here is arterial supply, not bone infection.

q: Women with brief jerky movements involving only upper limb
k: Seizure type by movement. Myoclonic: brief shock like jerks, seconds Clonic: rhythmic repeated jerking Tonic: sustained stiffening Atonic: sudden loss of tone, drop attack Absence: staring spells, few seconds
r: Brief, jerky, shock like movements lasting about a second, here limited to the upper limbs, are myoclonic seizures. Consciousness is usually preserved; they typically occur in the morning (juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, often with dropping things in the morning).
x: A. Atonic seizures are a sudden loss of muscle tone causing drop attacks or head drops, not jerks. | B. Clonic seizures are sustained, rhythmic, repetitive jerking that lasts longer, usually with impaired awareness, not single brief jerks. | C. Tonic seizures are sustained stiffening (increased tone) of the limbs and trunk, not jerky movements.

q: 46 years old female right handed, complaining of Sausage digits in the left hand and nail pitting , She Also Had morning stiffness and joint swelling in both PIPs and DIPs . what else you can find in the history?
k: Psoriatic arthritis clues. Dactylitis (sausage digits) Nail pitting, onycholysis DIP involvement, asymmetric oligoarthritis Skin psoriasis (may follow the arthritis) Pencil in cup deformity on X ray
r: Sausage digits (dactylitis), nail pitting and DIP joint involvement point to psoriatic arthritis. The history question that completes the picture is skin disease: a history of psoriatic plaques (scalp, extensor surfaces, natal cleft) or a family history of psoriasis.
x: B. Heat intolerance points to hyperthyroidism (thyroid acropachy can cause finger clubbing and swelling) but does not explain nail pitting, dactylitis and DIP arthritis. | C. Dyspnea from lung disease fits rheumatoid arthritis (interstitial lung disease) or scleroderma, not the dactylitis and nail pitting pattern of psoriatic arthritis.

q: A 62-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic stroke 1 month ago , presented to the Emergency Room complaining of central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours . She denied any dyspnea, palpitation, or change in consciousness. The patient is taking insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, lipitor, and aspirin. Examination revealed she is in pain. She was started on oxygen, morphine, and sublingual nitroglycerin (see image). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: ACS reperfusion choice. STEMI: primary PCI preferred Fibrinolysis only if PCI cannot be done in time and no contraindication Absolute contraindications include ischemic stroke within 3 months, any prior intracranial hemo
r: Multiple risk factors with 3 hours of continuous central chest pain treated with oxygen, morphine and nitrate is acute coronary syndrome. The definitive next step is urgent coronary angiography with PCI where indicated. Thrombolysis is not an option because of her ischemic stroke 1 month ago .
kw: central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours
x: A. IV magnesium is for torsades de pointes or hypomagnesemia related arrhythmias; it has no role in ACS here. | B. CT angiography is used when aortic dissection is suspected (tearing pain to the back, pulse or BP differential) or for stable low risk chest pain; it cannot treat and only delays reperfusion in an active ACS. | D. Fibrinolysis is contraindicated: ischemic stroke within the last 3 months is an absolute contraindication; it would be used for STEMI only when PCI is not available in tim

q: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis maintained on methotrexate 15 weekly . She is currently in remission. 4 months ago, her LFTs were normal but the most recent LFTs show: AST 300 (10x normal), ALT 280 (10x normal), Albumin 30 (low). What is the most appropriate action for her abnormal liver function tests?
k: Methotrexate and LFTs. Monitor LFTs regularly ALT/AST 1 to 3 times normal: reduce dose and recheck Above 3 times normal: stop methotrexate Give folic acid weekly to reduce toxicity
r: Her transaminases are about 10 times normal on methotrexate, with a falling albumin, after normal LFTs 4 months ago. Methotrexate is hepatotoxic, and a rise above 3 times the upper limit of normal requires stopping methotrexate to prevent further liver injury; she is in remission, so the drug can be
x: A. Liver ultrasound may be part of later workup, but the priority action is removing the offending drug. | B. Glucocorticoids treat autoimmune hepatitis or RA flares; they do not reverse drug induced liver injury and she is in remission. | D. Liver biopsy is invasive and considered only for persistent abnormalities after the drug is stopped, not as the first action.

q: lady in her fourties recurrent uti what is the best for prevention
k: Recurrent UTI prevention ladder. Behavioural: fluids, postcoital voiding, avoid spermicides Postmenopausal: vaginal estrogen Most effective: continuous or postcoital antibiotic prophylaxis
r: For a woman with recurrent UTI (2 or more in 6 months or 3 or more in a year), the most effective prevention is antibiotic prophylaxis , either continuous low dose or postcoital (for example nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole). It has the strongest evidence for reducing recurrences.
x: A. Cranberry products have weak and inconsistent evidence; they may be an option for women who wish to avoid antibiotics, but they are not the best. | B. Increased fluid intake is a reasonable first behavioural measure, but it is less effective than prophylactic antibiotics.

q: A patient presented with severe diarrhea . Which of the following is the most expected abnormalities ?
k: GI losses and acid base. Vomiting / NG suction: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis Diarrhea / fistula: normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia
r: Stool below the stomach is rich in bicarbonate and potassium . Severe diarrhea loses both, giving a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia ; volume depletion and secondary hyperaldosteronism worsen the potassium loss.
x: B. Metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia fits renal failure, type 4 RTA (hypoaldosteronism) or adrenal insufficiency, not GI loss of potassium. | C. Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia is the pattern of vomiting or gastric outlet obstruction (loss of HCl), or diuretics; diarrhea loses bicarbonate, not acid. | D. Metabolic alkalosis with hyperkalemia is an unusual combination and does not fit any GI loss.

q: Patient with diabetes, hypertension and renal failure . Blood pressure is around 159/105-110 and glucose around 7-8 . What is the cause of the renal failure?
k: Diabetic vs hypertensive kidney disease. Diabetic: long DM duration, albuminuria/nephrotic range proteinuria, retinopathy, normal or large kidneys Hypertensive: long HTN, mild proteinuria, small kidneys, other end organ
r: This recall is built on which disease drove the kidney damage. Blood pressure is markedly high and poorly controlled ( 159/105 to 110 ) while glucose is near target ( 7 to 8 ); in the earlier version, hypertension had been present for about 20 years versus only 2 to 3 years of diabetes. Diabetic nep
x: A. Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause of CKD overall, but it needs long standing (usually over 10 years), poorly controlled diabetes, with proteinuria and often retinopathy; here diabetes is short and controlled.

q: An (forget age) female patient with (memory impairment not sure about it )was admitted to the hospital and found elevated blood pressure ( 167/98 mmHg ). She was prescribed antihypertensive medication but refused to take it because she was concerned about its potential side effects. What complication could develop if she does not take her antihypertensive medication ?
k: Complications of uncontrolled hypertension. Heart: LVH, heart failure, coronary disease, atrial fibrillation Brain: stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic), vascular dementia Kidney: nephrosclerosis, CKD Eye: hypertensive reti
r: Untreated high blood pressure ( 167/98 ) increases afterload chronically, causing left ventricular hypertrophy , diastolic dysfunction and eventually heart failure . Hypertension is one of the commonest causes of heart failure, alongside stroke, coronary disease and CKD as the main complications of
kw: does not take her antihypertensive medication
x: A. Pericarditis is caused by viral infection, uremia, post MI or autoimmune disease, not by hypertension. | B. Amyloidosis can cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy, but it is a deposition disease, not a complication of high blood pressure. | D. Infective endocarditis is caused by bacteremia on damaged or prosthetic valves, IV drug use, or dental procedures; hypertension does not cause it.

q: An elderly patient presents with acute heart failure and has atrial fibrillation on ECG. What is the best next step?
k: AF rate control choice. Unstable: synchronized DC cardioversion Stable, normal LV: beta blocker or diltiazem/verapamil Acute heart failure or hypotension: digoxin or amiodarone WPW with AF: procainamide (avoid AV nodal b
r: AF in a patient with acute heart failure needs rate control without depressing contractility. Beta blockers (and non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) are negatively inotropic and are avoided in acute decompensated heart failure, so digoxin (positively inotropic, slows AV conduction) is the
x: B. Adenosine is used to terminate or unmask regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT); it does not control AF. | C. Beta blockers are first line rate control in stable AF and in chronic stable heart failure, but they can worsen acute decompensated failure. | D. Procainamide is used for AF with pre-excitation (WPW, irregular wide complex tachycardia) or stable VT, not rate control in heart failure.

q: A 49-years-old male smoker for many years came to clinic for lung cancer screening . What is the most appropriate screening tools ?
k: Lung cancer screening (USPSTF 2021). Age 50 to 80 At least 20 pack years Current smoker or quit within 15 years Test: annual low dose CT Stop when quit over 15 years or not fit for surgery
r: Lung cancer screening with annual low dose CT is offered to adults aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack years who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years (USPSTF). This smoker is 49 , below the starting age, so screening is not indicated yet; the priority is smoking cessation.
x: A. Low dose CT is the screening test, and becomes the answer at 50 or above with 20 or more pack years, or when 'no need' is not among the options. | B. Chest X ray is not used for screening; it has not been shown to reduce lung cancer mortality. | C. Bronchoscopy is a diagnostic test for a suspected lesion or symptoms such as hemoptysis, never a screening tool.

q: 23 yo female known case of SLE complaining of ll swelling and SOB. On exam she hs jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, prominent diastolic component, positive shifting dullness, and edema up to knees. Labs: - Creatinine 450 (high) - WBC: 3 (low) - ALT: 100 (high) - AST: 94 (high) -C3/C4: low Which SLE associated condition explains her symptoms?
k: Constrictive pericarditis.
r: Raised JVP + early diastolic knock + ascites = constriction; don't be pulled to liver or renal failure by the abnormal labs.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2022).

q: A male patient presents with a blood pressure of 160/90 mmHg and is scheduled to receive thrombolytic therapy. What should be done before administering the thrombolytic agent?
o: Lower the blood pressure to 140/60 mmHg before administering thrombolytic therapy.
r: Thrombolysis is allowed if BP < 185/110; 160/90 does not need lowering, give it immediately.
n: Target BP Before Administration Of tPa is 185/110

q: Patient came with SOB and fatigue. He was stable. ECG: showed bradycardia (same pic, Dx not written). Next step in the management?
k: Bradycardia algorithm (symptomatic, HR usually < 50).
r: Atropine is unlikely to work in a heart transplant patient or in infranodal (Mobitz II, complete) block; go to pacing.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6867).

q: A 38-year-old woman, mother of three, presents with fatigue and weight loss for the last few months. She was unable to breastfeed her last child and her menses did not return after giving birth. She has cold intolerance and loss of appetite. Examination reveals a croaky voice with delayed relaxation phase of her ankle jerks (see lab results) What is the next step in management?
o: Treat with levothyroxine 50 mcg per day
k: Sheehan syndrome: postpartum hemorrhage leads to pituitary necrosis.
r: In pituitary failure, give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine, and judge the thyroid by free T4, not TSH alone.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6197).
kw: menses did not return after giving birth

q: A 20-year-old woman, recently married, presents with burning micturition for one week. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?
r: Uncomplicated cystitis in a young woman: oral nitrofurantoin (or fosfomycin/TMP-SMX).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0163).

q: A 73-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by family members who noticed a change in her level of consciousness for 1 day. She is known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and liver cirrhosis. Examination reveals she is drowsy, with raised JVP, positive shifting dullness, and +2 lower limb edema (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Hyponatremia: first classify volume status.
r: Raised JVP + ascites + edema means diuretic, not fluids, even if the patient is drowsy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0332).
kw: raised JVP, positive shifting dullness, and +2 lower limb edema

q: A 23-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 7-month history of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and diarrhea that are sometimes associated with streaks of blood and ‘occasional audible peristalsis. He had fever and loss of appetite for the last 7 days. There is no history of allergy or chronic use of any medications. Examination reveals a thin, ill-looking patient with a tender but soft abdomen (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Chronic diarrhea + blood + systemic features (fever, weight loss) = organic inflammatory disease until proven otherwise.
r: Any blood in the stool, fever or weight loss removes IBS from the answer list.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9220).

q: A 61-year-old obese man presented with daytime somnolence, poor concentration, nocturia, and progressive shortness of breath. Examination reveals an obese patient with bilateral lower limb edema and normal vesicular breath sounds on lung auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
k: OSA: suspect clinically, confirm with polysomnography.
r: "Establish the diagnosis" asks for the cause (sleep study), not the consequence (echo).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8447).

q: A 26-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department 1 hour after having a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He has never had a seizure previously or any episode of jerking, staring, confusion, or memory loss. He has had no recent illness and has no history of neurological problems. Birth and development were normal. There is no family history of seizures or epilepsy. He takes no medication and does not use illicit drugs. His vital signs are normal. Neurological findings are unremarkable. Results of laboratory studies show a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
r: First unprovoked seizure in an adult: neuroimaging (head CT in ER) to exclude a structural cause; EEG later.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0055).
kw: normal complete blood count and metabolic panel

q: A 63-year-old man is evaluated for hemoptysis and a 5-kg weight loss over the last 2 months. He has a history of 30 pack- years of smoking but stopped 10 days ago (see reports). Chest X-ray: 5-cm irregular mass in the right upper lobe. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy: Tumor in the right upper lobe bronchus. Biopsy: Squamous cell carcinoma, Whole body FDG-PET scan: Negative for metastasis. Which of the following is the most appropriate action while preparing him for surgery?
k: Confirmed, staged, resectable lung cancer: next is fitness testing.
r: Recent smoking cessation and a large tumour make PFT even more important before lobectomy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3298).

q: A 60-year-old man with hypertension presents to the Emergency Room with sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain, dyspnea, and palpitations for 2 hours. His past medical history is significant for a non-hemorrhagic stroke 2 months ago (see lab results and report) ECG: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
r: STEMI with ischaemic stroke 2 months ago: fibrinolysis is contraindicated (stroke < 3 months) -> primary PCI.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0196).
kw: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
sudden onset of retrosternal chest pain

q: A 60-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with symptomatic hyponatremia. Which of the following is the most serious consequence of rapid correction of hyponatremia?
k: Sodium correction speed: Hyponatremia corrected too fast → central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination); Hypernatremia corrected too fast → cerebral edema; Symptomatic hyponatremia → hypertonic 3% saline, with a capped daily rise
r: Low to high too fast, the pons will fry; high to low too fast, the brain will blow (edema).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0629).

q: A 20-year-old woman is referred to Neurology Clinic because of an unsteady gait and transient loss of vision during a sports game at university. She has no history of fever, sweating, or recent trauma, and no past medical or drug history (see report). MRI Brain: Multiple demyelinating hyperintense lesions are seen distributed in the periventricular white matter and callososeptal regions bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Young woman, episodes of visual loss and ataxia separated in time = multiple sclerosis.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0171).

q: A 22-year-old woman was brought to the Emergency Room after ingesting 50 tablets of extra strength acetaminophen (500 mg each tablet) 3 hours ago. The patient is conscious and oriented (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Close monitoring of liver function tests
k: Paracetamol overdose: decontaminate early, NAC by level or by dose.
r: Large ingestion, early, alert patient = NAC plus charcoal; late or symptomatic = NAC alone.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2455).

q: A 42-year-old man presented to the hospital complaining of shortness of breath, fever, and fatigue for the past few days. Examination showed he has high JVP, pulsus paradoxus, and distant heart sounds. Lung auscultation was clear (see reports). ECG: Low voltage. Chest X-ray: An increase in cardiac silhouette Which area of the heart is most likely involved?
k: Tamponade = pericardial fluid compressing the heart.
r: Big heart shadow with clear lungs and low voltage = effusion, not failing myocardium.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6441).

q: A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 4-month history of fever, night sweats, fatigue, arthralgia, and lower back pain. He had a history of unpasteurized milk ingestion. His examination reveals right knee arthritis and limited spinal movements. His cardiopulmonary examination is unremarkable (see lab results and reports). Right knee joint aspiration: WBC 15,000 (0-200) Blood culture: Negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?
k: Raw milk + fever + sweats + back or joint pain = brucellosis until proven otherwise.
r: A negative blood culture does not exclude brucellosis; go to serology, not biopsy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2834).

q: A 44-year-old Saudi man is evaluated because of a 3-month history of fever and back pain that radiates to his legs. His examination reveals bony tenderness over the entire back. Blood culture shows gram-negative coccobacilli. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: + Written in Exam Drinking unpasteurized milk
r: Saudi man, fever + back pain (spondylitis), gram-negative coccobacilli, raw milk = brucellosis.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0090).
kw: 3-month history of fever and back pain
bony tenderness over the entire back

q: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was recently diagnosed with hypertension. Which of the following is the most appropriate antihypertensive medication?
r: Diabetes + hypertension: ACE inhibitor (ramipril) protects the kidneys.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0068).

q: A 60-year-old man is found to have elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup. He has no symptoms, and physical examination is unremarkable. ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, and urine analysis are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next option in management?
o: Repeat office blood pressure measurement in 6 months
k: Elevated office BP without urgency: confirm before treating.
r: One high clinic reading is not hypertension: confirm with ambulatory monitoring first.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9709).
kw: elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup

q: A 31-year-old woman known to have rheumatic mitral stenosis recently developed atrial fibrillation, for which she was placed on warfarin therapy. What is the most appropriate target of the international normalized ratio (INR) range?
k: Warfarin target INR 2 to 3 for AF (including AF with rheumatic MS), DVT and PE.
r: Rheumatic MS + AF = warfarin with INR 2 to 3; do not reach for a DOAC or a higher valve target.
n: ⚠ يشبه OCT-7054 لكن جوابه: 2.0-3.0.

q: A 70-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. Examination revealed a pulsatile abdominal mass felt on deep palpation with mild tenderness just above the umbilicus (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH Heart rate 76 /min; Respiratory rate 14 /min; Temperature 36.6 °C; Oxygen saturation 99 % Test Result Normal Values RBC 6.0 4.7–6.1 × 10¹²/L (Male) 4.2–5.4 × 10¹²/L (Female) Hb 135 130–170 g/L (Male) 120–160 g/L (Female) HCT 0.42 0.42–0.52 (Male) 0.37–0.48 (Female) Platelets count 155 150–400 × 10⁹/L WBC 13.5 4.5–10.5 × 10⁹/L Sodium 136 134–146 mmol/L; Potassium 4 3.5–5.1 mmol/L; Bicarbonate 25 21–28 mmol/L Upright chest x-ray: No air under diaphragm. Which the following is the most appropriate lab investigation to be ordered next?
r: ⚠ Pulsatile mass = AAA; the key chose amylase level (to exclude pancreatitis as the cause of pain). Keep the key as Alhomrani wrote it.

q: A 60-year-old man with known liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Department with progressively increasing abdominal distension and bilateral lower limb pitting edema. He has no history of fever, abdominal pain, or altered level of consciousness. He is not currently taking any medications. Physical examination reveals moderate ascites and bilateral pitting edema. His vital signs are stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Cirrhotic ascites, uncomplicated: salt restriction + spironolactone with furosemide (ratio 100:40).

q: Patient with back pain, worsening at morning and improving within an hour after movement, positive schober test. What examination should be done next?
k: Ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27): young male, inflammatory back pain > 3 months, morning stiffness improving with activity.
r: AS heart lesion is aortic regurgitation, not mitral; the most common extra-articular feature is the eye.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0630).
kw: worsening at morning and improving within an hour after movement

q: man presents to ER with fever, rigors and chills He also reports back pain, he has history of drinking unpasteurized milk. What is the most appropriate lab test?
k: Brucellosis: Gram negative coccobacillus from raw milk or livestock.
r: Raw milk in the stem = Brucella; the first test is serology, not imaging.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0027).

q: A 44-year-old man complains of dyspnea on exertion. Heart auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the base of the heart. The intensity and duration of the murmur increase during inspiration. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Step 1: systolic or diastolic. Step 2: left or right (respiration).
r: Same timing and site for AR and PR; only the respiratory change separates them.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2836).
kw: early diastolic murmur at the base

q: type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy was found in the clinic waiting area drowsy and excessively sweating. A quick measurement of blood glucose revealed a low level. Which of the following is the most appropriate action to be taken?
k: Hypoglycaemia treatment depends on the ability to swallow.
r: "Drowsy" is not "unconscious": if the stem does not say unable to swallow or unresponsive, oral glucose wins.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1203).
kw: blood glucose revealed a low level

q: A female patient presents with features of Cushing's syndrome for 4 months. Laboratory tests show High cortisol 8am =840, 4pm= 500 High ACTH = 15 (high) TSH =4 (normal) What is the most likely diagnosis ?
r: High cortisol with high/normal-high ACTH = ACTH-dependent; mild ACTH rise = pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease); very high = ectopic.

q: 56 years old man post op , c/o hemoptysis and SOB ECG: Sinus tachycardia and a new finding of a right bundle branch block. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?
r: Post-op hemoptysis, dyspnoea, tachycardia, new RBBB = pulmonary embolism: CT pulmonary angiography.

q: A 45-year-old man presented to the ER with palpitations. Initially conscious and oriented. After some time, he became less responsive, and his BP dropped to 80/45 mmHg. ECG: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
k: SVT ladder, decided by stability first: Unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure): synchronized cardioversion.; Stable: vagal maneuvers (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage).; Then adenosine (rapid IV push, escalating dose).
r: The stem changes mid-way: 'initially conscious' then hypotensive and drowsy; the LATEST state (unstable) decides the answer.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0652).

q: Women came with weakness, ECG (image show Afib), CT : shows infraction HR 300 what is the cause of the stroke?
k: AF and stroke. ECG: irregularly irregular, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline; Mechanism: left atrial appendage stasis -> thrombus -> embolism; CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 -> anticoagulate
r: Irregularly irregular with no P waves = AF; regular sawtooth = flutter, whatever rate is quoted.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-1003).

q: A 20-year-old woman presented to the clinic with dysuria and suprapubic pain. No fever. Urine dipstick done (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Send culture and wait for results
k: UTI management by type. Uncomplicated cystitis, afebrile young woman: empiric antibiotics, no culture; Fever, flank pain (pyelonephritis): culture plus empiric antibiotics; Men, pregnancy, children, complicated or recurrent UTI: culture
r: Adding fever to this same stem changes the answer to culture plus empiric antibiotics.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0934).

q: Patient with meningitis the doctor did passive flexion of the patient neck which caused involuntary flexion of the hips and knees while his supine sign Name ?
r: Neck flexion causes hip and knee flexion = Brudzinski sign (Kernig = pain on knee extension with hip flexed).

q: 25-year-old college student came for a routine checkup. He does not have any active complaints. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur increase when the patient leans forward in full expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Diastolic murmurs: ARMS on the left (AR, MS) and PaRTS on the right (PR, TS).
r: If only one option is diastolic, the timing alone answers the question.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6732).

q: A woman was incidentally found to have high blood pressure. She reports being prescribed antihypertensive medications previously but failed to comply. What is the side effect if her condition is left untreated?
k: Target organ damage of untreated hypertension.
r: Pericarditis comes from uremia, not hypertension; if CKD were the stem, uremic pericarditis would fit.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0139).

q: 50 year old man came in for cancer screening, which of the following is the appropriate cancer for screening at this stage?
k: Average-risk screening: colon cancer is the one every adult gets.
r: Lung cancer screening needs a smoking history in the stem; without it, colon wins.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0305).

q: A 62-year-old woman has DVT for which she has started on Warfarin. A few weeks after, she fell down and developed a subdural hematoma that requires evacuation (see lab result). Test Result Normal Values INR 3.9 0.8-1.2 Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Fresh frozen plasma and vitamin K
r: ⚠ Warfarin bleed needing surgery: best is 4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K; among these options the key is FFP (fast reversal).

q: A 40-year-old man with a history of recurrent painful attacks affecting the right big toe, was diagnosed with gout and started on allopurinol. He is also a known case of psoriasis for several years. He presented to the clinic with recurrent joint pain affecting the right big toe, left ankle, and bilateral knees. He is using allopurinol regularly as prescribed but has no improvement in his joint pain. Examinations revealed he has active arthritis at the left ankle and knee joints bilaterally (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause for his joint pain?
r: Known psoriasis + new arthritis while gout is controlled = psoriatic arthritis.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0001).
kw: no improvement in his joint pain
active arthritis at the left ankle and knee joints bilaterally

q: A patient with chronic hepatitis C infection and cirrhosis presents with mildly elevated bilirubin( and other abnormal liver function tests which I can't remember) . What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
Observation and repeat liver function tests
k: Chronic HCV: treat virtually everyone with viremia.
r: Cirrhosis does not stop HCV treatment; it makes it more urgent, and surveillance continues after cure.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0532).

q: A patient presents with numbness, and MRI of the brain shows white matter sclerosis in the periventricular area. Which of the following will support the diagnosis?
k: MS diagnosis: clinical episodes + MRI dissemination in space and time; CSF supports.
r: Central lesion = MRI and CSF; peripheral nerve = nerve conduction studies.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6648).
kw: white matter sclerosis in the periventricular area

q: A 73-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by family members who noticed a change in her level of consciousness for 1 day. She is known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and liver cirrhosis. Examination reveals she is drowsy, with raised JVP, positive shifting dullness, and +2 lower limb edema (see lab results). Na: 125 Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Hyponatremia: first classify volume status.
r: Raised JVP + ascites + edema means diuretic, not fluids, even if the patient is drowsy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0332).
kw: raised JVP, positive shifting dullness, and +2 lower limb edema

q: A diabetic patient admitted to the hospital follows different Social media diets and asks for advice. What’s the most appropriate advice?
o: Avoid all Social media information completely
Follow diets shared on Social media
Refer to a registered dietitian / diabetes educator
k: Diabetes diet questions: the answer is structured education.
r: Options that forbid or ignore the patient's wishes are rarely right; refer to the qualified professional.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0642).

q: age not recalled male presented to the emergency department with icterus and jaundice. Serology showed: Hepatitis A: + Anti-HAV IgM — positive + Anti-HAV IgG — positive Hepatitis B: + Anti-HBs (surface antibody) — positive + HBsAg (surface antigen) — negative + Anti-HBc (core antibody) — negative + HBeAg (e antigen) — negative What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute hepatitis A with immunization against hepatitis B
Acute hepatitis A with previous hepatitis B infection
r: Anti-HAV IgM + = acute hepatitis A; anti-HBs + alone = immune to hepatitis B (vaccine), not active B.

q: child with DKA mother is worried about his kidney Which investigation to monitor kidney function annually ?
k: Diabetic nephropathy screening = albuminuria, yearly.
r: If the options list both urine microalbumin and urine albumin/creatinine ratio, pick the ratio.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0010).

q: Patient present with chronic diarrhea started 6 months ago, cbc showed macrocytic anemia ,folate and b12 both below range, stool ova and parasite negative, negative occult blood history of travel to india and thailand 1 year ago ,what is the diagnosis?
k: Read the deficiency pattern to localize malabsorption.
r: Travel to the tropics plus folate AND B12 deficiency = tropical sprue; celiac spares B12 and has no travel clue.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0055).

q: 62-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and ischemic stroke 1 month ago, presented to the Emergency Room complaining of central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours. She denied any dyspnea, palpitation, or change in consciousness. The patient is taking insulin, lisinopril, metoprolol, lipitor, and aspirin. Examination revealed she is in pain. She was started on oxygen, morphine, and sublingual nitroglycerin (see image). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: ACS with a contraindication to lysis: urgent invasive coronary angiography with PCI.
r: In ACS stems, a recent stroke, bleed or surgery is the clue that removes thrombolysis and makes the cath lab answer correct.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-4468).
kw: central stabbing continuous chest pain for 3 hours

q: A 54-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with an acute exacerbation of COPD. Examination reveals the use of accessory muscles of breathing, diminished gag reflex, decreased breath sounds with wheezing heard throughout both lung fields. Oxygen, glucocorticoids, antibiotics, and nebulizers are started (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Close observations for the next 4-6 hours
Increase oxygen to 100% by non-rebreather mask
r: COPD exacerbation with reduced consciousness / lost gag reflex: cannot protect airway -> intubate (NIV contraindicated).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0188).
kw: use of accessory muscles of breathing
Oxygen, glucocorticoids, antibiotics, and nebulizers are started

q: A 40-year-old woman is under treatment for a recurrent helicobacter-associated duodenal ulcer. She noticed that her stool is turned non-tarry black (see lab result). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg Heart rate 70 /min Test Result Normal Values Hb 152 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) What drug is likely to be the cause of the black stools?
k: Normal vitals + normal Hb + non-tarry black stool on ulcer treatment = bismuth effect, reassure.
r: If the stem gave tarry stool, tachycardia or a falling Hb, the answer would shift to rebleeding (melena), not a drug effect.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9146).
kw: treatment for a recurrent helicobacter-associated duodenal ulcer

q: which of the following mosquitoes should be used in surveillance of malaria?
r: Malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles: use it for surveillance.

q: Pt presented with cough and fever with a history of travel 1 week back Lab:Na is low 112 approximately What is diagnosis?
k: Atypical pneumonia clues.
r: Pneumonia + hyponatremia + diarrhea or confusion = Legionella; order the urinary antigen.

q: Patient with back pain, worsening at morning and improving within an hour after movement, positive schober test. What examination should be done next?
k: Ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27): young male, inflammatory back pain > 3 months, morning stiffness improving with activity.
r: AS heart lesion is aortic regurgitation, not mitral; the most common extra-articular feature is the eye.
