q: A 30-year-old man is brought by his family because of behavioral changes. He has episodes of emotional lability, lip smacking, and grimacing. Sometimes, following these episodes, he becomes agitated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Temporal lobe (focal impaired awareness) seizure: aura (epigastric rising feeling, deja vu, fear, smell) then staring + automatisms then postictal confusion.
r: Automatisms + postictal confusion = temporal lobe; automatisms without postictal phase in a child = absence.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-4683).

q: Patient has SOB and came to the ER, fluid was transudative. What is the etiology?
k: Transudate = pressure problem (pleura normal); exudate = pleural disease (inflammation, infection, malignancy).
r: Transudate in an exam stem almost always means heart failure; any inflammatory or malignant cause makes it an exudate.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0641).

q: 60-years-old female asthmatic and alcoholic presented with bone pain that prevents her from performing activities. BMI: 31. What indicates osteoporosis screening?
k: Osteoporosis screening: all women ≥65; younger postmenopausal women with risk factors.
r: Obesity protects bone; low BMI is the risk. Steroids count only if LONG term.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1002).

q: An elderly person presented with a history of sudden-onset unilateral hemiparesis and facial droop two days ago. neurological symptoms subsequently resolved completely. A CT scan of the brain revealed a small infarct in the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: TIA vs stroke is defined by tissue, not by time.
r: Symptoms fully resolved but infarct on CT = stroke; resolved with normal imaging = TIA.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6888).
kw: sudden-onset unilateral hemiparesis and facial droop
small infarct in the middle cerebral artery

q: A 60-something-vear-old man with known COPD, controlled with bronchodilators, comes for a routine follow-up. He quit smoking 12 years ago. His oxygen saturation ranges from 89% to 91%. What is the most appropriate management?
r: All COPD patients should receive pneumococcal (and annual influenza) vaccination; long-term oxygen is indicated only for resting SpO2 88% or less / PaO2 55 mmHg or less (up to 59 mmHg with cor pulmonale or haematocrit >55%).
n: مكرر من القديم (NOV-039).

q: A 68-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension is admitted with extensive anterior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). had successful angioplasty and stenting to left anterior descending artery. Aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol and enalapril were started. Cholesterol (HDL) 1.0 > 1.03 mmol/L Cholesterol (LDL) 3.36 <3.36 mmol/L Total Cholesterol 5.0 <5.1 mmol/L Triglycerides 2.2 <2.16 mmol/L Which of the following is recommended?
k: Four statin benefit groups (age over 21).
r: After any MI, ignore the "normal" lipid panel: high-intensity statin is always indicated.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0411).

q: Female patient in her 40s developed left-sided weakness. As a child she had joint pain (they described it, word close to migratory?) and required high-dose aspirin. Which of the following is the most likely underlying arrhythmia causing her symptoms?
k: Rheumatic fever → mitral stenosis → left atrial dilation → AF → embolic stroke.
r: Rheumatic history plus stroke: the link is AF from mitral stenosis, and the anticoagulant is warfarin, not a DOAC.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0406).
kw: fleet joint pain and required high-dose aspirin

q: Patient come with history of blood transfusion AST = 20 ALT = 22 Serology: HBsAg + HBcAb IgM - HBcAb IgG + HBsAb - HBeAg + What is the diagnosis?
k: Rule: read HBsAg (infected?), then HBcAb IgM vs IgG (acute vs chronic), then anti HBs (recovered or vaccinated).
r: Anti HBc tells natural infection from vaccine: positive core antibody can never come from vaccination.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-5055).

q: A researcher wants to assess the relationship between birth weight and cognitive function r= +0.8 What is the interpretation of correlation coefficient?
o: Inc Weight birth causes cognitive function to be low
Inc Weight birth increase cognitive development
r: r = +0.8 = strong positive correlation: as one increases the other increases (association, not proof of causation).

q: A 65-year-old man with a known history of cardiovascular disease presents to the emergency department with fever, generalized weakness, and hypotension following a recent infection. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. Hemodynamic monitoring reveals the following findings: Parameter Finding Central venous pressure (CVP) Decreased Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) Decreased Cardiac output (CO) Decreased Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) Increased Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO) Increased What is the most likely type of shock?
k: Shock type by hemodynamic profile: Hypovolemic: CO low, CVP/PCWP low, SVR high, SvO2 low; Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high, SvO2 low; Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR LOW, SvO2 high
r: The infection history is a distractor: only a HIGH cardiac output with LOW SVR makes it septic.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3306). Septic Shock = High CO (initially) & Low SVR

q: A 67-year-old man a known case of HCV cirrhosis admiked to Emergency Room with massive hematemesis. Variceal bleeding is suspected. On examina;on, he is drowsy with tense ascites (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH, Heart rate 86 /min Oxygen satura;on 95 % Test Result Normal Values Hb 8 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) INR 1.3 0.8- 1.2 Which of the following management op;ons has a great benefit in reducing this pa8ent mortality?
r: Variceal bleed in cirrhosis: octreotide + prophylactic IV ceftriaxone (reduces mortality) + endoscopy; the key here is the antibiotic.

q: A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of gastroesophageal reflux disease on pantoprazole is evaluated in the clinic because of a 4-month history of intermittent dysphagia for solids. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
k: GERD with any alarm feature: go straight to endoscopy.
r: Dysphagia for liquids flips the answer toward barium swallow then manometry; dysphagia for solids in a GERD patient means endoscopy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0661).

q: A 38-year-old woman has fever and headache for 2 days. On examination, she has a scattered petichiae over her body. Peripheral smear done (see image and lab results).Temperature 38.6 °C Test Result Normal Values Hb 112 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) Reticulocyte 5.6 0.2-1.2 % Platelets count 32 150-400 x 109/L Indirect bilirubin 48 3.2-12.1 mol/L Total bilirubin 76 3.5-16.5 mol/L Lactate dehydrogenase 690 60-160 IU/L APTT 33 30-40 sec. INR 1.0 0.8-1.2 Prothrombin time 10 10-13 sec Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Thrombocytopenia + MAHA + normal coagulation = TTP or HUS.
r: Schistocytes with low platelets and NORMAL coags = TTP: plasma exchange, avoid platelets.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0711).

q: Old pt with uncontrolled hypertension suddenly became confused. He can move his eyes up and down only, dilated pinpoint pupills, Where is the site of the lesion?
r: Hypertensive bleed with pinpoint pupils and only vertical eye movements = pontine haemorrhage.

q: Anorexia Nervosa Case admitted to the hospital for feeding. After 3 days, all labs were low. What is the cause?
k: Refeeding syndrome: Clue: malnourished patient + feeding started + low electrolytes within days; Low phosphate, low K, low Mg; Can cause arrhythmia, heart failure, weakness, seizures
r: The timing link (labs fall only after feeding begins) is what separates refeeding from pre existing malnutrition or malabsorption.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6358).

q: Patient in 50s came at follow up clinic k/c of DM on metformin 500 mg PID and gliclazide. HbAlc: 5.8 (normal value 5.6) what to do?
o: Tell him he is at a high risk for cardiovascular disease
k: Follow-up decisions by HbA1c on treatment: Target for most adults: < 7%; At or below target: no change, reassure, continue; Above target: intensify (increase dose or add agent)
r: Same HbA1c 5.8% but BP 149/90 on repeated readings flips the answer to adding an ACE inhibitor.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2276).

q: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for a 4-month history of dry cough, which began 4 months ago when she noted a paroxysmal onset of persistent coughing spells that make it difficult to carry on a conversation. She was initially diagnosed with allergic rhinitis and was started on a glucocorticoid nasal inhaler with no improvement. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable except for a history of dust allergies. Examination revealed normal vital signs, slight nasal congestion, and dry cough are noted during the examination. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and abdominal examination findings are unremarkable (see reports). Chest radiograph: Normal. Spirometry: Slightly reduced FEV/FVC ratio of 70% which increased after bronchodilator challenge by 20%. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?
k: Asthma diagnosis ladder. First: spirometry with bronchodilator; reduced FEV1/FVC with FEV1 rise of at least 12% and 200 mL after bronchodilator confirms asthma; Normal spirometry but high suspicion: methacholine challenge; Negative methacholine largely excludes asthma
r: Methacholine is the classic answer when spirometry is NORMAL; when reversibility is already shown, the diagnosis is made.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8227).

q: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing, muscle cramping, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. A diagnosis of acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia is established. Which of the following is the most expected laboratory abnormality?
o: Blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio is elevated > 20
Presence of dysmorphic red blood cell (RBC) and RBC cast
k: Prerenal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices: BUN/Cr: prerenal >20; ATN <15; FENa: prerenal <1%; ATN >2%; Urine Na: prerenal <20; ATN >40
r: Each wrong option here describes intrinsic renal disease; only the high BUN/Cr ratio fits intact tubules saving volume.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-7478).

q: A 59-year-old man is evaluated in the hospital for progressive shortness of breath and hypoxia 20 hours after undergoing surgery for colonic adenocarcinoma with known liver metastases (see report). CT angiography: Shows a right lower lobe pulmonary embolism. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
k: Acute PE treatment depends on stability.
r: If the stem gives low BP, the answer flips to alteplase; if it gives ESRD, it flips to unfractionated heparin.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0729).
kw: colonic adenocarcinoma with known liver metastases

q: A 61-year-old obese man presented with daytime somnolence, poor concentration, nocturia, and progressive shortness of breath. Examination reveals an obese patient with bilateral lower limb edema and normal vesicular breath sounds on lung auscultation. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
k: OSA: suspect clinically, confirm with polysomnography.
r: "Establish the diagnosis" asks for the cause (sleep study), not the consequence (echo).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8447).

q: A 35-year-old Indian man presents to the Emergency Department with lethargy, weight loss, and headache for 3 months. He has a history of contact with a tuberculosis patient several years ago. His neurological and ophthalmologic examination are unremarkable. He has a positive polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and diuretics
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and acyclovir
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and dexamethasone
k: TB meningitis = anti-TB therapy plus steroid.
r: Same four drugs as pulmonary TB, but CNS involvement adds dexamethasone.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4470).

q: A 76-year-old man, known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 meters. He denied any history of syncope, chest pain, or palpitation. Precordium examination revealed a forceful apex beat and a crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids = aortic stenosis. Classic triad: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope Signs: slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, heaving apex Elderly: degenerative calcification;
r: An elderly man with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia), progressive exertional dyspnea , a forceful (heaving) apex from LV pressure overload and a crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids has calcific aortic stenosis.
n: مكرر من القديم (NOV-0845).

q: A 22-year-old man presented to the Emergency Room with left leg swelling and pain that started 2 days ago and is getting worse. It involves the whole left leg. He also complains of chest tightness and shortness of breath. Examination reveals left lower limb pitting edema extending to the thigh (see report). ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this time?
r: DVT with features of PE: start anticoagulation now with heparin (UFH/LMWH), warfarin later.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0135).
kw: chest tightness and shortness of breath
pitting edema extending to the thigh

q: A 70-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department complaining of increasing shortness of breath and a productive cough for the past 5 months. He has been a smoker for over 50 years. Over the course of 5 months, he complained of malaise, night sweats, fever, and has lost 10 kg over the last 3 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Rule: chronic cough + weight loss + heavy smoking in an elderly patient = lung cancer.
r: If TB is offered with a TB exposure clue (prison, homeless, apical cavity), TB beats cancer; a pure heavy smoker picture favours carcinoma.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2850).

q: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent seizures and cognitive dysfunction. She is subsequently diagnosed with glioblastoma multiforme (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatremia?
k: Causes of SIADH: CNS: tumors, trauma, meningitis, stroke, hemorrhage; Lung: small cell carcinoma, pneumonia, TB; Drugs: SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide
r: Any intracranial pathology plus low sodium in a euvolemic patient: think SIADH; cerebral salt wasting is the alternative only if the patient is volume depleted.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-7886).

q: A man in his 50s with a 10-year history of diabetes mellitus presents to the clinic for follow-up. His history and physical examination are unremarkable, and his vital signs are normal. Laboratory investigations show a normal urea level (5), serum creatinine of 130, and urinalysis positive for glucose (2+) and protein (2+). Which of the following medications is most appropriate to slow the progression of his condition?
k: Diabetic kidney disease: proteinuria or albuminuria means start RAAS blockade.
r: Normal blood pressure does not cancel the ACE inhibitor: it is given for the proteinuria; if the stem mentions ACE-inhibitor cough, switch to an ARB.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-7921).

q: A patient presents with diarrhea and weight loss. On examination, he has mouth ulcers, with no other systemic symptoms. What is the initial investigation?
o: Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) test for celiac disease
r: Diarrhoea, weight loss, mouth ulcers -> screen for celiac with tTG-IgA first; biopsy confirms.

q: Patient presents with 10 years history of HTN, and was diagnosed with DM and Dyslipidemia 5 months ago. He has a long-standing tension headache for which he takes paracetamol occasionally (2-3 times per month). Vitals: BP: 173/93 mmHg. Labs: Creatinine and BUN are both high. What is the most likely cause of his Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)?
r: Headache with BP 173/93 in a known hypertensive: uncontrolled hypertension is the cause.

q: A 55-year-old man presents with bright red blood per rectum. He has lost approximately 500 mL of blood over the past 2 hours, BP (85/55). What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with intravenous pantoprazole

Transfusion packed RBC 2 and iv crystalloid
k: GI bleeding: resuscitate first, localise second.
r: If one option is resuscitation and the others are diagnostic tests, an actively bleeding patient gets resuscitation first.

q: New Q 45 year old man came to clinic due to abnormal blood test, he is medically free , does not complain of anything ( totally normal) physical exam is normal, lab test was consistent with IDA ?
r: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man > 40 with no obvious cause: endoscopy (upper and lower) to exclude GI cancer.

q: A patient with mild dementia has requested to drive a car, but his family is concerned for his safety. How should the patient be evaluated?
r: Mild dementia and driving: assess with a formal on-road driving test.
n: On Road is Even Better Than CDR

q: a 67 years old male suffering from palpitation& irritability insomnia for 3 months MPHx afib depression HTN takes enalorpil fluoxetine amiodarone PE unremarkable what is the best next step in mx?

q: A 20 year old woman presented to the clinic with dysuria and suprapupic pain, no fever Urine analysis: Appears Turbid and yellow Positive nitrates Lymphocytes 12 What to do ?

q: A patient had an episode of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. He has no personal or family history of related diseases. He has been on warfarin for three months and is tolerating it very well. His current INR is 2.5. What is the appropriate management?

q: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Room with a 2-day history of headache, fever, photosensitivity, lethargy, and skin eruption. r: "Most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis" of meningitis = LP; "first action" in a purpuric child or adult = antibiotics.

q: A 55-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia on chemotherapy presents to the Emergency Room with a 1-day history of fever. His physical examination is unremarkable. His chest radiograph and urinalysis are normal. Blood and urinary cultures are taken (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Febrile neutropenia in haematological malignancy: IV antibiotics first, add others only for indications.
r: Day 1 of fever = IV antibiotics only; antifungal or antiviral options upfront are the trap.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-8122).

q: A 54 years old man presented with episodes of pallor, palpitations, and sweating. These episodes last for 20 minutes. During these episodes, his blood pressure reaches 180/100. The episodes are resistant to anti hypertension medications. Whats the most definitive management?
r: Episodic headache, palpitations, sweating, high BP = phaeochromocytoma: laparoscopic adrenalectomy after alpha-blockade.

q: A diabetic patient admitted to the hospital follows different social media diets and asks for advice. What's the most appropriate advice?
o: Follow diets shared on social media
Refer to a verified diet resources
r: Advise reliable, verified diet sources (dietitian/approved guidelines), not social media.

q: A patient came after a motor vehicle accident (MVA). He looks extremely pale and cold, with low blood pressure (hypotension). There is mild abdominal tenderness but no visible external bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
r: Trauma, pale, cold, hypotensive without external bleeding = hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock from internal bleeding.

q: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of fever and dysuria. She was treated for a urinary tract infection 6 months ago. Her mother asks how to reduce the risk of recurrent UTIs, Which of the following is the most important recommendation to help prevent future urinary tract infections?
r: Recurrent UTI in a toddler: treat constipation and good toilet habits (bladder-bowel dysfunction) is the key preventive step.
n: We Need To Revise Why Not “B” (Question) (Please Remember , This Is Pediatric , NOT Adult)

q: patient in his early twenties presents with intermittent diarrhea, sometimes, and abdominal pain. Colonoscopy with biopsy reveals skip lesions, areas of inflammation alternating with normal mucosa, and strictures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Skip lesions, strictures, transmural = Crohn's disease (UC is continuous from the rectum).

q: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with acute chest syndrome. While receiving a blood transfusion, he suddenly develops fever and chills. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
k: Any new symptom during a transfusion: STOP the transfusion first.
r: The sickle cell and acute chest syndrome background is a distractor; the lead-in is about what happens during the transfusion.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2303).

q: 17-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department for polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and an unintentional weight loss over the past month. He has abdominal pain and drowsiness for the last 21 hours. Hsi medical and family history are unremarkable. He is not of any medications. On physical examination, he looks sick with dry mucous membrane, tachypnea, and tachycardia with clear chest auscultation. Abdominal examination shows diffuse mild tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Intravenous 0.9% saline is initiated. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia 120/min. Chest radiograph si normal (see lab results). Blood pressure 95/53 mmHg. Heart rate 119 /min Respiratory rate 20 /min Temperature 37.2 C°Oxygen saturation 95 % BMI 19 kg/m2 Sodium 130 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 4.4 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Chloride 96 97-108 mmol/L Bicarbonate 10 21-28 mmol/L Blood urea nitrogen 15 2.8 to 8.9 mmol/L Creatinine 115 44-115 mol/L Random Glucose 25 3.9-5.5 mmol/L. ABG HCO3-10 22-28 mmol/L рН 7.10 7.36- 7.45. RBC 5 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x1012/L (Female) Hb 130 130- 170 gL/ (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) WBC 144.5-10.5×109/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?

q: A 67-year-old male presents with palpitations, irritability, and insomnia for the past 3 months. His medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation, depression, and hypertension. His current medications include enalapril, fluoxetine, and amiodarone. Physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Any patient on amiodarone with new symptoms: check thyroid function (and LFT, chest for lung toxicity).
r: Psychiatric looking symptoms plus amiodarone (or lithium) = check the thyroid first.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3273).

q: 55? Male, known case of AFib, HTN, depression, on amiodarone, enalapril, fluoxetine. Presents with 3 months of irritability, insomnia, palpitations. PE: Normal, vitals: 130/70, HR 76, O2 96%. Most appropriate next step?
k: Amiodarone and the thyroid: check TFTs at baseline and every 6 months, and whenever symptoms appear.
r: A new psychiatric-looking complaint in a patient on amiodarone is thyroid until proven otherwise.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6159).

q: Typical reactive arthritis case, arthritis after 2or 3 weeks from gastroenteritis managment?
r: Reactive arthritis after gastroenteritis: NSAIDs first line.

q: elderly with delirum and now agitated what to give?
r: Agitated delirium in an elderly patient: low-dose haloperidol; avoid benzodiazepines (worsen delirium).

q: Pt (he was young) has pneumonia 4 days ago and they give him treatment then discharge. Now present with no relief of S&S ( something like that ) and he was drowses. The put him on O2 and the O2 was 85%. What is the most appropriate next step?
r: Pneumonia with drowsiness and SpO2 85% despite oxygen: respiratory failure with low consciousness -> intubation.

q: A 60-year-old man with known liver cirrhosis presents to the Emergency Department with progressively increasing abdominal distension and bilateral lower limb pitting edema. He has no history of fever, abdominal pain, or altered level of consciousness. He is not currently taking any medications. Physical examination reveals moderate ascites and bilateral pitting edema. His vital signs are stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Cirrhotic ascites, uncomplicated: salt restriction + spironolactone with furosemide.

q: A 69-year-old man is evaluated during a routine examination.He reports his blood pressure to be around 150/84 mmHg on several occasions.He is known to have mild benign prostatic hyperplasia, and hyperlipidemia for which he is taking simvastatin.Cardiac examination is normal, and the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable.Laboratory studies show a normal chemistry panel;a urine dipstick demonstrates no blood or protein.An electrocardiogram shows no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy Blood pressure 147/86 mmHg Heart rate 80/min Respiratory rate 14/min Temperature 36.6°C Oxygen saturation 95% BMI 31 kg/m2 Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat blood pressure determination in 4 months
k: Mild hypertension without target organ damage in an older patient: lifestyle (weight loss, salt, exercise) first in this key; drugs if it fails.
r: Make the same patient younger than 60 (as in the 50-year-old sister recall) or add LVH, proteinuria or raised creatinine and the answer flips to starting a drug.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-3365).

q: A patient presents with progressively worsening bilateral lower limb weakness and urinary retention. Neurological examination reveals increased muscle tone and brisk deep tendon reflexes in both lower limbs. What is the most likely underlying cause?
r: Spastic weakness with brisk reflexes (UMN) + retention = spinal cord compression; cauda equina gives LMN (flaccid, areflexic).

q: A 26-year-old man with type I diabetes mellitus on insulin presents to the clinic for regular follow-up. He is asymptomatic (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Diabetes + albuminuria (micro or macro) = ACE inhibitor (ARB if not tolerated).
r: The lab card is hidden in this recall; the clue is "asymptomatic diabetic on follow-up, most appropriate treatment" = proteinuria = ACE inhibitor.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0927).

q: A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with productive cough, fever, and dyspnea for 3 days. Chest examination reveals evidence of consolidation at the right lower lung field. Baseline laboratory studies, two blood cultures, and sputum samples for cultures and gram stain are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial regimen?

q: Patient with wood stick injury question mentioned it involves the sclera and the eye was bleeding and patient was unable to move his eye and in severe pain. On examination, he has Teardrop pupil and Cloudy anterior chamber What is the type of injury? (It Was Metallic Object In Another Recall)

q: In a case of anencephaly , the doctor advised an abortion. The mother agreed to the procedure, but the father refused . What is the most appropriate action?
o: Consent taken from both mother and father
k: Consent rules to separate: Competent adult procedure on herself: patient alone consents Termination for lethal fetal anomaly (this recall): consent of both spouses Life-threatening emergency: treat without waiting for co
r: This recall is keyed to obtaining consent from both parents, in line with the local regulation that termination of pregnancy for a lethal fetal anomaly such as anencephaly requires the agreement of both spouses. When they disagree, the physician should counsel both, explain the diagnosis and prognos
x: A. The father's refusal alone is not the deciding factor; the issue is that consent for this procedure requires both parents. | B. For a procedure on her own body (for example surgery for an incomplete abortion), the competent woman alone consents; but in this recall termination for fetal anomaly is keyed as needing both spouses. | C. The doctor advises and counsels but never decides on behalf of competent patients in an elective procedure.

q: A hypertensive patient was prescribed hydralazin by his physician. However, due to a medication error , the nurse administered hydroxyzine instead. Which of the following is the most appropriate strategy to prevent this type of error from occurring in the future?
o: Write medications using Tall Man lettering
Use both written and verbal prescribing methods
Use brand names instead of generic names
Always include the dosage of the medications when prescribing
k: Look-alike, sound-alike drug errors: use Tall Man lettering. Examples: hydrALAZINE/hydrOXYzine, DOPamine/DOBUTamine, predniSONE/prednisoLONE Other measures: separate storage, barcode scanning, read-back of verbal orders
r: Hydralazine and hydroxyzine are a classic look-alike, sound-alike pair. Tall Man lettering (hydrALAZINE versus hydrOXYzine) capitalises the differing letters so the names cannot be misread, and it is the recommended system-level safeguard for exactly this error.
x: B. Written and verbal prescribing: verbal orders add sound-alike risk rather than removing it; verbal orders are discouraged except in emergencies. | C. Brand names instead of generic: brand names can also look alike, and generic prescribing is the standard; brand names do not fix the confusion. | D. Always include the dosage: good prescribing practice, but both drugs share similar doses (for example 25 mg), so the dose would not reveal the mix-up.

q: Patient with strong history of breast cancer come for screening , she request BRCA gene testing , after 2 says her sister asked about results of all the genetic testing she requested ,what will you do ?
o: Tell her only if it is positive , to support her sister
k: Confidentiality applies to relatives too. Disclose only with the patient's consent Encourage the patient to inform at-risk relatives herself Offer relatives their own genetic counselling and testing Exceptions to confide

x: B. Tell her only if positive: disclosing selectively still breaches confidentiality, and refusing only when negative effectively reveals the result anyway.

x: A. Refuse her: punishes her for exercising autonomy and exposes her to unintended pregnancy; refusal is justified only for a true medical contraindication. | B. Refer her to another doctor: abandons a reasonable request you can meet yourself; referral is for care outside your competence or a genuine conscientious objection.

kw: refused pelvic examination and screening for STD and Pap smear
x: A. Refuse her: denies effective contraception and risks unplanned pregnancy; refusal is justified only by a true contraindication. | B. Refer her to another physician: abandons a request you can safely meet; referral fits care outside your competence. | C. q: The treating physician has decided that a pediatric patient is a candidate for DNR (Do Not Resuscitate). Which of the following is true about DNR?

Sharing with the parents the availability of the DNR decision
It's made by one consultant and 3 specialists
k: Saudi DNR policy essentials. Decided by 3 consultants (including the treating consultant) Based on medical futility, documented in the file Family informed; consent not required Reviewed if the condition changes
r: Under the Saudi Ministry of Health DNR policy, a Do Not Resuscitate order is a medical decision that must be agreed upon by three consultants , including the treating consultant, who document that resuscitation would be futile. This safeguard keeps the decision from resting on a single physician. Fa

x: B. Presenting DNR to the parents as an available option to accept or refuse misrepresents the policy: the family is informed after the medical decision, it is not theirs to take. | C. One consultant plus three specialists is not the required composition; the policy calls for three consultants. | D. A DNR made by the attending physician alone lacks the required consensus of three consultants.

q: A 27-year-old man is scheduled for a tonsillectomy. He searches for a highly reputed surgeon. Decreased patient safety with increased surgical risk
Lower healthcare costs due to fewer mistakes
Shorter operative time due to efficiency

Human factors such as inattention and loss of situational awareness are a major cause of intraoperative errors, so operating with this surgeon means decreased patient safety and increased surgical risk , regardl

Lower costs from fewer mistakes is the opposite of what is expected: inattention increases errors, complications and costs. | D. Shorter operative time from efficiency is not expected; a distracted surgeon is less efficient and more error prone.

q: A patient with diabetes and hypertension on lisinopril is admitted for surgery; after the operation, he is transferred to the surgical ward and given only IV heparin , without continuation or documentation of his chronic lisinopril therapy; which of the following represents the critical mistake in this scenario?

q: 150 child , 30 developed food poisoning attack rate is ?
k: Attack rate = new cases ÷ population at risk during the outbreak × 100. Denominator = everyone exposed, not only the healthy ones Secondary attack rate = cases among contacts ÷ susceptible contacts (exclude the primary c
r: Attack rate = number who became ill ÷ number of people exposed (at risk) × 100. Here 30 ill out of 150 exposed children: 30/150 = 0.2 = 20% . Attack rate is the cumulative incidence used for outbreaks with a short, defined exposure such as food poisoning.
x: A. 15% would need about 22 or 23 cases out of 150; it does not match 30/150. | B. 10% would be 15 out of 150, or wrongly dividing 15 by 150; it halves the true number of cases. | D. 25% would need 37 or 38 cases, or comes from dividing ill by the well (30/120) instead of by everyone exposed.

x: A. Artificial tears: for dry eye or mild irritation with normal vision; they would only delay diagnosis of a vision threatening cause here. | B. Antiviral drops: for confirmed herpes simplex keratitis (dendritic ulcer on fluorescein); you need slit lamp examination first, and starting drops blindly is wrong. | C. Topical antibiotics: for bacterial conjunctivitis with purulent discharge and normal vision; the watery discharge plus visual loss and photophobia point away from it.

q: A new study was conducted to investigate the effect of HIV on mortality . The target group was recruited from hospitals and followed for 10 years to compare mortality between negative and positive HIV patients. What does ethics impose on this research ?

q: A patient with a "Do Not Resuscitate" ( DNR ) order was transferred to another hospital . What is the most accurate statement?

q: Pregnant lady which vaccine contraindicated ?

Placental issue: causes later complications such as abruption, growth restriction or late fetal death, not repeated losses at 6 weeks. | C. Genetic/genital infection: chromosomal abnormality is the most common cause of a single sporadic early miscarriage, and infection is not an accepted cause of recurrent loss; neither fits the recurrent pattern keyed here.

The definitive treatment is to end the pregnancy by delivery after maternal stabilization (magnesium s

Option not recalled; no basis to choose it.

q: A 34-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation is evaluated for a severe headache . Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Neurologic and cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Plasma exchange: first line for TTP (severe thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, neurologic signs, often normal liver enzymes and no hypertension); in pregnancy related HELLP the cure is delivery. | D. q: A 27-year-old woman presents with chronic pelvic pain and urinary urgency . The pain is relieved by voiding . She underwent laparoscopy, which ruled out endometriosis . What is the most appropriate next step?
k: Chronic pelvic pain: follow the symptom that relieves or triggers the pain. Cyclic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia: endometriosis (laparoscopy) Pain with bladder filling, relieved by voiding, urgency/frequency
r: Chronic pelvic pain with urinary urgency that is relieved by voiding , after laparoscopy has ruled out endometriosis , is the picture of interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome). The bladder is the source, so the next step is referral to urology for evaluation (urinalysis and culture to exclude
x: B. Hysteroscopy: evaluates the uterine cavity for abnormal bleeding, polyps, submucosal fibroids or septum; it does not assess bladder pain. | C. Colonoscopy: right when pelvic pain comes with bowel symptoms (rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, pain relieved by defecation as in IBS); here pain is relieved by voiding.

q: A 67-year-old woman presents for cervical cancer screening. She has a history of normal Pap smear results over the past 10 years . What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue Pap smear screening every 3 years
k: Cervical cancer screening (average risk). Start at 21 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years 30 to 65: co-test or primary HPV every 5 years (or cytology every 3) Stop after 65 if adequate negative prior screening History of CI
r: She is 67 years old (older than 65) with normal Pap results over the past 10 years , which counts as adequate negative prior screening. Cervical cancer screening stops after age 65 in women with adequate negative screening and no history of high grade lesions. Continuing screening adds no benefit at
kw: normal Pap smear results over the past 10 years
x: B. Pap every 3 years: the schedule for ages 21 to 29 (or 30 to 65 with cytology alone); it does not apply after 65 with negative history. | C. Annual Pap smear: not recommended at any age for average risk women; intervals are 3 to 5 years. | D. HPV testing: primary HPV or co-testing every 5 years is used between 30 and 65; after 65 with adequate negative screening no further testing is needed.

q: A pregnant woman in her first trimester presents with dyspnea . What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Reassure her that dyspnea is a normal physiological change during pregnancy due to increased blood volume.
Explain that it is due to physiological anemia of pregnancy and advise her to increase her intake of iron-rich foods.
k: Physiological dyspnea of pregnancy. Common from the first trimester Main driver: progesterone increases respiratory drive and tidal volume (mild respiratory alkalosis) Blood volume rises 40 to 45% by 32 to 34 weeks Red f
r: Breathlessness in early pregnancy without other alarming features is a common physiological change, so the appropriate advice is reassurance. Pregnancy brings major cardiorespiratory changes, including blood volume rising from about 6 weeks and increased ventilation, and many women feel short of bre
x: B. Physiological anemia of pregnancy: is a dilutional effect (plasma rises more than red cells) that does not usually cause dyspnea, and iron rich food advice would be for true iron deficiency, not this complaint.

q: A woman presents with amenorrhea for 9 months . Her evaluation is otherwise normal, except for an elevated Labs:- serum FSH level of 60 IU/L. LH 60 Testosterone, TSH ARE normal Which of the following long term complications is she most at risk of developing?
k: High FSH/LH + amenorrhea = ovarian failure = low estrogen = bone and heart risk. High FSH, high LH, low estrogen: POI / menopause, risk osteoporosis Normal or high estrogen, anovulation (PCOS): risk endometrial hyperplas
r: Secondary amenorrhea for 9 months with FSH 60 and LH 60 (both high) and normal TSH and testosterone means the ovaries have failed: hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, i.e. premature ovarian insufficiency in a young woman. The defining hormonal problem is estrogen deficiency , and the classic long term c
x: A. Endometrial cancer is driven by unopposed estrogen (anovulation as in PCOS, obesity, estrogen-only HRT); here estrogen is low, so the endometrium is not stimulated. | B. Ovarian cancer risk rises with incessant ovulation, nulliparity and BRCA mutations; ovarian failure does not raise it. | D. Fourth option not recalled; any choice not linked to estrogen deficiency would not fit this hormone picture.

q: Pregnant woman BMI 37 , will do total hysterectomy what is the best VTE prophylaxis

r: This woman stacks major VTE risk factors: pregnancy (a hypercoagulable state), obesity (BMI 37) and major pelvic surgery (hysterectomy) . High risk surgical patients need pharmacological prophylaxis, and LMWH is the agent of choice in pregnancy and the puerperium because it does not cross the placen
x: B. Compression stockings alone are for patients with low risk or a contraindication to anticoagulation (active bleeding, high bleeding risk); with this many risk factors they are an adjunct to LMWH.

q: Missed abortion at 8 weeks what is the management:

Expectant management is not offered, so medical evacuation with misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 analogue that ripens the cervix and ca
x: B. Hysterectomy is never a treatment for miscarriage; it is reserved for life threatening hemorrhage not controlled by other means. | C. Methotrexate is for an ectopic pregnancy (stable, unruptured, criteria met) or for some gestational trophoblastic disease, not an intrauterine miscarriage. | D. Hypertonic saline instillation is an obsolete second trimester termination method with serious risks; it has no role at 8 weeks.

q: 39wks gestation Spontaneus rupture for 24 hours ; everything else is normal. What is the next step:

The risk of chorioamnionitis and neonatal infection increases with time from rupture, and at term there is no benefit to prolonging the pregnancy, so with a cephalic fetus and otherwise normal findings the next step is inducti
x: A. Conservative (expectant) management is an option only for a short period after term PROM, or is the standard for preterm PROM (PPROM) without infection where fetal maturity is the aim; after 24 hours at term it raises infection risk.

q: 21 years old female , complains of heavy menstrual bleeding for the previous 2 years. Low hb There is US pic of uterus What is the diagnosis:

r: A young woman with heavy menstrual bleeding for 2 years causing anemia and an ultrasound showing a uterine lesion fits uterine leiomyoma (fibroid). Fibroids, especially submucosal ones, enlarge the endometrial surface and impair contraction, causing heavy regular periods; ultrasound is the initial i

Ovarian cysts are adnexal masses that usually cause pain or no symptoms, not heavy regular menstrual bleeding with a uterine lesion. | C. Endometrial cancer typically presents with postmenopausal bleeding in older women with estrogen excess; very unlikely at 21.

q: female with vulvar pain, on examination there is an ulcer in labia minora , ragged edges , necrotic center , and regional lymphadenopathy (pic provided) What is the Diagnosis?

Think HIV when there is fever, generalized nodes and opportunistic infections such as oral candidiasis. | C. Genital herpes (HSV) would show multiple small painful shallow ulcers on an erythematous base.

q: A 28-year-old woman complains of pelvic pressure and heavy bleeding .after marriage . On examination, she has pelvic tenderness . What is the diagnosis?

r: This recall's key is PID because of the young age (28) , onset after marriage (new sexual exposure) and pelvic tenderness . Pelvic pressure is nonspecific and occurs in subacute PID, and abnormal or heavy uterine bleeding is reported in a substantial share of PID patients. Adenomyosis is less likely

Choose it for a nulliparous woman with the 3 Ds or a chocolate cyst on ultrasound.

q: Baby delivered dead at 38 wks ( Stillbirth case). Placenta and baby appear normal Which of the following is best to sent for investigations for chromosomal analysis ?

r: After a stillbirth, fetal cells in blood and skin may be nonviable, so culture often fails. Placental tissue (a sample of the chorionic plate near the cord insertion) has the highest yield of viable cells for karyotype or chromosomal microarray after delivery, even when the placenta looks normal, be
x: A. A segment of umbilical cord is an acceptable additional sample, but it gives a lower yield of viable cells than placental tissue. | B. Amniotic fluid (by amniocentesis) is the best sample before delivery, when the fetal death is diagnosed in utero; after the baby is delivered it is no longer available. | C. Fetal cord blood is often clotted and contains no viable dividing cells after fetal death, so it frequently fails to culture.

q: Question about 30 years G2p1 with past hx of pph and now 50% singlton pregnancy What the risk of pph in her current pregnancy

x: B. Multiple pregnancy overdistends the uterus and causes atony, but this pregnancy is a singleton; choose it when twins are described. | C. Grand multiparity (usually 5 or more births) is a risk factor, but she is only para 1. | D. Advanced maternal age (35 or older) raises PPH risk; at 30 she is not in that group.

q: Patient with ovarian cancer asking what is the best form of contraception?

r: Ovarian cancer is Category 1 (no restriction) for combined hormonal contraception in the medical eligibility criteria, because combined pills do not worsen ovarian cancer and in fact long-term use lowers ovarian cancer risk. The compiler's key is the OCP as a safe, highly effective method while the
x: A. The vaginal ring is also combined hormonal contraception and has the same eligibility category; it is not wrong medically, but the classic expected answer in this recall is the OCP. | B. Male condoms are safe for anyone but have a much higher typical-use failure rate, so they are not the best form when an effective hormonal method is allowed.

q: A 25-year-old woman, known to have a left ovarian cyst , presented to the Emergency Room with 3 hours of severe left lower quadrant pain associated with nausea. Ultrasound Doppler: Diminished blood flow toward the left ovary . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?

x: A. Conservative management: delay leads to ovarian necrosis and loss; conservative care fits an uncomplicated simple cyst with normal flow. | B. Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours: wastes the window to salvage the ovary; repeat imaging is for a stable, asymptomatic simple cyst. | D. Ultrasound-guided drainage: does not untwist the pedicle and simple cysts recur; it has no role in torsion.

q: A woman in her thirties had a Pap smear 3 years ago that was negative . She now asks about cervical cancer screening. What is the recommended screening?

k: Cervical screening (average risk): Under 21: no screening 21 to 29: Pap (cytology) every 3 years 30 to 65: Pap every 3 years, HPV every 5 years, or co-test every 5 years Over 65 with adequate negative history: stop After
r: For a woman in her thirties with a negative last Pap, the accepted screening intervals are cytology alone every 3 years , primary HPV testing every 5 years, or co-testing every 5 years. Of the listed options only Pap smear every 3 years matches a recommended schedule.

x: A. HPV testing every year alone: primary HPV testing is done every 5 years from age 30 (25 in some guidelines), not yearly. | C. Co-testing every year: co-testing is every 5 years; annual screening adds harm without benefit. | D. No further screening: screening continues to 65 provided prior results are adequate and negative.

q: A female with a history of ectopic pregnancy is asking about the chance of recurrence in a future pregnancy. What is the chance of recurrence?
k: Ectopic pregnancy recurrence and risk factors. General population: about 1 to 2% of pregnancies After one ectopic: about 10 to 15% After two or more: about 25% or higher Strongest risk factor: previous ectopic; commonest
r: After one previous ectopic pregnancy the risk of recurrence in a later pregnancy is about 10 to 15% , which falls within the 6 to 15% option. It rises further (around 25% or more) after two ectopics, so early ultrasound is advised in every future pregnancy.
x: A. 1-5%: closer to the background rate of ectopic pregnancy in the general population (about 1 to 2%), not the risk after a previous ectopic. | C. 50-60%: greatly overstates the risk; most women with a prior ectopic go on to have an intrauterine pregnancy. | D. (forgot): the option was not recalled; the accepted figure of about 10 to 15% still points to 6 to 15%.

q: A 25-year-old woman was diagnosed with a complete abortion at 10 weeks of gestation. She is a heavy smoker , smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day, and was not taking any folic acid or dietary supplements. Which of the following is the most likely risk factor that caused the miscarriage?
o: Smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day
k: Miscarriage risk factors. Most common cause overall: fetal chromosomal abnormality Maternal age over 35 and prior miscarriage Smoking, alcohol, cocaine, heavy caffeine Uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid disease, antiphosphol
r: Of the options, heavy smoking (over 20 cigarettes a day) is the identifiable, established risk factor for first-trimester miscarriage. Nicotine and carbon monoxide cause placental vasoconstriction and uteroplacental insufficiency, raising the risk of miscarriage, growth restriction and abruption.
x: A. Diet low in carotene: not an established cause of miscarriage. | B. Diet low in folic acid: folate deficiency mainly raises the risk of neural tube defects; it is not the main miscarriage risk here. | C. No known risk factor: most sporadic early losses are chromosomal, but this stem gives a clear modifiable risk factor, so this is not the best answer.

q: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 had an uneventful pregnancy and went into spontaneous vaginal delivery. She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g. After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in managing this patient?

Send blood tests and manage accordingly
Take her to the operating room for surgical management

r: Heavy bleeding after placental delivery is primary postpartum hemorrhage, an obstetric emergency where the first actions are to call for help (mobilize the team) and secure blood by cross-matching , alongside checking uterine tone, IV access and uterotonics. Among the options, this is the initial st
kw: After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily
x: A. Emergency O negative transfusion is for massive hemorrhage with instability when cross-matched blood is not yet available; it is not the first step in a patient not yet assessed. | B. Sending blood tests and waiting to 'manage accordingly' delays active resuscitation; labs are drawn while the team acts, not before. | C. Theatre (surgical management) is for PPH that fails uterine massage, uterotonics and balloon tamponade, or for retained tissue or tears needing repair under anesthesia.

q: A 33-year-old G3 at 24 weeks of gestation presents with vaginal discharge and PPROM is assessed by sterile speculum examination. Which protein helps diagnose PPROM?

PPROM is primarily diagnosed clinically by sterile spe
x: A. Placental protein 14 (glycodelin) is a decidual/endometrial protein not used to diagnose ROM; do not confuse it with placental protein 12 (IGFBP-1), which is the other validated rupture test besides PAMG-1. | B. Placental alkaline phosphatase is a placental enzyme (and tumor marker) with no role in diagnosing membrane rupture. | C. Placental vasopressinase degrades ADH and explains transient diabetes insipidus of pregnancy; it is not used to diagnose PPROM.

q: 40 years old woman with lower abdominal pain , no bleeding , pregnancy test was negative on examination cervical motion tenderness and closed What the diagnosis
k: PID diagnosis (minimum criteria in a sexually active woman with pelvic pain): Cervical motion tenderness, OR uterine tenderness, OR adnexal tenderness Supportive: fever, mucopurulent discharge, raised WBC or CRP Always r
r: Lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test (ectopic excluded) is the classic picture of pelvic inflammatory disease. Cervical motion tenderness reflects inflammation of the upper genital tract and is a minimum clinical criterion for PID; a closed cervix and no
x: B. UTI: causes dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain; it does not produce cervical motion tenderness on pelvic examination. | C. Cystitis: a lower UTI with suprapubic pain and urinary symptoms, again without cervical motion tenderness. | D. Forgot (recaller says it was not ectopic): ectopic would require a positive pregnancy test; endometriosis, if offered, fits cyclic pain, dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia, not acute pain with CMT.

q: woman in her 30s presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure. On examination, an enlarged uterus with irregular a palpable mass in the uterine fundus is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

r: A woman in her 30s with heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure and an enlarged, irregular uterus with a palpable fundal mass has a leiomyoma (uterine fibroid). Uterine cancer: classically postmenopausal bleeding in an older woman with risk factors (obesity, diabetes, unopposed

q: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic complaining of heavy menstrual bleeding lasting more than 10 days . Pregnancy test is negative , and pelvic ultrasound is normal . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

r: Heavy bleeding for more than 10 days with a negative pregnancy test and a normal ultrasound is acute abnormal uterine bleeding without structural cause, in a patient not described as unstable. Medical therapy comes first, and tranexamic acid (an antifibrinolytic) is the only effective medical option
kw: heavy menstrual bleeding lasting more than 10 days
x: A. Dilatation and curettage: reserved for severe or refractory bleeding, or hemodynamic instability, after medical treatment fails; in a 45-year-old, endometrial sampling is also indicated for diagnosis, but it is not the first management here. | B. Hysterectomy: definitive treatment for chronic AUB after failed medical and conservative therapy when fertility is not desired; not the first step for an acute episode with a normal uterus. | D. Oxytocin: a uterotonic for postpartum hemorrhage; it ha

q: pregnant woman with preeclampsia has just delivered and has a lax uterus with moderate postpartum hemorrhage . Physical examination reveals no laceration or retained product of conception. Which of the following medical therapies is most recommended?
o: 20 units oxytocin in a 500 mL of D5W given intravenous
k: Uterotonic ladder for atonic PPH (with uterine massage, call for help, cross-match): 1st: oxytocin IV or IM 2nd: ergometrine 0.5 mg IM or methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM; avoid in hypertension or preeclampsia 3rd: carboprost
r: A lax uterus after delivery with no laceration or retained tissue means atonic PPH, and oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic. The patient has preeclampsia , which rules out ergometrine because it causes vasoconstriction and can provoke a hypertensive crisis, so an IV oxytocin infusion is the correc
x: A. 5 units of oral oxytocin: oxytocin is not given orally because it is destroyed in the gut; it is given IV or IM. | B. 0.2 mg intravenous ergometrine: an effective second-line uterotonic in normotensive women, but contraindicated in preeclampsia or hypertension. | C. 0.5 mg intramuscular ergometrine: the correct route and dose for ergometrine in a normotensive woman, but ergot alkaloids are contraindicated in preeclampsia or hypertension because they cause vasoconstriction and can provoke a hy

q: 23-year-old woman develops postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) following a normal vaginal delivery, with an estimated blood loss of 1500 mL . All uterotonic medications have been administered but failed to control the bleeding. Which of the following is the first-line surgical intervention ?
k: Refractory atonic PPH escalation: Massage plus uterotonics, tranexamic acid Intrauterine balloon tamponade Laparotomy: compression sutures (B-Lynch), uterine or internal iliac artery ligation Embolization if stable and a
r: After a vaginal delivery with atonic PPH and failure of all uterotonics , the next step is the least invasive mechanical measure, intrauterine balloon tamponade (for example a Bakri balloon). It is quick, can be placed at the bedside, often stops the bleeding, and preserves fertility in a 23-year-ol
kw: All uterotonic medications have been administered
x: A. Uterine artery embolization: an option when the patient is stable and interventional radiology is immediately available, usually after tamponade fails. | B. Hysterectomy: the last resort when all conservative and surgical measures fail or life is threatened; it ends fertility in a young woman. | D. Dilatation and curettage: used for retained products of conception, not for atony after uterotonics have failed.

q: Pregnant female with fetal hydrobe and they ask which of the following arteries is used to detect fetal anemia ?
k: Fetal Doppler: which vessel for which question: MCA PSV: fetal anemia (>1.5 MoM = moderate to severe), then cordocentesis and intrauterine transfusion Umbilical artery: placental insufficiency in IUGR Ductus venosus: fet
r: Fetal hydrops can result from severe fetal anemia (for example alloimmunization). Doppler of the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the non-invasive test for fetal anemia: anemic blood is less viscous and the fetus increases cardiac output, so MCA flow velocity rises, and a value above
x: B. Renal artery: not used to assess fetal anemia. | C. Umbilical artery: Doppler assesses placental resistance in fetal growth restriction (absent or reversed end-diastolic flow), not anemia. | D. Hepatic: not a standard vessel for anemia screening.

q: 6 weak pregnant woman has a previous child with hydrocephalus . What dose of folic acid should she take?
k: Folic acid dose by NTD risk: Average risk: 0.4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester Moderate risk (family history of folate-sensitive anomalies such as hydrocephalus, diabetes): 1
r: A previous child with hydrocephalus (a folate-sensitive congenital anomaly, but not a neural tube defect itself) places her at moderate risk. Moderate risk women take 1 mg (1,000 micrograms) folic acid daily until 12 weeks, then drop to the standard 0.4 mg; she is 6 weeks , so she is still in the hi
x: A. 400 micrograms: the dose for average-risk women, and the dose for this moderate-risk woman after 12 weeks (another recall at 16 weeks was keyed 400). | C. 5000 micrograms: the high-risk dose (4 to 5 mg) for a previous pregnancy with a neural tube defect, antiepileptic drug use, sickle cell disease or similar. | D. 2000 micrograms: not a standard recommended dose.

q: year-old primigravida at 12 weeks ; electrolytes and renal function were requested. Most expected finding? (p. 147)
k: Normal pregnancy dilutes and filters more: most renal markers go DOWN. GFR and renal plasma flow: up about 50% Creatinine: down (by about 0.3 mg/dL) BUN: down Sodium and osmolality: down slightly Albumin: down about 1 g/
r: Early in pregnancy renal plasma flow and GFR rise sharply (by about 50%), so creatinine is cleared faster and its serum level falls . At 12 weeks this change is already established, making a lower creatinine the most expected result on routine renal function.
x: B. Plasma sodium falls slightly in pregnancy because water retention exceeds sodium retention (dilution); it does not rise. | C. BUN also falls with the higher GFR and plasma dilution; a raised BUN would suggest dehydration or renal impairment, not normal pregnancy. | D. BUN is not unchanged; it drops in the first trimester for the same reason creatinine does.

q: 25-year-old woman in her mid-trimester of pregnancy presents with a sudden unexpected rupture of membranes followed by painless expulsion of the products of conception. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Painless second trimester dilation or loss = cervical incompetence. Risk factors: prior cone biopsy/LEEP, repeated dilation, cervical trauma, previous mid-trimester loss Diagnosis: history plus short cervix on transvagin
r: Mid-trimester loss that begins with sudden unexpected rupture of membranes and ends in painless expulsion is the classic picture of cervical incompetence: the weak cervix dilates silently without contractions. The absence of pain, fever and preceding bleeding is the decisive clue.
x: A. Septic miscarriage presents with fever, uterine tenderness and foul discharge, usually after retained products or instrumentation; this patient is painless and well. | C. Threatened miscarriage is bleeding with a closed os and a continuing pregnancy; here the products have already been expelled. | D. Incomplete miscarriage is an open os with partial passage of tissue and usually painful bleeding with cramps; it describes the outcome of passage, not a painless second trimester mechanism.

q: A 30-year-old woman is referred by a medical clinic with a complaint of vulvar pain . Examination reveals one ulcer on the left lower labia majora. The lesion has a ragged edge , necrotic base , and palpable adenopathy on the left inguinal region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Genital ulcers: decide by pain and base. Syphilis: single, painless, clean indurated base, rubbery non-tender nodes Chancroid: painful, ragged undermined edge, necrotic/purulent base, tender suppurative nodes Herpes: mul
r: A painful vulvar ulcer with a ragged edge , necrotic base and tender unilateral inguinal adenopathy is chancroid, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi . The undermined, dirty base and painful node (which may suppurate into a bubo) are the decisive features.
x: A. Primary syphilis gives a painless ulcer with a clean, indurated base and sharp margins with non-tender nodes; this ulcer is necrotic and ragged. | C. Herpes causes multiple small painful vesicles that erode into shallow ulcers, often with systemic symptoms; it is not a single necrotic ulcer. | D. A Bartholin abscess is a tender fluctuant swelling at the 4 or 8 o'clock position of the posterior vestibule, not an ulcer on the labia majora.

q: A 35-year-old woman, G3P2 diabetic patient at 38 weeks of gestation, is planned to have induction of labor. She has no abdominal or pelvic pain, and no vaginal loss. Examination revealed the uterine size corresponds to gestational age, soft, and not tender. Pelvic examination shows the cervix is closed and uneffaced . CTG is done . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Read a CTG with DR C BRAVADO; reassuring = all features normal. Baseline 110 to 160 bpm Variability 5 to 25 bpm Accelerations present No decelerations Early: head compression (benign); Variable: cord; Late: placental ins
r: The woman is not in labour : no pain, no vaginal loss, soft non-tender uterus and a closed uneffaced cervix. Without contractions there is nothing to cause periodic decelerations, and the trace with a baseline of about 140 bpm is reassuring. Induction is planned only because of diabetes at 38 weeks.
x: A. Late decelerations start after the contraction peak and reflect uteroplacental insufficiency; they need contractions and an abnormal trace, neither described here. | B. Early decelerations mirror contractions from head compression, typically in active labour with an engaged head; this woman has no contractions. | D. Variable decelerations are abrupt dips from cord compression (e.g. cord prolapse, oligohydramnios); nothing in the stem suggests this.

q: Recently married women with sudden iliac fossa pain ?
k: Acute pelvic pain in a woman of childbearing age: hCG first, then pelvic US. Positive hCG + empty uterus + adnexal mass/free fluid = ectopic Sudden pain + adnexal mass + vomiting = torsion (Doppler) Ruptured cyst: free f
r: A recently married woman of reproductive age with sudden iliac fossa pain must have pregnancy related and adnexal causes excluded first: ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst. Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal, with beta hCG) is the first imaging test: it is fast, radiation
x: A. CT pelvis uses radiation that is undesirable in possible pregnancy and is inferior for adnexal and early pregnancy assessment; it is reserved for unclear cases or suspected non gynaecological pathology. | B. Erect and supine abdominal X ray is used for suspected obstruction or perforation, not for sudden iliac fossa pain in a woman of childbearing age.

q: Endometriosis defenetive management
k: Endometriosis management ladder. Diagnosis gold standard: laparoscopy (visualisation ± biopsy) First line pain control: NSAIDs + combined pill or progestin Second line: GnRH agonist with add back HRT Fertility wish: lapa
r: The lead in asks for the definitive management of endometriosis. Endometriosis is oestrogen dependent, so removing the uterus and both ovaries ( TAH with BSO ) with excision of visible disease is the treatment with the lowest recurrence; it is reserved for women who have completed their family and f
x: B. Endometrial ablation destroys the uterine lining to treat heavy menstrual bleeding; it does not treat ectopic endometrial implants. | C. Not recalled; if it was laparoscopic excision or ablation of implants, that is first line surgery and preserves fertility but is temporising, with many patients needing reoperation. | D. Not recalled; if it was medical therapy (combined pill, progestins, GnRH agonists), that suppresses symptoms but is not curative and symptoms recur after stopping.

q: infertility laparoscop show absence of dye filling bilateral tubal blockage management
k: Infertility treatment by cause. Tubal patency: HSG first, laparoscopy and dye confirms Bilateral tubal block: IVF Unilateral block with ovulation issue: clomiphene Anovulation (PCOS): letrozole or clomiphene, then gonado
r: Laparoscopy with dye showing no spill from both tubes confirms bilateral tubal blockage : sperm and egg cannot meet, so any treatment that relies on the tubes will fail. IVF bypasses the tubes by fertilising the egg outside the body and transferring the embryo to the uterus.
x: A. Clomiphene induces ovulation in anovulatory women (e.g. PCOS) or is used with one patent tube; ovulation is useless if both tubes are blocked. | C. IUI places sperm in the uterus and still needs at least one patent tube; it suits mild male factor or unexplained infertility. | D. Gonadotropin ovulation induction is for anovulation resistant to clomiphene/letrozole; it cannot overcome blocked tubes.

q: 67 yr women with negative 3 pap smear. A 67 year old woman , had 3 consecutive negative pap smear and no evidence of CIN 2 (or 3, im not sure), which one of the following is the recommended step:
o: pap smear and HPV co-testing every 5 years
k: Cervical screening schedule: Start at 21 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years (or cytology every 3) Over 65 with adequate negative history and no CIN 2+ in 25 years: stop After hysterectomy fo
r: Cervical screening stops after age 65 in a woman with adequate prior negative screening (for example 3 consecutive negative Pap smears, or 2 negative co-tests, within the past 10 years) and no history of CIN 2 or worse in the last 25 years. She is 67 with 3 consecutive negative smears, so she needs
x: A. Not recalled; whatever it was, it cannot beat stopping screening once the age and negative history criteria are met. | B. Pap smear every 3 years is the schedule for ages 21 to 29 (and an option up to 65); it does not apply after 65 with adequate negative history. | C. Co-testing every 5 years is the preferred schedule for ages 30 to 65, not for a 67 year old who qualifies to stop.

q: after abortion risk of reoccurrence. Female had one ABORTION , risk of 2nd abortion ?
k: Miscarriage recurrence after one loss ≈ baseline risk. Baseline clinical miscarriage: about 10 to 15% under 35 Risk rises with each further loss and steeply with maternal age over 40 Recurrent miscarriage = 3 or more con
r: After a single sporadic miscarriage, the risk of miscarriage in the next pregnancy is about the same as the background rate, roughly 15 to 20% (mainly from random chromosomal errors), and rises only modestly with more losses. 10 to 25% is the range that contains this figure, and the card notes it as
x: A. 1 to 9% is below even the baseline miscarriage rate of clinically recognized pregnancies (about 10 to 15% under age 35). | C. 25 to 45% fits a woman after two or three consecutive losses (recurrent miscarriage) or of advanced maternal age, where the risk rises steeply after 40; it does not apply after one abortion.

q: A 26-year-old G4 P3 presented at 31 weeks gestation with labor pain. She had preterm premature rupture of membranes 4 weeks ago . Today, the cervix is 3 cm dilated with clear liquor noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: High vaginal swab for bacterial culture and sensitivity

Immediate caesarean section is for obstetric indications such as fetal distress, cord prolapse or malpresentation; chorioamnionitis itself is an indication for delivery, usually vaginal, not for caesarean. | D. q: A 23-year-old single woman presented with heavy menstruation during the first 4 days of her period for the last 2 years (see image and lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Heavy menstrual bleeding causes (PALM-COEIN): Structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy Non structural: coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified Fibroid on US: well defined hypoechoic
r: Heavy menstrual bleeding for 2 years with an ultrasound showing a uterine mass (arrow) points to uterine leiomyomas (fibroids), the commonest cause of structural menorrhagia. Submucosal and intramural fibroids enlarge the endometrial surface and cause heavy, regular periods; ultrasound is the first
x: A. Pregnancy causes amenorrhoea, not 2 years of regular heavy periods; bleeding in pregnancy would suggest miscarriage or ectopic with a positive hCG. | B. An ovarian cyst is an adnexal mass, usually asymptomatic or causing pain or torsion, and does not typically cause heavy periods. | C. Endometrial cancer presents mainly with postmenopausal bleeding in older women with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, unopposed oestrogen); it is very unlikely at 23.

q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of infertility for 6 years complains of severe dysmenorrhea unrelieved by naproxen . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Endometriosis: cyclic pain + infertility. 3 Ds: dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia (deep), dyschezia Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodules Diagnosis: laparoscopy (powder burn, red/white lesions); endometrioma = cho
r: Infertility (6 years) plus severe dysmenorrhoea not relieved by NSAIDs (naproxen) in a woman of 30 is the classic combination for endometriosis ; the laparoscopic photo of peritoneal "powder burn" lesions confirms it. Endometriosis causes the 3 Ds (dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia) and infertil
x: A. Endometritis is an infection of the endometrium, usually after delivery, miscarriage or instrumentation, with fever, pelvic pain and discharge; it is not years of cyclic pain. | B. Leiomyomata mainly cause heavy menstrual bleeding and pressure symptoms; submucosal ones can affect fertility, but refractory dysmenorrhoea with powder burn lesions is endometriosis. | D. Pelvic congestion syndrome is chronic dull pelvic pain worse on standing and premenstrually, with pelvic varices, typically in m

q: A woman comes to the clinic for having a history of increasing pelvic pain. which is cyclic in nature and increasing in intensity just before menses . Which of the following is an acceptable method for diagnosing endometriosis ?
k: Endometriosis diagnosis: Initial: transvaginal ultrasound (endometrioma = chocolate cyst, ground glass) Gold standard / confirmatory: laparoscopy ± biopsy MRI: deep infiltrating disease, surgical planning CA-125 may rise
r: Cyclic pelvic pain building just before menses suggests endometriosis, and the question asks for an acceptable method of diagnosing it. Diagnostic laparoscopy with direct visualization (ideally with biopsy of lesions) is the gold standard and confirmatory test, because peritoneal implants are usuall
kw: increasing in intensity just before menses
x: A. MRI helps map deep infiltrating endometriosis and endometriomas before surgery, but it misses superficial peritoneal disease and cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis. | C. Endometrial biopsy samples the uterine lining and is the test for abnormal bleeding over 45 or suspected hyperplasia/cancer; endometriosis lies outside the uterus. | D. Transvaginal ultrasound is the initial test and can show an endometrioma (ground glass cyst), but a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis.

q: A 33-year-old woman, nulliparous , complaining of cyclic pelvic pain and dyschezia underwent diagnostic laparoscopy (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Cyclic pain + dyschezia/dyspareunia + infertility = endometriosis. Most common site: ovary; then uterosacral ligaments, pouch of Douglas Exam: fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodularity Adenomyosis: older, multipar
r: A nulliparous woman with cyclic pelvic pain and dyschezia has two of the 3 Ds of endometriosis (dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia); dyschezia reflects implants in the pouch of Douglas or rectovaginal septum. Laparoscopy, the confirmatory test, shows the typical peritoneal implants (powder burn,
x: A. Pelvic TB causes infertility, menstrual disturbance (often amenorrhoea) and constitutional symptoms, with tubercles and dense adhesions at laparoscopy, usually in endemic settings; not cyclic pain. | B. Adenomyosis is endometrium within the myometrium, seen in older multiparous women with heavy painful periods and a bulky tender uterus; it is not visible as peritoneal lesions on laparoscopy. | D. PID gives non cyclic pelvic pain, fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness in a sexually a

q: Mother pregnant with twin , in U/S there's lambda sign What type of twins pregnancy ?
k: Chorionicity on ultrasound: Lambda (twin peak) sign, thick membrane: DCDA T sign, thin membrane: MCDA No membrane: MCMA Different sexes or two separate placentas: dichorionic Cleavage timing: 0 to 3 days DCDA, 4 to 8 day
r: The lambda (twin peak) sign is a triangular projection of placental tissue into the base of a thick inter twin membrane; it means two separate chorions, i.e. dichorionic diamniotic twins. It is best assessed in the first trimester (around 11 to 14 weeks), when chorionicity is most reliable.
x: A. Monochorionic monoamniotic twins have no dividing membrane at all and are recognized by cord entanglement in a single sac. | B. Monochorionic diamniotic twins show the T sign: a thin membrane meeting the single placenta at a right angle, without placental tissue between the layers. | D. Conjoined twins have no membrane and fused fetal bodies that move together; they result from very late cleavage (after about day 13).

q: 36 week G3P4 singleton pregnancy with frank breech . All previous normal vaginal. Would like to have a vaginal delivery. Which week should ECV be preformed
k: ECV timing: 36 weeks nullipara, 37 weeks multipara. Frank breech: hips flexed, knees extended Contraindications: placenta previa or APH, ruptured membranes, abnormal CTG, need for CS anyway, major uterine anomaly, multip
r: External cephalic version is offered from 36 weeks in nulliparous women and from 37 weeks in multiparous women. This woman is G3P4 with previous normal vaginal deliveries, so she is multiparous and ECV should be performed at 37 weeks. Before then spontaneous version is still likely in a multipara, a
kw: Which week should ECV be preformed
x: A. 36 weeks: the timing for a nulliparous woman; in a multipara spontaneous turning is still common, so waiting to 37 weeks is preferred. | C. 38 weeks: later than recommended; less amniotic fluid and a larger baby lower success, and labor may start before the attempt. | D. 39 weeks: too late as the planned time; it delays the attempt with a growing risk of spontaneous labor in breech.

q: 32 YO (G2P3) undergoing repeat elective C section . Previous C section was uncomplicated. What is the most evidence based method to reduce the risk of post operative endometritis
k: Cesarean infection prevention: antibiotics before incision. Cefazolin within 60 minutes before skin incision Add azithromycin for CS in labor or after ruptured membranes Vaginal cleansing: adjunct, mainly in labor Endome
r: The single most evidence based measure to reduce post cesarean endometritis and wound infection is prophylactic antibiotics given before the skin incision (typically a first generation cephalosporin), which substantially cuts infectious morbidity in both elective and emergency cesarean sections. The
x: A. Vaginal iodine prep: also lowers endometritis, mainly in women in labor or with ruptured membranes, but it is an adjunct with weaker evidence than antibiotic prophylaxis. | C. Daily wound checking: detects wound infection after it happens; it does not prevent endometritis. | D. Monitoring for post operative fever: a detection strategy for infection that has already occurred, not prevention.

q: To reduce the occurrence of adhesions in pregnant women undergoing elective Cesarean sections , which of the following strategies can be employed?
o: Add an adhesion barrier before closing the wound
k: Match the measure to the complication asked at CS: Adhesions: meticulous hemostasis, gentle handling Endometritis and wound infection: antibiotics before incision Elective CS timing: ≥39 weeks Routine drains: not recomme
r: Adhesions form where there is tissue trauma, ischemia, blood and fibrin left in the peritoneal cavity. Careful surgical technique with meticulous hemostasis (gentle tissue handling, removing clots, avoiding excess dry packing) is the simplest well accepted measure to reduce adhesions at cesarean sec
x: A. Perform the C section preterm: delivering early adds neonatal prematurity risks and does nothing to reduce adhesions; elective CS is timed at ≥39 weeks. | B. Using drains: routine drains do not reduce adhesions or infection after CS and are a foreign body; they are kept for specific bleeding concerns. | C. Adhesion barrier: evidence that barriers reduce clinically significant adhesions after cesarean is limited and inconsistent, so they are not the recommended standard measure.

q: 20 y/o wemon complaining of worsening menstrual cramping , resulting of absence of the university frequent, tried NSIDs with patrial relief . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start oral combined oral contraceptive pills
k: Dysmenorrhea ladder: Step 1: NSAIDs Step 2: hormonal therapy (COCP, progestin, LNG IUS) Step 3: failure of both: laparoscopy for endometriosis Secondary signs: onset after years of painless periods, dyspareunia, abnormal
r: A 20 year old with worsening menstrual cramps causing missed university and only partial relief from NSAIDs has dysmenorrhea that has failed first line therapy.
