The next step is hormonal therapy, usually combined oral contraceptive pills, which suppress ovulation and endometrial prostaglandins; lapa
x: B. Diagnostic laparoscopy: for suspected endometriosis after failure of NSAIDs plus hormonal therapy (3-6 months), or with abnormal findings. | C. Refer to pain clinic: for chronic pain refractory to medical and surgical management, not after one partly effective drug. | D. Pelvic MRI: for a suspected structural cause such as adenomyosis or a mass after abnormal examination or US; not the next step here.

q: 35 y/o wemon diagnosed with left tube ectopic pregnancy, managed with MTX , she remined asymptomatic with plautuing on day 4,7 b-hcg Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
k: Methotrexate monitoring for ectopic pregnancy: Measure β hCG on day 4 and day 7 Fall ≥15%: weekly β hCG until negative Fall <15% or plateau: second dose methotrexate Rupture, instability, or failure of second dose: surge
r: After single dose methotrexate, β hCG is measured on day 4 and day 7, and it should fall by at least 15% between them. A plateau between days 4 and 7 in an asymptomatic , stable woman means inadequate response, so the next step is a second dose of methotrexate, with repeat monitoring.
x: A. Laparoscopic salpingectomy: for rupture, hemodynamic instability, severe pain, or failure after a second methotrexate dose; she is asymptomatic. | B. Repeat β hCG in 48 h: serial 48 hour testing is for a pregnancy of unknown location before diagnosis, not the protocol after methotrexate. | C. Repeat β hCG in 1 week: correct only if the day 4 to 7 fall is ≥15% (weekly follow up until negative).

q: A 44-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding ( PB 95/47 , HR 107, Hb 68 , B-hch 3). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute AUB management: Stable: IV conjugated estrogen first line; COCP, oral progestin or tranexamic acid Severe, unstable or refractory: D&C (or balloon tamponade) Age ≥45 or risk factors: endometrial sampling Definitive
r: A 44 year old with heavy bleeding, hypotension (95/47) and tachycardia (107) , and Hb 68 has severe acute abnormal uterine bleeding with hemodynamic compromise; β hCG 3 excludes pregnancy. After resuscitation, D&C rapidly stops bleeding that is too severe for medical therapy and gives endometrial ti
x: A. Hysterectomy: definitive for refractory bleeding or structural disease (adenomyosis, fibroids) once she is stabilised and the cause is known, not as the first emergency step. | B. Mefenamic acid: an NSAID for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding or dysmenorrhea; too weak for unstable acute bleeding. | C. Insert hormonal IUD: excellent for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, but it acts over months and cannot control acute hemorrhage.

q: 45-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks, planned C-section . BMI 32 , no previous DVT/ PE, no significant PMH, and no DVT signs. What is the appropriate prophylaxis?
k: Peripartum VTE prophylaxis: Risk factors: age >35, BMI ≥30, parity ≥3, smoking, CS, immobility, preeclampsia, previous VTE, thrombophilia Agent of choice: LMWH (safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding) Add mechanical: compre
r: Pregnancy and the puerperium are prothrombotic, and cesarean section is a major added VTE risk. This woman has several risk factors: age 45 (>35), BMI 32 (≥30) and a planned C section . That combination warrants pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH (enoxaparin) after delivery, with graduated compre
x: B. Warfarin: teratogenic in pregnancy and not used for routine peripartum prophylaxis; it can be used postpartum for longer term anticoagulation, including in breastfeeding, but LMWH is the standard. | C. No prophylaxis: right only for a low risk woman with no or minimal risk factors; age >35 and obesity plus CS put her at increased risk.

q: A 32-year-old woman with twin pregnancy , presented at 38 weeks of gestation in active labor. Examination revealed twin A is in vertex presentation , and twin B is also in vertex presentation . Both fetal heart rates are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Twin delivery by presentation: Vertex vertex: vaginal delivery Vertex non vertex: vaginal delivery possible (breech extraction or ECV of twin B) or CS Twin A non vertex: cesarean section Monochorionic monoamniotic: cesar
r: Twins at 38 weeks in active labor with twin A vertex and twin B vertex and normal fetal heart rates have the most favourable twin presentation. Vertex vertex twins are delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery, with continuous monitoring and readiness for intervention for the second twin.
kw: twin A is in vertex presentation
twin B is also in vertex presentation
x: A. Forceps delivery: only for specific second stage indications (prolonged second stage, fetal distress with a low head); there is no indication here. | B. Cesarean section: right when twin A is non vertex, in monoamniotic twins, or with usual obstetric indications such as fetal distress. | C. Ventouse delivery: an assisted delivery needing an indication in the second stage; none is present.

q: 30 weeks pregnant all normal came for prenatal visit what vaccine I can give ?
k: Vaccines in pregnancy: Recommended: Tdap at 27-36 weeks each pregnancy; inactivated influenza any trimester If at risk: hepatitis A, hepatitis B Contraindicated (live): MMR, varicella, BCG, live intranasal influenza DTaP
r: At 30 weeks a healthy pregnant woman should receive the inactivated Tdap vaccine (printed here as 'dtap'), ideally between 27 and 36 weeks in every pregnancy. Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn against pertussis before the infant's own vaccines start at 2 months.
x: A. MMR: a live attenuated vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy; give it postpartum to rubella non immune women. | C. Hepatitis A: inactivated and can be given in pregnancy if at risk (travel, exposure, liver disease), but it is not routine for a healthy woman. | D. Varicella: live attenuated, contraindicated in pregnancy; offer postpartum if non immune.

q: A 40-year-old woman came in labor with her seventh child . Following delivery, she developed postpartum hemorrhage due to failure to deliver the placenta (retained placenta). What is the type of postpartum hemorrhage ?
k: PPH classification is by TIME, not cause. Primary: within 24 hours of delivery (atony, trauma, retained placenta, coagulopathy) Secondary: 24 hours to 12 weeks (retained products, endometritis) Grand multiparity and age
r: This recall's key is secondary PPH, reasoning that retained products of conception are a classic cause of secondary (late) PPH. However, PPH type is defined by timing, not cause: bleeding following delivery because the placenta has failed to deliver happens within 24 hours, which is primary PPH. The
x: A. Primary: bleeding within 24 hours of delivery; a retained placenta right after birth fits this timing, so many sources would key it here (see concern). | C. Tertiary: not a standard PPH category; PPH is only primary (within 24 hours) or secondary (24 hours to 12 weeks).

q: 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days . Now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued and sometimes faints . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: Heavy bleeding with symptoms of anemia: assess severity first (CBC), exclude pregnancy (hCG). Then stabilize: transfusion if Hb low and symptomatic Then imaging (pelvic US) and endometrial sampling if age ≥45 or risk fac
r: A 45-year-old still in reproductive age with 15 days of bleeding who is now drowsy, fatigued and fainting has symptomatic anemia. The first step is to measure the hemoglobin (CBC) to judge need for transfusion and to exclude pregnancy with beta-hCG, since pregnancy-related bleeding changes the whole
kw: period has not stopped for the past 15 days
x: A. Ultrasound: needed to look for structural causes (fibroids, endometrial thickness) but comes after stabilization and excluding pregnancy. | B. Urine pregnancy test: excludes pregnancy but ignores the anemia that is causing her symptoms; CBC plus hCG covers both. | C. Dilatation and curettage: used for acute uncontrolled bleeding or tissue sampling after initial assessment; not the first step before labs.

q: A pregnant woman attending antenatal care has pre-existing type 1 diabetes mellitus with a HbA1c of 12% . What is the most common complication in this case?
k: Pregestational diabetes: high HbA1c at conception = congenital anomalies. HbA1c is the best predictor of fetal anomaly risk in early pregnancy Typical anomalies: cardiac defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression La
r: In pre-existing type 1 diabetes with a very high HbA1c of 12% , hyperglycemia during organogenesis in the first trimester markedly raises the risk of congenital malformations (cardiac, neural tube, caudal regression). The recaller notes she was at 12 weeks, so the early-pregnancy complication is key
x: B. Polyhydramnios: a common complication of diabetes later in pregnancy (fetal polyuria from hyperglycemia); it is the answer when the stem is in the second or third trimester or describes a large-for-dates uterus.

q: A woman required oxytocin for augmentation of labor . Physicians were discussing how to prevent PPH in her case.
o: Monitor for signs of uterine atony
Active management of 3rd stage of labor
k: PPH prevention = active management of the third stage for every birth. Uterotonic: oxytocin is first line Controlled cord traction Uterine tone check after placental delivery Atony risks: augmentation, prolonged labor, o
r: Oxytocin augmentation of labor is a risk factor for uterine atony, the most common cause of PPH. The proven measure to prevent PPH is active management of the third stage of labor : a prophylactic uterotonic (oxytocin) after delivery, controlled cord traction and uterine assessment.
x: A. Monitor for signs of uterine atony: surveillance detects PPH after it starts but does not prevent it. | C. Delayed cord clamping: benefits the newborn (iron stores, preterm outcomes); it does not prevent maternal PPH and is compatible with active management.

q: A 34-year-old G2P1 has a fetus with a single umbilical artery .
k: Single umbilical artery: normal cord has 2 arteries and 1 vein. Associations: multiple pregnancy, maternal diabetes Fetal: renal and cardiac anomalies, aneuploidy, growth restriction Management: detailed anatomy scan, co
r: The stem asks what is associated with a single umbilical artery . Multiple pregnancy is a recognized risk factor (more common in twins), so it is the keyed association among these options. At 34 years she is not of advanced maternal age, and parity is not a risk factor.
x: A. Age: advanced maternal age has been linked in some studies, but 34 years is below the usual threshold and age is not the classic association here. | B. Parity: G2P1 is not a recognized risk factor for single umbilical artery. | D. Hypothyroidism: not an established association; the classic maternal disease associated is diabetes.

q: A 12-week pregnant woman presents with exertional dyspnea. She is otherwise healthy, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows monochorionic twin pregnancy with evidence of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses
k: TTTS occurs in monochorionic twins (shared placenta with vascular anastomoses). Donor: oligohydramnios, growth restriction; recipient: polyhydramnios, heart failure Staging by Quintero About 16 to 26 weeks, stage II or m
r: This recall's key is amnioreduction , following the compiler's reasoning that fetoscopic laser ablation is performed only from about 16 weeks , so at 12 weeks it is not yet an option. Removing excess amniotic fluid from the recipient sac relieves the maternal symptom ( exertional dyspnea from uterin
x: A. Termination of pregnancy: may be discussed in severe early TTTS with poor prognosis, but it is not the default first step in a healthy mother. | B. Expectant management with observation only: appropriate for mild disease (Quintero stage I) with no maternal symptoms; here the mother is symptomatic. | C. Laser photocoagulation: the definitive treatment for moderate to severe TTTS between about 16 and 26 weeks; another candidate chose it regardless of gestation, but at 12 weeks it is too early.

q: A 24-year-old woman primigravida undergoes an uneventful vaginal delivery at term. After placental delivery, she has 1000 cc of vaginal bleeding . She is alert, and her vital signs are stable, with the uterus noted to be firm . Which of the following is the most common cause?
k: PPH causes: the 4 Ts. Tone (atony): most common, soft boggy uterus Trauma: lacerations with a firm uterus Tissue: retained placenta or products Thrombin: coagulopathy Firm uterus with bleeding: inspect cervix, vagina, pe
r: 1000 cc of bleeding after placental delivery is PPH. The decisive clue is a firm uterus , which means normal tone and excludes atony; with an uneventful delivery and stable patient, the next most common cause is genital tract laceration (cervical, vaginal, perineal).
x: A. Uterine atony: the most common cause of PPH overall, but the uterus would be soft and boggy; a firm uterus excludes it. | B. Coagulopathy: suspected with oozing from puncture sites, abruption, preeclampsia/HELLP, amniotic fluid embolism or massive transfusion; none here. | D. Retained products of conception: suggested by an incomplete placenta and a uterus that does not stay contracted; usually atony coexists.

q: 30-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism is taking levothyroxine 125 µg daily. Her thyroid function tests are within the normal range. She is newly diagnosed with pregnancy . What is the most appropriate management of her levothyroxine dose?
o: Continue the same dose without any change
k: Hypothyroidism in pregnancy: increase the dose on confirmation. Typical step: about 25 to 30% increase (e.g. two extra doses per week) Check TSH every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy Return to pre-pregnancy dose a
r: Pregnancy raises thyroxine requirements (higher thyroid-binding globulin, placental deiodination, fetal dependence on maternal T4 in the first trimester). A woman with known hypothyroidism should therefore increase her levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with normal pre-pregnancy t
x: B. Decrease the dose: requirements rise, not fall, in pregnancy; decreasing risks maternal hypothyroidism and impaired fetal neurodevelopment. | C. Continue the same dose: would be acceptable only with close TSH monitoring showing she stays on target; standard advice is to increase pre-emptively. | D. Stop levothyroxine: levothyroxine is safe in pregnancy and stopping it harms the fetus.

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with a very heavy period. She is morbidly obese and diabetic . Her periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months . She had her period 2 weeks ago and it has not stopped, with heavy clots. Pregnancy test is negative . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Irregular, infrequent cycles + heavy prolonged bleeding = anovulatory AUB (unopposed estrogen). Risk: obesity, diabetes/insulin resistance, PCOS Regular heavy periods: think fibroids, adenomyosis, coagulopathy Always exc
r: The decisive clues are "morbidly obese and diabetic" (insulin resistance, PCOS picture), periods "every 3-4 months" (oligomenorrhea = anovulation) and a negative pregnancy test. Without ovulation there is no progesterone, so the endometrium keeps building under unopposed estrogen until it sheds irre
x: A. Fibroids: cause heavy but REGULAR cyclical periods (menorrhagia), often with a bulky irregular uterus; they do not explain cycles every 3-4 months. | B. Bleeding disorder: suspect in an adolescent with heavy bleeding since menarche or a personal/family history of bruising and mucosal bleeding; nothing here suggests it. | C. Incomplete abortion: needs a positive pregnancy test, open os and passage of tissue; the pregnancy test here is negative.

q: A 46-year-old woman is complaining of heavy menstruation lasting for 14 days every period. She is morbidly obese and has type 2 diabetes mellitus (see lab results and report). Ultrasound: Endometrial thickness of 18 mm . Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: AUB over 45, or under 45 with unopposed estrogen risk / failed treatment = endometrial biopsy. Office (pipelle) sample is first line Hysteroscopy-guided biopsy if sample inadequate or bleeding persists TVUS assesses thic
r: She has abnormal uterine bleeding at "46" (over 45) with strong unopposed estrogen risk factors ("morbidly obese", "type 2 diabetes") and a thickened endometrium of 18 mm. Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma must be excluded, and the next step is tissue: an office (pipelle) endometrial sample, whic
x: A. Pelvic CT: used for staging once cancer is confirmed, not for diagnosing the cause of AUB; it cannot give histology. | B. Pelvic MRI: helps characterise adenomyosis or fibroids or stage a known endometrial cancer; it does not replace tissue diagnosis. | C. Hysteroscopy: chosen when office sampling fails, is non-diagnostic or bleeding persists despite a benign sample, or for a focal lesion such as a polyp; it is not the first step here.

q: A 27-year-old G4P3 woman is seen in labor at 39 weeks of gestation. Examination revealed the cervix is 5 cm dilated with clear amniotic fluid draining. Cardiotocography shows that the baseline is 140 beats per minute, no accelerations, good variability, and no decelerations . The uterine contractions are regular and strong, occurring at a rate of 3 to 4 in 10 minutes . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Reassurance and reassessment in 30 to 60 minutes
k: Normal active labor + reassuring CTG + adequate contractions = continue and reassess. Adequate contractions: 3-5 in 10 minutes Not in labor + indication: induction In labor, weak contractions, slow progress: augmentation
r: At "5 cm dilated" with regular strong contractions she is in the active first stage of labor. The CTG is reassuring (baseline 140, good variability, no decelerations; absent accelerations alone in labor is not worrying) and contractions are adequate at "3 to 4 in 10 minutes". Labor is progressing no
x: A. Induction of labor: starts labor in a woman who is NOT in labor (e.g. post-term, unripe cervix); she is already in active labor. | B. Augmentation of labor: for slow progress with inadequate contractions (fewer than 3 in 10 min); her contractions are adequate. | C. Emergency cesarean section: for fetal distress (bradycardia, reduced variability, late decelerations) or obstructed labor; the CTG here is reassuring.

q: A newly married woman is presented to the gynecology clinic for a routine examination and checkup. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value ?
k: Bimanual pelvic exam = highest-yield component of the gynecological examination. Assesses uterus (size, position, mobility) and adnexa Detects cervical motion and adnexal tenderness Virgin patient: avoid digital vaginal
r: In a routine gynecological check the bimanual (digital pelvic) examination gives the most diagnostic information: uterine size, shape, position and mobility, adnexal masses and cervical or adnexal tenderness. A "newly married" woman is sexually active, so a digital pelvic exam is acceptable.
x: A. Vaginal inspection: shows only the external genitalia and vaginal walls (discharge, lesions); it cannot assess the uterus or adnexa. | B. General appearance: part of every exam but nonspecific for pelvic pathology. | C. Abdominal examination: detects only large pelvic masses rising out of the pelvis; small uterine or adnexal pathology is missed.

q: A 27-year-old woman delivered 2 weeks ago and presented with a painful, hard mass in the right breast. She received a 4-day course of antibiotics with no improvement . Examination revealed she is febrile, and a breast abscess is suspected . Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Mastitis that fails antibiotics, or a fluctuant/hard mass = think abscess: ultrasound + drainage. Mastitis: antistaphylococcal antibiotic (e.g. flucloxacillin, cephalexin), continue breastfeeding Abscess: US-guided aspir
r: Two weeks postpartum with a "painful, hard mass", fever and "no improvement" after 4 days of antibiotics = mastitis that has progressed to a suspected abscess. Antibiotics cannot sterilise a pus collection, so ultrasound is needed to confirm it and a surgical review for drainage (needle aspiration o
kw: 4-day course of antibiotics with no improvement
x: A. Change antibiotics: changing the drug does not treat a collection; it only fits mastitis with no abscess (or a resistant organism such as MRSA) once an abscess is excluded. | B. Stop breastfeeding: not needed for mastitis or abscess; continued emptying helps resolution (feeding from the other side or expressing if drainage is near the nipple). | C. Encourage breastfeeding: correct supportive advice, but it does not address a suspected abscess, so it is not the most appropriate management.

q: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL Day 7: 2100 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
k: Methotrexate monitoring: compare day 4 vs day 7 hCG. Fall ≥15%: weekly hCG until negative Fall <15% or plateau: second MTX dose Clearly rising hCG or failure after repeat dosing: surgery Unstable / rupture signs: immedia
r: After single-dose methotrexate, hCG is compared between day 4 and day 7. Here it RISES from 1200 to 2100 (about 75%), which means treatment failure with an actively growing ectopic and rising rupture risk. This recall's key is that a clearly rising hCG after methotrexate = failed medical treatment,
x: A. Repeat beta-hCG in 1 week: correct only when hCG falls by ≥15% between day 4 and day 7 (successful response, weekly follow-up until negative). | C. Administer a second dose of methotrexate: the response to a plateau or fall of less than 15% between day 4 and day 7; a marked rise suggests failure of medical treatment. | D. Admit for multiple methotrexate regimen: a different protocol chosen from the start, not the response to a sharply rising hCG on single-dose therapy.

q: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 had an uneventful pregnancy and a spontaneous vaginal delivery after 2 hours of labor , just making it to the hospital . She delivered a healthy boy weighing 3000 g . After placental delivery, she started to bleed heavily. Which of the following was her risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage?
k: PPH causes = 4 Ts: Tone (most common), Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Atony risks: overdistension (macrosomia, twins, polyhydramnios) Labor: precipitous OR prolonged, oxytocin use Grand multiparity, chorioamnionitis Precipito
r: Delivery "after 2 hours of labor, just making it to the hospital" is precipitous labor (less than 3 hours). Very rapid labor predisposes to uterine atony (and genital tract trauma), the commonest cause of PPH. She is only para 1 and the baby is 3000 g, so the other options do not apply.
kw: just making it to the hospital
x: A. Grand parity: requires high parity (around 5 or more deliveries); she is G2 P1. | B. Prolonged labor: also a risk for atony, but her labor was very short, not prolonged. | C. Macrosomic baby: means about 4000 g or more (uterine overdistension); 3000 g is a normal weight.

q: A 30-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 presented to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with profuse vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain . CTG showed a normal heart rate with regular contractions . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Antepartum hemorrhage: classify by pain. Painful bleeding + tender/hard uterus: abruption Painless bright red bleeding: placenta previa Painless bleeding at membrane rupture + fetal distress: vasa previa Previa suspected
r: Third-trimester bleeding with "abdominal pain" is PAINFUL antepartum hemorrhage = placental abruption. Bleeding from the separating placenta irritates the uterus, causing regular (often frequent) contractions; the fetal heart may still be normal when the separation is small.
kw: profuse vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain
x: A. Labor: at 30 weeks this would be preterm, and labor gives only a show (mucus with streaks of blood), not profuse bleeding. | B. Preterm labor: contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; it does not explain profuse bleeding, which here comes from the abruption. | C. Placenta previa: bleeding is classically PAINLESS with a soft, non-tender uterus; this patient has pain.

q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman in her 8th week presented to the Emergency Room with bleeding and reported passing vesicles . After assessing, her uterine size appears larger than the date . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Bleeding + uterus larger than dates + vesicles = molar pregnancy. Very high hCG: hyperemesis, early preeclampsia (<20 weeks), hyperthyroidism, theca lutein cysts US: snowstorm, no fetus (complete mole) Treatment: suction
r: First-trimester bleeding with "passing vesicles" (grape-like hydropic villi) and a uterus "larger than date" is the classic triad of a hydatidiform (complete) mole. Confirm with very high hCG and the snowstorm pattern on ultrasound, then suction evacuation and hCG follow-up.
kw: uterine size appears larger than the date
x: B. Missed abortion: non-viable pregnancy with a closed os; the uterus is SMALLER than dates and there is no vesicle passage. | C. Ectopic pregnancy: pain and spotting with an empty uterus; the uterus is not larger than dates and vesicles are not passed. | D. Threatened abortion: bleeding with a closed os and a viable fetus; uterine size matches dates.

q: A 25-year-old G1 P0 woman presented to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with abdominal pain. There was no leaking or bleeding. The CTG shows a normal heart rate with regular contractions 4 in 10 minutes . Which of the following is the most appropriate way to diagnose if she has preterm labor ?
o: History only is enough to diagnose
CTG showing regular contractions is diagnostic
If there is no leaking, then she isn't in preterm labor
k: Preterm labor = regular contractions + cervical change, at 20-37 weeks. Digital exam only after previa excluded and membranes intact PPROM suspected: sterile speculum, avoid digital exam Confirmed under 34 weeks: steroid
r: Preterm labor is regular contractions PLUS cervical change (dilation and/or effacement) before 37 weeks. She has contractions "4 in 10 minutes" and no bleeding or leaking (so no contraindication to a digital exam), and the missing piece is cervical change, which a digital exam for dilation provides.
kw: diagnose if she has preterm labor
x: B. History only is enough: history cannot separate true preterm labor from false (Braxton Hicks) contractions; objective cervical change is required. | C. CTG showing regular contractions is diagnostic: contractions alone are not enough; without cervical change it may be false labor. | D. No leaking means not in preterm labor: wrong, preterm labor can occur with intact membranes; leaking relates to PPROM, a separate diagnosis.

q: A 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days and now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Manage the bleeding and send her home
k: Acute heavy AUB: ABC and stabilise first, then stop bleeding, then find the cause. Transfuse: Hb below 7 g/dL, or higher if symptomatic or unstable Medical: IV estrogen, COCP or high-dose progestin, tranexamic acid D&C:
r: Fifteen days of continuous bleeding at "45" with "drowsy and easily fatigued" means symptomatic anemia; the labs (not shown in the recall) are keyed as a low hemoglobin. A symptomatic, drowsy patient must be stabilised first, so the next step is blood transfusion, then control of the bleeding and en
kw: not stopped for the past 15 days
x: A. Ultrasound: part of the AUB workup (structural causes, endometrial thickness) but done after the patient is stabilised, not before treating symptomatic anemia. | B. Dilatation and curettage: for severe bleeding that fails medical therapy or in an unstable patient after resuscitation; it is not the first step and does not correct anemia. | D. Manage the bleeding and send her home: unsafe in a drowsy woman with symptomatic anemia; it fits only a stable patient with mild bleeding and acceptable

q: A 28-year-old woman presented with mild pelvic pain and spotting. She was diagnosed with an ectopic pregnancy and offered medical management . Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to treat this patient?
k: Methotrexate for ectopic: needs ALL of the following. Hemodynamically stable, no rupture No fetal cardiac activity, small mass Low hCG (lower levels = higher success) Reliable follow-up; no liver, renal or blood disease,
r: "Mild pelvic pain and spotting" describes a stable, unruptured ectopic, and she was "offered medical management". The medical treatment of ectopic pregnancy is methotrexate, a folate antagonist that stops the rapidly dividing trophoblast; it is usually given as single-dose IM with hCG checks on days
x: A. Oxytocin: a uterotonic used for induction/augmentation of labor and for PPH; it has no effect on a tubal pregnancy. | B. Carboprost: a PGF2-alpha used for PPH due to atony (avoid in asthma); not a treatment for ectopic pregnancy. | C. Misoprostol: used for medical management of missed or incomplete miscarriage and for induction; it empties the uterus, not the tube.

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. She is 20 weeks pregnant and known to have SLE . She has been symptom-free for the past 2 years. She is taking Plaquenil daily . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer to Rheumatology to stop the medication
k: Well-controlled chronic disease on a pregnancy-safe drug = continue it. SLE safe: hydroxychloroquine, low-dose steroids, azathioprine SLE avoid: methotrexate, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide Epilepsy controlled: continue
r: Hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil) is safe in pregnancy and is recommended to be continued in SLE. She is in remission ("symptom-free for the past 2 years") ON it; stopping it raises the risk of a lupus flare, which is far more dangerous for mother and fetus than the drug.
x: A. Stop Plaquenil: withdrawal increases flare risk in pregnancy; the drug is not teratogenic. | B. Switch it to steroids: steroids are for active flares; switching a well-controlled patient adds risks (diabetes, hypertension, PPROM) with no benefit. | D. Refer to Rheumatology to stop the medication: co-management is reasonable, but the plan to STOP is wrong.

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the clinic unsure of her gestational age. She missed her period 3 months ago but her periods are irregular (see report). Ultrasound: Determined gestational age as 11 weeks . Which of the following was measured in the ultrasound to determine gestational age?
k: Ultrasound dating by trimester. Up to 13+6 weeks: CRL (most accurate) From 14 weeks: HC/BPD, with FL Growth and fetal weight: AC (most sensitive) Earliest scans: gestational sac / yolk sac
r: Her dates are unreliable ("irregular" periods) and the scan gives "11 weeks", which is first trimester. Crown-rump length is the most accurate dating parameter in the first trimester (up to 13+6 weeks), with an error of only about 5-7 days.
x: A. Femur length: a second and third trimester biometry measure used with BPD, HC and AC; not for first-trimester dating. | C. Abdominal circumference: used after the first trimester; it is the most sensitive parameter for fetal growth and weight (IUGR, macrosomia), not for dating. | D. Biparietal diameter and head circumference: used for dating from about 14 weeks onwards, when CRL is no longer valid.

q: A 45-year-old woman P6 is complaining of chronic pelvic pain and heavy menstruation (see report). Pelvic MRI: Diffuse thickened myometrium . Which of the following is the most definitive treatment for her condition?
k: Adenomyosis = endometrial glands within the myometrium. Typical: multiparous, 40s, dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia Exam: diffusely enlarged, boggy, tender, symmetric uterus Imaging: TVUS then MRI (thickened junctional zone) S
r: Chronic pelvic pain, heavy menstruation and a "diffuse thickened myometrium" on MRI in a multiparous woman ("P6") at 45 = adenomyosis. Medical options only control symptoms; the only definitive cure is hysterectomy, appropriate here because her family is complete.
x: B. Hormonal IUD: effective first-line SYMPTOM control (reduces bleeding and pain) and fertility-sparing, but not definitive. | C. Oral contraceptive pills: symptomatic control of bleeding and dysmenorrhea only; disease persists. | D. Dilatation and curettage: removes endometrium for diagnosis or acute bleeding; it cannot reach adenomyosis, which lies within the myometrium.

q: A 43-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months (see report). Ultrasound: A 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
o: Hysteroscopy and removal of the structure
k: Endometrial polyp: intermenstrual bleeding + focal echogenic lesion. Best test to confirm: saline sonography or hysteroscopy Symptomatic or 1 cm or more: hysteroscopic polypectomy Small and asymptomatic (premenopausal):
r: "Intermenstrual bleeding" with a discrete "13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium" is an endometrial polyp. It is symptomatic and over 1 cm, so it should be removed; hysteroscopic polypectomy both treats the bleeding and provides tissue for histology.
x: A. Endometrial sample: a blind pipelle sample can miss a focal lesion; it suits diffuse thickening (e.g. AUB over 45), not a discrete polyp. | B. Repeat the ultrasound in 6 weeks: observation fits only small (under 1 cm), asymptomatic polyps; she is symptomatic. | C. Cyclic progesterone for 3 months: a treatment for anovulatory bleeding or hyperplasia without atypia; it does not remove a polyp.

q: A 30-year-old woman is complaining of yellowish , fishy-smelling vaginal discharge and itching . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Vaginal discharge by its key feature. Fishy odor, thin gray, clue cells, pH over 4.5: BV (metronidazole, no partner treatment) White curdy, itchy, odorless, pH normal: Candida (azoles) Frothy yellow-green, strawberry cer
r: The decisive clue is "fishy-smelling": a fishy (amine) odor, worse after intercourse and positive on the whiff test with KOH, is the defining feature of bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella and anaerobes, clue cells, pH over 4.5). This recall's key treats the odor as decisive over the color and the itch
x: A. Candida vaginitis: thick white cottage-cheese, ODORLESS discharge with marked itching and normal pH (under 4.5). | C. Vaginal gonorrhea: mainly causes cervicitis (mucopurulent cervical discharge, often asymptomatic); no fishy odor. | D. Vaginal trichomoniasis: frothy yellow-green discharge with itching, dyspareunia and strawberry cervix; motile flagellates on wet mount, treat partners too.

q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman with 7 weeks' amenorrhea presented to the clinic with a history of passing tissue at home and vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed mild vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix . Which of the following is the most likely abortion type?
k: Abortion types by cervix and tissue passage. Closed, no tissue: threatened (or missed if non-viable) Open, no tissue: inevitable Open, tissue passed: incomplete Closed, tissue passed: complete Missed: non-viable fetus re
r: Use the 2x2 rule: tissue passed? cervix open or closed? She "passed tissue at home" and now has only "mild" bleeding with a "closed cervix" = all products expelled = complete abortion. Confirm an empty uterus on ultrasound; no evacuation is needed.
x: B. Inevitable: OPEN cervix but NO tissue passed yet. | C. Threatened: closed cervix with bleeding but no tissue passed and a viable pregnancy. | D. Incomplete: tissue passed but the cervix is still OPEN with retained products and often heavier bleeding.

q: A 37-year-old G3 P1011 at 28 weeks ' gestation had vaginal spotting 2 weeks ago but no abdominal cramping or passing any clots or tissue. Examination reveals fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks ' size. Ultrasound confirms lack of fetal heart activity and no fetal movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Fetal death is named by gestational age. Under 20 weeks: missed abortion 20 weeks or more: IUFD / fetal demise Retained IUFD: risk of DIC, check coagulation Management: induction of labor (misoprostol) or expectant
r: The key word is "28 weeks". Absent fetal heart activity and movement on ultrasound at 20 weeks or more (or fetal weight above about 350-500 g) is intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD), not an abortion. The fundal height of only 18 weeks shows the fetus stopped growing weeks ago, and the earlier spotting
x: B. Missed abortion: the same picture (non-viable, retained, closed os, small for dates) but BEFORE 20 weeks. | C. Incomplete abortion: requires passage of tissue with an open cervix; she passed no tissue. | D. Gestational trophoblastic disease: uterus LARGER than dates, very high hCG and snowstorm ultrasound; here the uterus is small and a fetus is seen.

q: A 24-year-old primigravida presents at 12 weeks gestation to an antenatal visit. Blood electrolytes and renal function tests were requested 3 days earlier. Which of the following is the most expected finding on her blood tests?
o: A fall in serum creatinine level
An increase of plasma sodium level
Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level
Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level
k: Renal physiology in pregnancy: GFR up about 50%. Creatinine and BUN: decrease Sodium and osmolality: slight decrease Uric acid: falls early (rise suggests preeclampsia) Glycosuria and mild proteinuria can be physiologica
r: Renal plasma flow and GFR rise by up to about 50% from early pregnancy, so creatinine is cleared faster and serum creatinine FALLS (and so does BUN). By "12 weeks" this fall is already measurable; a "normal" nonpregnant creatinine may actually indicate renal impairment in pregnancy.
x: B. An increase of plasma sodium level: plasma sodium falls slightly in pregnancy (hemodilution and a reset osmostat). | C. Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level: BUN falls with the higher GFR; a rise suggests renal impairment or dehydration. | D. Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level: BUN does change; it decreases from the first trimester.

q: A 35-year-old G9 P6026 at 8 weeks' gestation presents to the hospital with vaginal spotting associated with very mild lower abdominal pain. She has noticed some dark brown clots. Examination reveals she is comfortable in bed with no abdominal tenderness appreciated. Pelvic examination reveals minimal dark-red clots in the introitus and cervical os closed (see report). Transvaginal ultrasound: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step of management plan?
k: Missed abortion (closed os, non-viable, small for dates). Stable, under 13 weeks: expectant management Medical: misoprostol (up to about 20 weeks) Surgical (suction evacuation): heavy bleeding, instability, infection, fa
r: At "8 weeks" by dates the scan shows a "5-week gestational size with no fetal heart" and the "cervical os closed": a non-viable pregnancy retained in the uterus = missed abortion (early pregnancy loss). She is stable, "comfortable", non-tender with only minimal bleeding and no infection, and under 1
kw: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart
x: A. Suction curettage: chosen for heavy bleeding, instability, infection, failed expectant/medical management or patient preference; none is present here. | B. Prostaglandin E2: used for cervical ripening before induction of labor at term; for medical management of miscarriage the agent is misoprostol (PGE1). | D. Abortifacient agent with antibiotic: implies septic abortion (fever, foul discharge, tenderness); she has no signs of infection.

q: A 34-year-old healthy woman presents with recurrent symptoms, including headache, anxiety, and mastalgia , that start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: PMS = cyclic symptoms in the luteal phase, gone soon after menses begin. Symptom-free week after menses is required Diagnosis: clinical, prospective diary for 2 cycles Severe mood symptoms impairing function: PMDD Treatm
r: Physical (headache, mastalgia) and emotional (anxiety) symptoms that "start 8-10 days before menstruation and improve afterward", recurring each cycle in a healthy 34-year-old, are luteal-phase symptoms = premenstrual (tension) syndrome. It is a clinical diagnosis, best confirmed with a prospective
x: A. Endometriosis: dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain and subfertility; it does not cause cyclic anxiety and mastalgia that resolve with menses. | B. Perimenopausal symptoms: hot flushes, night sweats and irregular cycles, usually after 45; not tied to the week before each period. | C. Pelvic congestion syndrome: dull pelvic aching from pelvic varices, worse on standing and after intercourse, usually in multiparous women; no breast or mood symptoms.

q: A 36-year-old G4 P3003 is admitted in preterm labor at 36+5 weeks with polyhydramnios . Fetal bradycardia is noted after spontaneous rupture of membranes . Which of the following needs to be excluded by a prompt vaginal examination?
k: Cord prolapse: sudden bradycardia or variable decelerations right after ROM. Risks: polyhydramnios, malpresentation, prematurity, high head, multiple pregnancy Confirm: vaginal exam (cord felt/seen) Act: call for help, e
r: "Fetal bradycardia" immediately "after spontaneous rupture of membranes" in a woman with "polyhydramnios" (gush of fluid sweeps the cord down) and a preterm, possibly high presenting part is cord prolapse until proven otherwise. A prompt vaginal exam confirms it by feeling the cord below the present
x: B. Breech presentation: a risk factor for cord prolapse but not itself a cause of sudden bradycardia; it is not what the urgent exam needs to exclude. | C. Placental abruption: painful bleeding with a tender hard uterus; a digital exam does not diagnose it. | D. Shoulder/arm prolapse: occurs with transverse lie; it does not cause sudden bradycardia after membrane rupture the way cord compression does.

q: A 32-year-old G2 Pi AO at 12 weeks of gestation . She is a known case of IDDM for 12 years and attended the Antenatal Clinic. Which of the following will most likely increase markedly in this patient?
k: Pregestational DM vs gestational DM. Pregestational: congenital anomalies (cardiac, NTD, caudal regression), miscarriage Both: macrosomia, polyhydramnios, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia GDM begins after organog
r: She has long-standing pregestational diabetes ("IDDM for 12 years"). Hyperglycemia during organogenesis in the first trimester markedly raises the risk of congenital malformations (cardiac defects, neural tube defects, caudal regression), and this is the complication most strongly increased compared
x: A. Preeclampsia: increased in pregestational diabetes (especially with vasculopathy or nephropathy), but the marked, organogenesis-related increase is in malformations. | B. Polyhydramnios: also more common in diabetes (fetal polyuria), but it is a later, less specific complication. | C. Postpartum hemorrhage: may rise slightly through macrosomia and overdistension, but it is not the markedly increased risk.

q: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 40 weeks of gestation was diagnosed with DVT and started on a therapeutic dose of heparin. The patient had a normal vaginal delivery. Shortly after a heparin injection , she sustained postpartum hemorrhage. The uterus was contracted and examination revealed no lacerations . Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: PPH 4 Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin. Heparin (UFH, partly LMWH) reversal: protamine sulfate Warfarin reversal: vitamin K + PCC or FFP DIC: FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets ITP with bleeding: platelets + steroids/IVIG
r: The uterus is "contracted" (not tone) and there are "no lacerations" (not trauma), leaving thrombin as the cause, and the bleeding started "shortly after a heparin injection" at a therapeutic dose. Heparin-related hemorrhage is reversed with its specific antidote, protamine sulfate.
x: A. Vitamin K: reverses warfarin (vitamin K antagonists), not heparin; it also acts slowly. | B. Tranexamic acid: an antifibrinolytic recommended early in PPH generally, but it does not neutralise heparin; the targeted treatment is protamine. | D. Fresh frozen plasma: replaces clotting factors in DIC or warfarin reversal; it does not reverse heparin effect.

q: A 22-year-old PG at 33 weeks of gestation newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes . Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy ?
k: GDM treatment ladder. 1st: diet + exercise + self-monitoring 2nd: insulin (preferred drug, does not cross placenta) Alternative: metformin (or glyburide in some settings) Screening: OGTT at 24-28 weeks
r: She is "newly diagnosed" with gestational diabetes. First-line therapy is medical nutrition therapy (diet) with exercise and glucose self-monitoring; most women reach targets this way. Medication is added only if targets are not met within about 1-2 weeks.
x: B. Metformin: an alternative or add-on when diet fails (or insulin is declined); not first-line at diagnosis. | C. Intravenous insulin: for DKA or intrapartum glucose control on a sliding scale; not for routine GDM. | D. Subcutaneous insulin: the preferred drug if diet and exercise fail to control glucose, but not the first step.

q: Pregnant came and asked about what vaccine to take in first trimester . Best answer
k: Pregnancy vaccines: inactivated yes, live no. Influenza (inactivated): any trimester Tdap: 27 to 36 weeks of every pregnancy Contraindicated: MMR, varicella, live intranasal influenza Live vaccines: avoid pregnancy for a
r: The decisive phrase is "first trimester" : the inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for every pregnant woman at any gestational age, including the first trimester. It protects the mother from severe influenza and the newborn through transferred antibodies.
x: A. MMR: a live attenuated vaccine, contraindicated in pregnancy; given postpartum to rubella non-immune women. | B. Varicella: also live attenuated and contraindicated in pregnancy; give after delivery if non-immune. | C. DTAP: DTaP is the paediatric formulation; pregnant women receive Tdap, and it is timed at 27 to 36 weeks, not the first trimester.

q: Pregnant lady in labor her bishop score is 3 , what would you do?
k: Bishop score decides the induction method. Low score (unfavourable): ripen first with prostaglandin or a balloon catheter High score (≥8, favourable): amniotomy and oxytocin Components: dilation, effacement, station, con
r: A Bishop score of 3 means an unfavourable cervix (score below 6 to 8). Before oxytocin or amniotomy can work, the cervix must be ripened, and prostaglandin (E2 dinoprostone or E1 misoprostol) is the agent used for cervical ripening.
x: A. Oxytocin: used to induce or augment labour once the cervix is favourable (Bishop ≥8) or after ripening; on a closed cervix it usually fails. | B. Amniotomy: needs a dilated, accessible cervix with an engaged head; not possible or effective with a low Bishop score. | C. Progestrone: used to prevent preterm birth (short cervix, prior preterm birth); it maintains pregnancy rather than ripening the cervix.

q: Pregnant with previous history of hydrocephalus . What is the dose of folic acid you will give her at this time? No GA Mentioned
k: Folic acid dose depends on NTD risk and timing. Low risk: 400 micrograms from before conception to 12 weeks High risk (previous NTD, antiepileptics, sickle cell): 4 to 5 mg Neural tube closes by about 4 weeks after conce
r: A previous history of hydrocephalus (often linked with a neural tube defect) raises NTD risk, and no gestational age is given , so the compiler treats her as being in early pregnancy, when the neural tube is still forming. Following his rule (<12 weeks: 1000 micrograms, >12 weeks: 400 micrograms), t
x: A. 400 micrograms: the routine low risk dose, and the keyed answer in the lookalike that states 16 weeks, after neural tube closure. | C. 2 mg: not a standard folic acid regimen in any guideline. | D. 5 mg: the high dose for high risk women (previous NTD-affected pregnancy, antiepileptic drugs, sickle cell disease, diabetes, obesity), ideally started before conception.

q: A 39-year-old primigravida a ended her routine prenatal visit at 39 weeks ' gestation. She denied any headache, visual changes, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain. Urinalysis Was Negative for protein (see lab results). Vital signs at this visit: Blood pressure 160/90 mmHg, Heart rate 84 /min. Vitals signs at all other visits: Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, Heart rate 68 /min. Labs: HCT 0.34 (0.7t-0.48), Platelets count 165 (150-400 x10^9/L), Alanine aminotransferase 12 (5-40 IU/L), Aspartate aminotransferase 22 (12-40 IU/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Hypertension in pregnancy is defined by timing and end-organ signs. Before 20 weeks or pre-pregnancy: chronic hypertension After 20 weeks, no proteinuria or organ damage: gestational hypertension After 20 weeks + protein
r: Her BP was 120/70 at all previous visits and is now 160/90 at 39 weeks, so the hypertension is new and after 20 weeks. There is no proteinuria , no symptoms, and normal platelets and liver enzymes, so there is no end-organ involvement: this is gestational hypertension.
x: A. Eclampsia: requires new onset seizures in a woman with hypertensive disease of pregnancy; she has no seizures. | B. Chronic hypertension: BP elevated before pregnancy or before 20 weeks; her earlier readings were normal. | D. Superimposed preeclampsia: needs pre-existing chronic hypertension plus new proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; she has neither.

q: First time pregnant mom came for her first antenatal visit . Which vaccine should she be given?
k: Antenatal vaccines: inactivated influenza any trimester, Tdap at 27 to 36 weeks. Influenza: any gestational age, every pregnancy Tdap: 27 to 36 weeks, every pregnancy Live vaccines (MMR, varicella): avoid in pregnancy, g
r: At the first antenatal visit (no gestational age given, so early pregnancy) the vaccine that can be given now is inactivated influenza , which is recommended for every pregnant woman at any gestational age. It protects the mother, who is at higher risk of severe influenza, and gives the newborn pass
x: A. Tdap is given in every pregnancy but timed for 27 to 36 weeks to maximise antibody transfer to the baby; it would be the answer if the stem said she is at about 28 weeks. | C. Pneumococcal vaccine is not routine in pregnancy; it is given only for specific indications such as asplenia or chronic disease. | D. Meningococcal vaccine is reserved for specific risks (asplenia, complement deficiency, outbreaks, travel such as Hajj); it is not a routine antenatal vaccine.

q: A 25-year-old woman presents at 10 weeks of gestation for booking in the antenatal clinic. She gave a history of previous intrauterine death with multiple congenital anomalies . Which of the following is the most appropriate time for a detailed anomaly scan ?
k: Antenatal ultrasound timing. Dating scan: about 10 to 13 weeks Nuchal translucency: 11 to 13+6 weeks Detailed anomaly scan: 18 to 22 weeks Growth scans: third trimester if indicated
r: The detailed anomaly (morphology) scan is done at 18 to 22 weeks , when fetal organs are large enough to be assessed in detail and there is still time for counselling and decisions. A previous IUFD with multiple anomalies raises concern but does not change the timing of the detailed scan; she is boo
kw: previous intrauterine death with multiple congenital anomalies
x: A. 10 to 12 weeks is the dating scan window (and nuchal translucency at 11 to 13+6 weeks); organs are too small for a detailed anatomy survey. | B. 14 to 16 weeks is too early for a full anatomy survey; this window is used for second trimester serum screening or amniocentesis, not the detailed scan. | D. 24 to 28 weeks is too late: anomalies found then leave little time for counselling and options; this window is for the glucose challenge test.

q: Which of the following is the recommended folic acid daily dose for a HEALTHY (low-risk) woman who wants to conceive and has no prior diseases or risk factors?
k: Folic acid dose depends on NTD risk. Low risk: 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily, from at least 1 month before conception to 12 weeks High risk: 4 to 5 mg daily High risk = prior NTD, antiepileptics, diabetes, obesity, hemol
r: For a healthy, low risk woman the preconception folic acid dose is low dose, 400 micrograms (0.4 mg) daily, started at least one month before conception. Among the options, 1000 micrograms (1 mg) is the only low dose choice and the closest to the standard low risk dose; only 4000 micrograms correspo
x: B. 2000 micrograms is not a standard regimen for either risk group. | C. 3000 micrograms is not a standard regimen for either risk group. | D. 4000 micrograms (4 mg, or 5 mg in some guidelines) is the high dose for high NTD risk: previous NTD baby, antiepileptic drugs, pregestational diabetes, obesity, sickle cell disease; she has none of these.

q: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea and recurrent cyclic lower abdominal pain . On examination, a bluish/purplish bulging membrane is seen at the vaginal opening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Outflow tract obstruction with normal secondary sexual characteristics. Imperforate hymen: bluish bulging membrane at introitus Transverse vaginal septum: short blind vagina, no bulge at introitus Vaginal (Mullerian) age
r: A 14 year old with primary amenorrhea , cyclic lower abdominal pain (menstruating behind an obstruction, hematocolpos) and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is classic imperforate hymen. Treatment is hymenotomy (cruciate incision) to drain the retained blood.
x: B. Primary amenorrhea is the presenting complaint, not a diagnosis; the question asks for its cause. | C. Endometriosis causes cyclic pain in women who already menstruate and has no bulging membrane at the vaginal opening. | D. Transverse vaginal septum also causes cryptomenorrhea with cyclic pain, but the obstruction is higher in the vagina, so no bulging bluish membrane is seen at the introitus; it does not bulge with Valsalva.

q: Pregnant women at 31 weeks of gestation diagnosed with pretrm premature rupture of membrane CTG shows late deceleration , on examination baby found in the vaginal cavity , what is the best next step?
k: Fetal distress: choose the fastest safe route. Not fully dilated or head high: emergency cesarean Fully dilated, head low (station +2 or below): instrumental delivery Preterm below 34 weeks: forceps, not vacuum Face pres
r: There is fetal compromise (late decelerations) and the head is already low in the vaginal cavity , so the fastest safe delivery is an operative vaginal delivery. At 31 weeks the vacuum is avoided (risk of scalp and intracranial bleeding in the preterm fetus, generally not used below about 34 weeks),
kw: baby found in the vaginal cavity
x: A. Ventouse is contraindicated in a preterm fetus below about 34 weeks; it would be a choice at term with a low head and full dilatation. | C. Cesarean section is right for fetal distress when the cervix is not fully dilated or the head is high; with the baby in the vaginal cavity, an instrumental delivery is quicker and safer.

q: A 44-year-old woman presented with heavy vaginal bleeding and a blood pressure of 93/73 mmHg . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Acute AUB management. Resuscitate (ABC, IV access, blood if needed) Medical: IV estrogen, high dose COCP or progestin, tranexamic acid Severe, unstable or failed medical: D&C Then long term: LNG IUD, ablation, hysterecto
r: This is acute, heavy abnormal uterine bleeding with borderline low blood pressure (93/73) , so the priority is to stop the bleeding quickly. Dilatation and curettage stops severe or refractory bleeding rapidly, and at 44 it also provides endometrial tissue to exclude hyperplasia or cancer.
x: A. Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for refractory bleeding, completed family, or structural disease such as adenomyosis or fibroids, but it is not the first step in an acute bleed. | B. Mefenamic acid (NSAID) modestly reduces chronic heavy menstrual bleeding; it is too weak for acute heavy bleeding with low blood pressure. | C. Hormonal IUD (levonorgestrel) is first line for chronic heavy menstrual bleeding, not for acute heavy bleeding with hemodynamic compromise.

q: A 23-year-old single woman presented with heavy menstruation during the first 4 days of her period for the last 2 years (see image and lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Heavy but regular menses + enlarged/irregular uterus or uterine mass on US = fibroids.
r: Heavy bleeding at the time of menses (cyclical) suggests a structural uterine cause such as a fibroid; irregular bleeding suggests anovulation or endometrial pathology.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0715).

q: A 37-year-old G3 P1011 at 28 weeks’ gestation had vaginal spotting 2 weeks ago but no abdominal cramping or passing any clots or tissue. Examination reveals fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks’ size. Ultrasound confirms lack of fetal heart activity and no fetal movement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Gestational age decides the name: pregnancy loss before 20 weeks is abortion, from 20 weeks on it is fetal demise (IUFD).
r: Same picture at 16 weeks would be missed abortion; the 20 week line is the whole question.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4948).
kw: fundal height equivalent to 18 weeks' size

q: To reduce the occurrence of adhesions in pregnant women undergoing elective Cesarean sections, which of the following strategies can be employed?
o: Add an adhesion barrier before closing the wound
k: Adhesion prevention at CS = good surgical technique.
r: If antibiotics appear as an option, they prevent wound infection and endometritis, not adhesions.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2761).

q: A 24-year-old primigravida presents at 12 weeks gestation to an antenatal visit. Blood electrolytes and renal function tests were requested 3 days earlier. Which of the following is the most expected finding on her blood tests?
o: A fall in serum creatinine level
An increase of plasma sodium level
Increased plasma blood urea nitrogen level
Unaffected serum blood urea nitrogen level
k: Pregnancy: GFR up about 50% from the first trimester, so filtered solutes fall.
r: A non-pregnant 'normal' creatinine in a pregnant woman may already mean impaired renal function.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1312).

q: A 35-year-old woman underwent suction curettage for a molar pregnancy, and her beta-hCG level was 70,000 mIU/mL prior to the procedure. She was followed up with weekly beta-hCG levels for 5 weeks: 1st week post-evacuation: 576 mIU/mL 2nd week post-evacuation: 350 mIU/mL. 3rd week post-evacuation: 180 mIU/mL 4th week post-evacuation: 70 mIU/mL 5th week post-evacuation: 1 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
r: After molar evacuation: weekly beta-hCG until negative 3 times, then monthly; still falling -> repeat in 1 week.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0443).

q: A 33-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presented with vaginal itching, burning, and irritation. Examination revealed a thick discharge with the appearance of cottage cheese in the vagina, Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
k: Candidiasis treatment by context.
r: Pregnancy is the word that turns oral antifungal into topical antifungal.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4799).
kw: thick discharge with the appearance of cottage cheese

q: A 43-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months (see report). Ultrasound: A 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
o: Hysteroscopy and removal of the structure
k: Endometrial polyp management depends on symptoms and size.
r: One criterion is enough: either symptoms or size over 1 cm sends the polyp for hysteroscopic removal.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0701).
kw: 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium

q: A 25-year-old pregnant woman presented with a history of vaginal bleeding and passe tissue at home. Examination revealed an open cervix. Ultrasound: Intrauterine tissue. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion she had?
k: Classify miscarriage by cervix + what has passed + what US shows.
r: Passed tissue + open os + tissue on US = incomplete; passed tissue + closed os + empty uterus = complete.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4988).

q: A 33-year-old 7 weeks' pregnant woman presented with mild vaginal bleeding. Examination revealed a closed cervix. Ultrasound: A 7-week viable intrauterine pregnancy. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion she had?
k: Classify by cervix (open or closed) and tissue (passed or not), plus viability.
r: Closed os + viable fetus = threatened; closed os + dead fetus = missed. Viability is the only fork.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0745).

q: A 17-year-old primigravida presents to the clinic for the first time, missing her period. LM was 9 weeks ago, and she had a positive home pregnancy test. Pelvic examination reveals a closed cervical os with mild bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography: Intrauterine gestational sac with a crown-rump length of 9 wee of gestation with positive embryonic heartbeat. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion?
k: Early pregnancy bleeding: check the cervical os first, then viability on US, then tissue passage.
r: Same stem with an OPEN os becomes inevitable; same stem with no heartbeat (and no bleeding) becomes missed.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1316).

q: A 23-year-old primigravida is admitted with threatened preterm labor at 30 weeks’ gestation and has received antenatal corticosteroids. Which of the following is the rationale behind corticosteroid administration in this case?
k: Preterm labor bundle: steroids for lungs, magnesium for brain, tocolysis to buy time.
r: Tocolytics do not improve neonatal outcome by themselves; their purpose is to buy time for steroids.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0738).

q: A 32-year-old G2 P1 A0 at 12 weeks of gestation, She is a known case of IDDM for 12 years and attended the Antenatal Clinic. Which of the following will most likely increase markedly in this patient?
k: Pregestational versus gestational diabetes.
r: If the stem said gestational diabetes, malformations would NOT be increased; the answer then shifts to macrosomia or polyhydramnios.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4663).

q: A 22-year-old PG at 33 weeks of gestation newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
r: Gestational diabetes: diet and exercise first; insulin if targets not met.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0227).

q: A 23-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound showed fetal hydrops with high peak systolic velocity more than 1.8 MOM in the middle cerebral artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Hydrops + high MCA PSV = fetal anemia = think alloimmunization (anti-D, anti-Kell) or other anemia causes.
r: Normal MCA Doppler with hydrops points away from anemia; look for a structural or chromosomal (non-immune) cause.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1613).

q: A 30-year-old Primigravida is found to have hyperthyroidism during her pregnancy. Which of the following is the most contraindicated?
k: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy: choose the drug by trimester, and never use radioiodine.
r: Separate absolute contraindications in pregnancy (radioiodine) from trimester preferences (methimazole avoided in the first trimester).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3538).

q: A 30-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with an acute monoarthritis, where joint aspiration was performed. Based on the presence of crystals in the synovial fluid, he was diagnosed with gout. Which of the following is the most likely type of the crystals seen?
k: Gout vs pseudogout crystals.
r: Gout = Negative and Needles; the rhomboid, Positive crystals are Pseudogout.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0403).

q: A 37-week pregnant woman with placenta previa presents asking for advice on how to prevent vaginal bleeding. What is the most appropriate advice?
r: Placenta previa: avoid intercourse and vaginal examination.

q: A 39-year-old woman presented at 37 weeks of gestation with scanty vaginal bleeding. She is a known case of placenta previa totalis with a history of two previous episodes of vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most advisable time for admission?
o: If she has another episode of bleeding
r: Placenta previa totalis at 37 weeks with bleeding: admit immediately (and plan CS).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0509).
kw: two previous episodes of vaginal bleeding

q: A 33-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills with strong androgenic progestin is seen in the clinic with a positive pregnancy test, where she is unaware of this pregnancy. Which of the following is the main teratogenic effect on the external genitalia of a female fetus?
r: Androgenic progestins in pregnancy can cause masculinisation of a female fetus.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0504).
kw: oral contraceptive pills with strong androgenic progestin
teratogenic effect on the external genitalia of a female fetus

q: A 32-year-old woman with twin pregnancy, presented at 38 weeks of gestation in active labor. Examination revealed twin A is in vertex presentation, and twin B is also in vertex presentation. Both fetal heart rates are normal Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: Twins, both vertex, at term, normal FHR: spontaneous vaginal delivery.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0483).
kw: twin A is in vertex presentation
twin B is also in vertex presentation

q: A 39-year-old woman, a known case of chronic hypertension, presented at 37 weeks of gestation to the antenatal clinic for follow-up. Examination revealed that the uterine fundal height lags more than 3 cm behind the gestational age. What is the single most effective parameter for predicting fetal weight?
r: IUGR suspected (fundal height lagging): abdominal circumference is the most sensitive single measure of fetal growth.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0484).
kw: uterine fundal height lags more than 3 cm behind the gestational age

q: A 23-year-old woman presented at 10 weeks of gestation with a history of vaginal bleeding, cramp-like pain, and passage of some placental tissue through the cervix. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion?
k: Classify miscarriage by cervix + what has passed + what US shows.
r: Tissue already passed excludes threatened and inevitable; then ask whether the uterus is empty (complete) or not (incomplete).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4987).
kw: passage of some placental tissue through the cervix

q: A 30-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL, Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL, Day 7: 800 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
k: Methotrexate follow-up rule (day 4 vs day 7).
r: The rise from day 1 to day 4 is a trap; judge only day 4 to day 7.
n: ⚠ يشبه OCT-0599 لكن جوابه: Administer a second dose of methotrexate.
kw: methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy

q: A 31-year-old woman G2 P1 was admitted at 41 weeks gestation in active labor. She had received pethidine and promethazine earlier. The cervix is 9 cm dilated, and meconium-stained liquor is draining. Non-stress test done shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?
o: Change the position of the patient
k: Labor with meconium: decide by the CTG.
r: Same scenario with an abnormal CTG (late decelerations) makes change of position clearly correct.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0847).

q: gets pregnant?
o: Continue on ACE inhibitors as it is safe
Continue because the benefit outweighs the risk
Cannot be stopped, so she should not get pregnant
Switch to alternative antihypertensive due to fetal kidney teratogenicity
k: Preconception medication review: ACE inhibitor or ARB: switch to labetalol, methyldopa or nifedipine; Well controlled antiepileptic not absolutely contraindicated: continue; Hydroxychloroquine in SLE: continue
r: ACE inhibitor = switch before conception; the 'fetal kidney' wording confirms the option.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-6945).
kw: hypertension and is on ACE inhibitors

q: A 32-year-old woman G2 P1 L1. She is 39 weeks pregnant with normal prenatal care, presented to the Emergency Room with headache and blurred vision (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit for observation and repeat testing
r: Term (39 weeks) with headache and blurred vision = preeclampsia with severe features: deliver (after MgSO4 and BP control).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0399).

q: A 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days and now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued (see lab results), Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Manage the bleeding and send her home
r: Prolonged heavy bleeding with drowsiness/fatigue = symptomatic anaemia: stabilise first with blood transfusion, then investigate.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0379).
kw: period has not stopped for the past 15 days

q: A 43-year-old woman with a history of pulmonary embolism 3 years ago is seeking an effective family planning method. Which of the following is the most appropriate method?
k: Prior VTE / PE: no estrogen.
r: Pill, patch and ring all contain estrogen; after a clot, go straight to an IUD.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-5627).

q: An 18-year-old girl complains of severe lower abdominal pain and back pain on the first 2 days of her cycle every period. She has a regular cycle and is medically free. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: Primary dysmenorrhea ladder: lifestyle (heat, exercise) then NSAIDs then combined OCP, then laparoscopy if still refractory.
r: Check whether the stem says NSAIDs were already tried: untried = NSAIDs, failed = OCP.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-5608).
kw: severe lower abdominal pain and back pain on the first 2 days of her cycle

q: A 33-year-old 7 weeks’ pregnant woman presented with mild vaginal bleeding Examination revealed a closed cervix. Ultrasound: A 7-week viable intrauterine pregnancy. Which of the following is the most likely type of abortion she had?
k: Classify by cervix (open or closed) and tissue (passed or not), plus viability.
r: Closed os + viable fetus = threatened; closed os + dead fetus = missed. Viability is the only fork.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0745).

q: A 34-year-old healthy woman presents with recurrent symptoms, including headache, anxiety, and mastalgia, that start 8- 10 days before menstruation and improve afterward. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: PMS = cyclic symptoms in the luteal phase that resolve early in menses.
r: If symptoms persist after menses or throughout the cycle, it is not PMS: think of an underlying mood or anxiety disorder.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0478).

q: A 26-year-old woman primigravida at 16 weeks’ gestation presents to the clinic complaining of nausea and vomiting, Which of the following is the most likely cause of this condition?
r: ⚠ Garbled recall. Key: folate deficiency (poor intake with vomiting, increased demand in pregnancy).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0271).

q: A 23-year-old primigravida admitted for induction of labor. The cervix is closed and 3.5 cm long. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent to be given to her for cervical ripening?
k: Before induction, assess the Bishop score.
r: Closed and long cervix = ripen first (prostaglandin); oxytocin alone is for a favorable cervix.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2500).

q: A 22-year-old PG at 33 weeks of gestation newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
r: Gestational diabetes: diet and exercise first; insulin if targets not met.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0227).

q: A pregnant woman with preeclampsia has just delivered and has a lax uterus with moderate postpartum hemorrhage. Physical examination reveals no laceration or retained product of conception. Which of the following medical therapies is most recommended?
o: 20 units oxytocin in a 500 mL of D5W given intravenously
k: Atonic PPH: uterine massage plus uterotonics in order.
r: Preeclampsia plus PPH: skip ergometrine and go to carboprost if oxytocin fails; asthma plus PPH: skip carboprost.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1772).

q: A 34-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation is evaluated for a severe headache. Her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. Neurologic and cardiopulmonary examination is normal. She has a gravid uterus and 2+ edema of the lower extremities. No petechiae or ecchymoses are seen (see lab results and report). Peripheral smear: Occasional fragmented erythrocytes without platelet clumping Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
r: Severe preeclampsia/HELLP at 38 weeks: the cure is delivery, emergently.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0065).

q: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Asthma Clinic. She currently uses a salbutamol inhaler 100 mcg prn combined with a beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 400 mcg bd. Despite this, she is having frequent exacerbations of her asthma that required frequent courses of prednisolone and hospitalization three times in the last 6 months. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start to take the salbutamol regularly
r: Asthma not controlled on moderate ICS: step up by adding a LABA (salmeterol).
n: ⚠ يشبه GB-0020 لكن جوابه: Add long-acting B2 agonist (Salmeterol).
kw: hospitalization three times in the last 6 months

q: A 30-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with an acute monoarthritis where joint aspiration was performed. Based on the presence of crystals in the synovial fluid, he was diagnosed with gout. Which of the following is the most likely type of the crystals seen?
k: Gout vs pseudogout crystals.
r: Gout = Negative and Needles; the rhomboid, Positive crystals are Pseudogout.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0403).

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the clinic unsure of her gestational age. She missed her period 3 months ago but her periods are irregular. Ultrasound: determined gestational age as 11 weeks. Which of the following was measured in the ultrasound to determine gestational age?
r: Dating before 14 weeks: crown-rump length is the most accurate.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0367).

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with a very heavy period. She is morbidly obese and diabetic. Her periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months. She had her period 2 weeks ago and it has not stopped, with heavy clots. Pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Irregular, infrequent cycles + heavy prolonged bleeding = anovulatory AUB (AUB-O).
r: The rhythm decides it: irregular cycles point to ovulatory dysfunction, regular heavy cycles point to a structural or bleeding cause.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0747).

q: A 45-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room complaining that her period has not stopped for the past 15 days. Now she is feeling drowsy and easily fatigued and sometimes faints. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
k: Heavy prolonged bleeding with anemia symptoms: labs first, then act.
r: If the stem already gives Hb and BHCG (SWR-2230), the answer moves away from ordering labs.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2231).
kw: period has not stopped for the past 15 days

q: - Pat with ectopic pregnancy, received a dose of MTX, beta hCG is 1000 then 1200 then 1100, best management?
o: Measure beta hCG in one wee
r: Ectopic after methotrexate with hCG plateau (not falling ≥15%): give a second dose of methotrexate.

q: A 26-year-old average-size woman has delivered a baby boy within the last 24 hours. During the morning round in the post-partum ward, it was found that her blood group is B-, her husband is O+, and her son is A+. A 300-g dose of anti-D immunoglobulin was prescribed. Which of the following volume of fetal blood will be protected by the prescribed dose?
k: 300 micrograms anti-D = 30 mL fetal whole blood = 15 mL fetal RBCs.
r: "Average size" means a standard bleed; a large hemorrhage needs Kleihauer-Betke and extra doses.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4590).

q: PPROM at 31 weeks of gestation. The doctor decided on conservative management. At 35 weeks, the mother developed contractions. What is the most likely fetal complication?
r: Long latency after PPROM: the main fetal risk is infection (sepsis/chorioamnionitis).

q: A 45-year-old P5+3 presented with abnormal uterine bleeding, regular cycle, associated with clots and pain not relieved by simple analgesia. Previous myomectomy and 3 surgical evacuations. Pelvic exam: bulky, tender uterus, no adnexal mass. BMI 40. Most likely explanation?
r: Painful heavy periods, bulky tender uterus, previous uterine surgery = adenomyosis.

q: G1p0 pt in 28 weeks came for routine follow up and found fetal stillbirth (absent heartbeat) what the most indicate diagnose chromosomal abnormality in fetus sample of ?
k: Fetal demise karyotyping: sample type follows timing.
r: Ask first: has the baby been delivered? No = amniotic sampling; yes = placental tissue.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0728).

q: Country conduct study of maternal mortality found there is 450 maternal death due to complication of pregnancy and childbirth , and there is in the same year 200,000 life birth. Which of the following is representing maternity mortality rate?
r: Maternal mortality ratio = deaths / live births × 100,000 = 450/200,000 × 100,000 = 225.

q: 20 years old single woman present with pelvic pian for 2 months (not sure of duration) CA-125 was 12 (0-35 U/mL) CT scan of pevis shows: Solid, multiloculated, complex ovarian cyst of 4 cm (not sure of size) what is the most appropriate management?
k: Adnexal mass management: Simple, asymptomatic, 5 cm or less, premenopausal: observe, repeat US in 6 to 8 weeks; Complex, symptomatic, larger than 5 cm, or found at surgery: cystectomy; Postmenopausal or high CA-125 with a complex mass: gynecologic oncology work-up
