r: Young woman + complex cyst: cystectomy (ovary-sparing), not oophorectomy.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0565).

q: A newly married woman presents with pelvic pain and amenorrhea for 6 weeks. Ultrasound shows a right-sided tubal mass measuring 4 cm. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Expectant management with follow up of bhcg
k: Tubal ectopic: MTX if all criteria met, otherwise surgery.
r: 4 cm is the cutoff: below 4 cm can be methotrexate, 4 cm or more goes to surgery.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0526).

q: A 28-year-old primigravida presents for an ultrasound scan. Ultrasound shows a single viable fetus with significant oligohydramnios. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Amniotic fluid volume = fetal urine in minus fetal swallowing out.
r: Things the fetus cannot swallow or that increase urine output cause polyhydramnios; things that reduce urine output cause oligohydramnios.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0696).

q: Pregnant 32 weeks with HTN 160/110, headache, and blurred vision No proteinurea what's the management?
k: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP ≥160/110 or severe symptoms (headache, visual change, epigastric pain), with or without proteinuria.
r: A seizure flips the answer to MgSO4 (after ABC), even with a BP of 160/110.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0021).

q: A woman planning to become pregnant has mild fatigue. TSH is 7 with normal T3/T4. What is the appropriate management?
o: Start levothyroxine when she becomes pregnant
k: Planning pregnancy with high TSH and normal T4: the TSH level decides when to start.
r: Check the TSH number: above 10 flips the answer to starting levothyroxine now.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0049).

q: What is the most common risk factor for abruptio placenta?
r: Most common risk factor for placental abruption = maternal hypertension (preeclampsia).

q: What is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage?
k: Causes of PPH, the 4 Ts in order of frequency: Tone: uterine atony, most common (soft, boggy uterus); Trauma: genital tract lacerations, second (bleeding with a FIRM uterus); Tissue: retained placenta or products
r: Most common = atony; second = trauma. A firm uterus flips the answer to trauma.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-5042).

q: Pregnant 32 weeks with HTN 160/110, headache, and blurred vision No proteinurea what's the management?
k: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP ≥160/110 or severe symptoms (headache, visual change, epigastric pain), with or without proteinuria.
r: A seizure flips the answer to MgSO4 (after ABC), even with a BP of 160/110.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0021).

q: postpartum woman had DIC whats the commonest cause?
r: Commonest obstetric cause of DIC = placental abruption.

q: 30-year-old female at 38 weeks of gestation presents in labor. Cervical examination shows 4 cm dilatation with ruptured membranes. Abdominal examination reveals breech presentation, with the presenting part 1 cm above the ischial spines. CTG is reassuring. Ultrasound estimates fetal weight at 2.9 kg from previous US. There has been no progression for 2 hours. What is the next step in management?
k: Breech in labour plus failure to progress means caesarean section, even when the criteria for vaginal breech birth are met.
r: The same failure to progress in a cephalic labour with weak contractions would be oxytocin. The breech presentation is the clue that makes it caesarean section.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0464).

q: cesarean section (CS) patient refuses the procedure and asks for a second opinion. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Both consents are not needed in the ER
Respect her wish and refer for a second opinion
Try to persuade her against her will
r: Competent woman refusing CS: respect her decision and offer a second opinion; husband's consent is not a substitute.

q: 30-year-old woman presents with chronic pelvic pain and urinary urgency, which is relieved by voiding. Diagnostic aparoscopy was performed to rule out endometriosis, but the findings were normal. What is the next best step in management?
k: Pelvic pain plus urgency relieved by voiding = bladder pain syndrome until proven otherwise.
r: Pain that improves after emptying the bladder is a bladder problem: send to urology, not back to theatre.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-2191).
kw: chronic pelvic pain and urinary urgency, which is relieved by voiding

q: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Asthma Clinic. She currently uses a salbutamol inhaler 100 mcg prn combined with a beclometasone dipropionate inhaler 400 mcg bd. Despite this, she is having frequent exacerbations of her asthma that required frequent courses of prednisolone and hospitalization three times in the last 6 months. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Start to take the salbutamol regularly
r: Asthma not controlled on moderate ICS: add a LABA (salmeterol).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0020).
kw: hospitalization three times in the last 6 months

q: A 25-year-old woman is seen for a routine prenatal evaluation; she is 12 weeks pregnant. This is her second pregnancy; the first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Medical history is notable for sickle cell disease requiring 1 to 2 hospitalizations per year for painful events. She has no history of stroke or acute chest syndrome. Her only medication is a folic acid supplement. Cardiac examination reveals a grade $2/6$ systolic flow murmur (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Stable SCD in pregnancy: high risk, so close multidisciplinary follow-up; no routine transfusion.
r: Hydroxyurea is the trap: it is the right answer for frequent crises or ACS in a NON-pregnant patient, but is teratogenic in pregnancy.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1299).
kw: 1 to 2 hospitalizations per year for painful events
no history of stroke or acute chest syndrome

q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented to the Emergency Department with 3-hour continuous retrosternal heaviness associated with profuse sweating. Physical examination reveals tachycardia and an S4 gallop on heart auscultation. The patient is commenced on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin infusion (see reports). Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block. Previous ECG was normal. Cardiac enzymes: Pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Wait for the results of cardiac enzymes
r: STEMI within 12 h and no PCI available: thrombolysis without waiting for enzymes.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0113).

q: female patient on isotretinoin for acne wishes to conceive. What should the physician tell her about the appropriate time?
o: She can conceive as soon as she stops isotretinoin
She can conceive while taking isotretinoin
She can conceive 3 months after stopping isotretinoin
k: Retinoids: know the washout.
r: Do not confuse isotretinoin (1 month) with acitretin, whose washout is measured in years.
n: ⚠ يشبه OCT-4761 لكن جوابه: She can conceive after 1 month of stoppi. If There is 1 Month , Then Go For It

q: Patients post Rhematic fever have Moderate to sever MR with HF symptoms What is the best??
r: Rheumatic severe MR with heart failure symptoms: surgery (mitral valve repair/replacement); drugs only bridge.
n: Option “A” is Just A Stabilizing Procedure For HF Symptoms Till Valve Replacement Is Ready Q: What If It Says Next? A: NEXT For Symptomatic Valvular Heart Disease is [SURGERY]

q: Female 39 week gestation came in labour Cervix 6 cm 80% effacement -1 stage Fetal HR 140 Ealy declaration What to do?
r: Early decelerations = head compression, benign: continue normal labour monitoring.

q: A 30-year-old Primigravida at 17 weeks of gestation is known to have epilepsy and is on valproic acid. She was concerned about the possible risks to her baby. Which of the following fetal abnormalities is markedly increased?
k: Antiepileptic teratogens: Valproate: neural tube defects (highest risk), also neurodevelopmental delay; Carbamazepine: neural tube defects (lower risk); Phenytoin: fetal hydantoin syndrome
r: Match drug to defect: valproate = neural tube defect, phenytoin = fetal hydantoin syndrome, lithium = Ebstein anomaly, warfarin = nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3312).

q: A 23-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound showed fetal hydrops with high peak systolic velocity more than 1.8 MOM in the middle cerebral artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
k: Hydrops + high MCA PSV = fetal anemia = think alloimmunization (anti-D, anti-Kell) or other anemia causes.
r: Normal MCA Doppler with hydrops points away from anemia; look for a structural or chromosomal (non-immune) cause.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1613).

q: A 23-year-old PG at 28 weeks of gestation known case of tricuspid regurgitation complaining of slight limitation of physical activity. What is her heart failure class based on the New York Heart Association classification?
k: NYHA classifies by symptoms with activity.
r: Slight = II, marked = III, at rest = IV; the underlying valve lesion does not set the class.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-1934).

q: A 23-year-old primigravida is admitted with threatened preterm labor at 30 weeks' gestation and has received antenatal corticosteroids. Which of the following is the rationale behind corticosteroid administration in this case?
k: Preterm labor bundle: steroids for lungs, magnesium for brain, tocolysis to buy time.
r: Tocolytics do not improve neonatal outcome by themselves; their purpose is to buy time for steroids.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0738).

q: A 25-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks' gestation presents with generalized pruritus and yellowish discoloration of the sclera and skin. Which of the following is the most important investigation?
o: Bile acids and liver function tests
k: Itch without rash in the third trimester, worse on palms and soles = cholestasis of pregnancy.
r: Pruritus with jaundice in late pregnancy: order bile acids, not an imaging or fetal growth test.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-9710).
kw: yellowish discoloration of the sclera and skin

q: A 38-year-old woman, known for low-lying placenta, delivered a normal vaginal delivery. One hour post-delivery, she had postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: PPH causes = 4 Ts, in order of frequency.
r: If the stem says the uterus is FIRM and contracted, atony is out and genital tract trauma becomes the answer.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0740).

q: A 50-year-old woman is complaining of hot flashes and insomnia. Which of the following is the most appropriate first- line management?
k: Choose HRT over lifestyle only when the stem shows moderate to severe symptoms.
r: Local estrogen is for vaginal symptoms; systemic estrogen is for flushes.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0920).

q: 45-year-old woman came to the clinic complaining of heavy periods lasting more than 10 days. Pregnancy test is negative and ultrasound is normal. Which of the following medication is the most appropriate to use?
k: Acute or heavy AUB management ladder: Unstable, acute heavy bleeding: IV conjugated estrogen; Stable: COCP or oral progestogen; Non-hormonal: tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic), NSAIDs (mefenamic acid)
r: If every other option is a uterotonic (oxytocin, carboprost, misoprostol), the non-pregnant patient gets tranexamic acid.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-0739).
kw: heavy periods lasting more than 10 days

q: A 23-year-old woman came to the clinic complaining of severe pain the day prior to menses, continuing for 2 days. The pain is so severe that she misses work. Which of the following is the most appropriate to control her pain so that she can go to work?
r: Severe primary dysmenorrhoea: NSAIDs or combined hormonal pills (suppress ovulation); here the COC.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0381).
kw: severe pain the day prior to menses

q: A 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy had an ultrasound confirming Dichorionic Diamniotic twins. What was the time interval between ovulation and cleavage?
k: Later split = more shared membranes.
r: Read the membrane type in the stem carefully: other versions ask MCDA (4-8 days) or MCMA (9-12 days).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-3452).

q: A 32-year-old woman G2 P1 L1. She is 39 weeks pregnant with normal prenatal care, presented to the Emergency Room with headache and blurred vision (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
o: Admit for observation and repeat testing
r: Term with headache and blurred vision = severe preeclampsia: admit for delivery.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0399).

q: A 30-year-old woman G2 P1 L1 presented 3 days ago to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with preterm premature rupture of membranes. She was managed expectantly and today she started to have fever and abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: PPROM complications and management.
r: A sibling version asks the next step: antibiotics and deliver, not continued expectant care.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-5351).

q: 50-year-old woman was managed conservatively for the last 6 months for grade 3 posterior vaginal prolapse, experiencing mild to moderate pelvic discomfort. Examination today shows similar findings with no progression or improvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
k: Prolapse is treated by symptoms, not grade alone.
r: Same grade 3 prolapse: asymptomatic = reassure; still symptomatic after 6 months of conservative care = counsel for surgery.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-4813).

q: A 20-year-old woman at 6 weeks gestation is receiving methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy. The first dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM was administered one week ago. The human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels on days 1, 4, and 7 were as follows: Day 1: 1000 mIU/mL Day 4: 1200 mIU/mL Day 7: 1100 mIU/mL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
k: Methotrexate follow-up rule (day 4 vs day 7).
r: The rise from day 1 to day 4 is a trap; judge only day 4 to day 7.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0599).
kw: methotrexate treatment for an ectopic pregnancy

q: A 33-year-old patient presents with vaginal spotting for the last 3 days. She is 7 weeks pregnant, and the transvaginal scan does not reveal an intrauterine or extrauterine gestational sac. Which of the following is the most appropriate next action?
o: Repeat lab and ultrasound evaluation in 48 hours
k: PUL = positive pregnancy test with no sac seen anywhere on TVUS.
r: Never give methotrexate or operate before the pregnancy is located, unless the patient is unstable.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2270).
kw: does not reveal an intrauterine or extrauterine gestational sac

q: A 17-year-old primigravida presents to the Emergency Department complaining of mild vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping. Her last period was 9 weeks ago, and she has a positive home pregnancy test (see report). Transvaginal Ultrasonography: Intrauterine gestational sac with a crown-rump length corresponding to 9 weeks' gestation with a positive heartbeat. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
r: First-trimester bleeding: assess with pelvic (speculum) examination to see if the os is open and confirm the type of miscarriage.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0456).
kw: mild vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping

q: A patient presents at 32 weeks of gestation with sudden vaginal bleeding of 700 cc. Which of the following is this type of bleeding?
k: Classify obstetric bleeding by its timing relative to delivery.
r: Same 32 weeks bleed becomes intrapartum if the stem says she is in labor (e.g. cervix 7 cm).
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-2222).

q: A 42-year-old P4+2 presented with severe, progressive secondary dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. Pelvic examination demonstrated a tender, diffusely enlarged uterus (see report). Endometrial biopsy: Normal endometrium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
r: Secondary dysmenorrhoea + menorrhagia + diffusely enlarged tender uterus, normal endometrium = adenomyosis.
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0497).

q: A 21-year-old woman with primary infertility for the last 4 years is seen in the clinic for follow-up. Investigation showed that her hormonal profile is normal and her husband's semen analysis is also normal. The hysterosalpingogram showed proximal blocked tubes bilaterally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
r: Unexplained infertility with normal hormones/semen: diagnostic laparoscopy and dye test (tubal patency, endometriosis).
n: مكرر من القديم (GB-0541).
kw: primary infertility for the last 4 years

q: A 25-year-old woman has been seeking fertility for the last 3 years. She had 2 unsuccessful in vitro fertilization trials. Pelvic Ultrasound: Multiple uterine fibroids of variable sizes. Which of the following will most likely increase her chance of reaching a successful pregnancy?
o: GnRH injection to reduce the size of the fibroid
k: Fibroids + infertility → myomectomy.
r: "Wants pregnancy" removes UAE and hysterectomy from the list; "most likely increase chance" means the definitive fertility-sparing step.
n: مكرر من القديم (OCT-0754).

q: A 30-year-old woman was diagnosed to have a complete abortion at 10 weeks of gestation. The patient is a heavy smoker and smokes more than 20 cigarettes a day. She was not taking any folic acid or dietary supplements. Which of the following is the most likely risk that caused the miscarriage?
o: Smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day
k: Miscarriage risk question: choose the established risk factor given in the stem.
r: "Not taking folic acid" is the distractor; it answers an NTD question, not a miscarriage question.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-4203).

q: A patient had colorectal cancer and does not wish to do the surgery. The Patient Is Alert And Fully Aware Of His Condition And He Refuses To Be Operated On. After SEVERAL WEEKS , The Patient Deteriorated And Developed Decreased Consciousness. His wife and son Approach You And Request You To Operate On Him , What is the most appropriate management?
o: Do the surgery if The Request In Writing
Refuse the surgery as the patient wishes
Honer Family's Wishes And Do The Surgery
r: A competent patient's refusal stays valid after he loses capacity: respect his prior wish, do not operate.

q: A 24-year-old single woman presents with dysmenorrhea and a feeling of pelvic heaviness. On pelvic examination, a firm, palpable mass in the pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Firm pelvic mass + heaviness or heavy bleeding in a reproductive age woman = fibroid; ultrasound is initial and diagnostic.
r: Firm uterine mass = fibroid; cyclic pain with a fixed retroverted uterus and uterosacral nodules = endometriosis instead.
n: مكرر من القديم (SWR-3350).
kw: firm, palpable mass in the pelvis

q: Postpartum woman Rh-negative, newborn also Rh-negative. Appropriate management?
o: Does not require any dose of anti-D
Administer anti-D only if mother develops symptoms
k: Postpartum anti-D: Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive baby, within 72 hours.

q: A child was admitted to the PICU with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). His condition initially improved with treatment, but he suddenly developed confusion and neurological signs . What is the most appropriate next step in management?

r: A term IUGR newborn has low glycogen stores and little fat, so after birth it cannot maintain glucose, making hypoglycemia the most common and most concerning metabolic complication. q: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother. q: A young patient presents complaining of recurrent urinary tract infections . What investigation should the doctor do in order to look for kidney scarring as a complication of recurrent UTIs. What's the investigation?
k: Pediatric UTI imaging by question: First febrile or recurrent UTI: renal and bladder ultrasound Hydronephrosis or suspected reflux: VCUG (MCUG) Renal scarring: DMSA scan Posterior urethral valves in boys: VCUG
r: The question asks specifically for kidney scarring . A DMSA scan (technetium labelled dimercaptosuccinic acid) is taken up by functioning cortical tubular cells, so scars appear as photopenic defects; it is the gold standard to detect renal scarring, ideally done months after the acute infection.
x: A. Renal ultrasound is the first investigation after a febrile or recurrent UTI to look for hydronephrosis and structural anomalies, but it is insensitive for cortical scars. | B. Contrast voiding urosonography (or micturating cystography) detects vesicoureteral reflux, the cause of recurrent UTI, not the scarring itself. | D. Voiding cystourethrogram is the test for vesicoureteral reflux and posterior urethral valves; choose it when ultrasound shows hydronephrosis or the question asks for reflu

q: A preterm delivered at 34 weeks of gestation with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) failed weaning from mechanical ventilation , what is the most appropriate next step ?

q: A newborn has not passed meconium within 48 hours and develops abdominal distension. Rectal examination causes explosive passage of stool and temporarily relieves the symptoms. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

q: A child presents with symptoms of celiac disease and has positive anti-tTG IgA and positive anti-endomysial antibody (EMA) . Which of the following is considered the confirmatory test ?

The lead-in asks for the confirmatory test,
x: A. Skipping further testing relies on the no-biopsy pathway (very high tTG with positive EMA on a separate sample), which is not universally accepted; the standard confirmatory step is biopsy. | C. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 typing has a high negative predictive value and is used to exclude celiac disease, not to confirm it. | D. Repeating serology is used to monitor adherence to a gluten-free diet after diagnosis, not to confirm the diagnosis.

q: Name of the reflex ?
k: Primitive reflexes, stimulus and disappearance: Rooting: stroke cheek, mouth turns to stimulus; gone by about 4 months Stepping: soles on surface, walking movements; gone by about 2 months ATNR (fencing): head turned, fa
r: The picture shows a finger stroking the cheek and the infant's mouth turning toward the finger. A tactile stimulus at the side of the mouth that makes the infant turn and seek the stimulus is the rooting reflex, present from birth to help locate the nipple for feeding.
x: B. Stepping reflex: the infant is held upright with the soles touching a surface and makes alternating walking movements; it involves the legs, not the mouth.

q: (Recall context from the page: a picture of the rooting reflex.) Time of disappearance ?
k: Match the reflex to its disappearance age: Stepping: about 2 months ATNR: about 3 months (2 accepted in recalls) Rooting, Galant: about 4 months Moro, palmar grasp: about 6 months Babinski: 12 to 18 months Parachute: app
r: The picture is the rooting reflex (stroking the cheek, mouth turns toward it). It is present from birth and disappears by about 4 months , as voluntary head control and feeding behaviour take over.
x: A. By 2 months: the age usually quoted for disappearance of the stepping reflex, and the age the ATNR (fencing) question accepts; too early for rooting. | C. By 6 months: disappearance age of the Moro and palmar grasp reflexes, not rooting.

q: A 24-month-old baby is brought in with a right sided red inflamed hemiscrotum. On exploration, the right tests is viable however; the cord is thick and oedematous . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Acute scrotum in children: Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex; explore immediately Appendage torsion: upper-pole tenderness, blue dot, cremasteric reflex present; analge
r: At exploration the testis was viable (not twisted or ischemic) and the cord was thick and edematous . Inflammation that thickens the cord and epididymis with a healthy testis is epididymo-orchitis; the red, inflamed hemiscrotum fits the inflammatory process.
x: A. Testicular torsion: exploration would show a twisted cord and a dusky or necrotic testis; a viable, untwisted testis excludes it. | C. Incarcerated inguinal hernia: there would be bowel or omentum in a hernial sac extending up into the groin, not just an edematous cord. | D. Torsion of a testicular appendage: shows a small infarcted appendage at the upper pole (blue dot sign) with a normal cord, usually in boys aged 7 to 12.

q: 6 year Child fully vaccinated came with injury from rusty nail What the propriate mangement additional to ab
k: Tetanus prophylaxis in wounds: Clean minor wound: vaccine if last dose >10 years or unknown Dirty or tetanus-prone wound: vaccine if last dose >5 years Unknown or fewer than 3 doses: vaccine, plus tetanus immunoglobulin
r: A fully vaccinated 6-year-old has just completed (or recently received) the DTaP booster at 4 to 6 years, so the last dose is well within 5 years even for a tetanus-prone rusty-nail wound. No vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed; what every wound still needs is thorough cleaning and irrigation (with
x: A. Td: the booster for children 7 years and older and adults; it would be given for a dirty wound if more than 5 years have passed since the last dose. | B. DTaP: the formulation for children under 7, given for a dirty wound only if the series is incomplete or the last dose was more than 5 years ago. | C. Nothing: wrong because wound cleaning and irrigation are always required, even when no tetanus prophylaxis is needed.

q: 1-week-old infant presents with a history of conjunctivitis associated with white eye discharge . Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
k: Ophthalmia neonatorum by onset: Within 24 hours: chemical (prophylaxis drops) 2 to 5 days: Neisseria gonorrhoeae, hyperpurulent, risk of corneal perforation; IV/IM ceftriaxone 5 to 14 days: Chlamydia trachomatis; oral er
r: Neonatal conjunctivitis appearing at 1 week (typical window 5 to 14 days) with watery to mucoid discharge fits Chlamydia trachomatis acquired from the birth canal. The timing is the key: gonococcal infection starts earlier (2 to 5 days) with profuse purulent discharge, and chemical conjunctivitis ap
x: A. Haemophilus influenzae: causes bacterial conjunctivitis in older infants and children (often with otitis media); not the classic organism at 1 week. | B. Adenovirus: causes viral conjunctivitis with fever, pharyngitis or diarrhea in older children; uncommon in the first week of life.

q: Which of the following cerebral palsy type is associated with Kernicterus ?
k: Cerebral palsy type by lesion site: Spastic (pyramidal tract): diplegia in prematurity/PVL, hemiplegia after stroke, quadriplegia after severe HIE Dyskinetic (basal ganglia): kernicterus, HIE at term Ataxic (cerebellum)
r: Kernicterus is deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem nuclei. Basal ganglia injury produces dyskinetic (athetoid or choreoathetoid) cerebral palsy, often with sensorineural hearing loss and upward gaze palsy.
x: A. Spastic: the most common type, from upper motor neuron (pyramidal) injury such as periventricular leukomalacia in preterm infants (diplegia) or stroke (hemiplegia). | B. Ataxic: results from cerebellar damage, giving wide-based gait and intention tremor. | C. Hypotonic: a nonspecific early or atonic picture, not the classic consequence of kernicterus.

q: Child diagnosed with meningococcal , contact with brother and sister. What is the most appropriate chemoprophylaxis for household members ?
k: Meningococcal chemoprophylaxis for close contacts: Rifampicin twice daily for 2 days (common choice in children) Ciprofloxacin single oral dose Ceftriaxone single IM dose (preferred in pregnancy) Hib contacts: rifampicin
r: Household contacts of a meningococcal case need chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible, regardless of vaccination. Accepted regimens are rifampicin for 2 days, a single IM dose of ceftriaxone, or a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin ; of the listed options only ciprofloxacin is given with the correct r
x: A. Penicillin and rifampicin for 1 week: penicillin does not eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a 2 day course, not a week. | C. Ceftriaxone IM 3 doses: ceftriaxone is effective but given as a single IM dose (useful in pregnancy); multiple doses are not needed.

q: picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia , the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue , CBC shows microcytic hypochromic RBC , What is the treatment ?
k: Microcytic + koilonychia = iron deficiency, treat with oral iron. Clues: pallor, pica, angular cheilitis, koilonychia, thrombocytosis Labs: low MCV, low ferritin, high RDW Common cause in children: excess cow's milk, poo
r: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic film is iron deficiency anaemia. First line treatment in a child is oral ferrous sulfate , continued for about 3 months after Hb normalises to refill stores.
x: A. Parenteral iron is reserved for malabsorption, intolerance or non-adherence to oral iron, or failure of oral therapy; it is not first line. | C. Folic acid treats folate deficiency, which causes a macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia, not a microcytic one. | D. B12 treats megaloblastic anaemia with high MCV and possible neurological signs; it does not correct a microcytic picture.

q: Young boy under 10 with fatigue dsypnea and palpitations during physical activity . His physical examination is normal. His older brother has a history of sudden cardiac death . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Family history of sudden death in the young = exclude HCM (echo + ECG). Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation Murmur: ejection systolic at left sternal edge, louder with Valsalva/standing Symptoms: exertional syncope, ch
r: Exertional fatigue, dyspnoea and palpitations in a child with an older brother who had sudden cardiac death point to an inherited cardiomyopathy, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in the young. A normal examination does not exclude it, since many have no mu
kw: older brother has a history of sudden cardiac death
x: A. PDA gives a continuous machinery murmur and bounding pulses; it is not familial and is not linked to sibling sudden death. | B. AVSD is usually detected in infancy (often with Down syndrome) with a murmur and heart failure; the exam would not be normal. | C. VSD produces a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge; a normal exam and family sudden death argue against it.

q: -5m infant is brought by his mother, who has noticed decreased activity and that he no longer smiles . He has repeated crusts of sudden brief flexion-extension spasms , each lasting 1-2 seconds, with about 20 spasms per cluster . An EEG is ordered. Which finding is expected?
k: West syndrome triad: spasms + hypsarrhythmia + developmental arrest. Onset: usually 3 to 12 months Spasms in clusters, often on waking Causes: tuberous sclerosis, hypoxic injury, metabolic, idiopathic Treatment: ACTH or
r: A 5 month old with clusters of brief flexion extension spasms (1 to 2 seconds, about 20 per cluster) and developmental regression (stopped smiling, less active) has infantile spasms (West syndrome). The characteristic EEG is hypsarrhythmia : chaotic, high voltage, disorganised background with multif
x: B. Centrotemporal spikes are seen in benign rolandic epilepsy of school-age children with nocturnal facial or oropharyngeal seizures. | C. Slow spike and wave below 3 Hz is the EEG of Lennox Gastaut syndrome, which begins later in early childhood with multiple seizure types; infantile spasms may evolve into it. | D. Generalised 3 Hz spike and wave is the pattern of childhood absence epilepsy with staring spells in school-age children.

q: mother brought her 2month baby with squint next assessment ?didn't mention sudden or hx of truma
k: Infant squint: confirm with the corneal light reflex first. Reflex displaced temporally = esotropia; displaced nasally = exotropia Intermittent squint can be normal up to about 4 months Constant squint at any age or any
r: The first assessment of an infant with a squint is the corneal light reflex (Hirschberg test) : a penlight at both eyes should give symmetrical, centred reflections, and a displaced reflex in one eye confirms a true deviation and separates it from pseudostrabismus (broad epicanthal folds). It needs
x: B. The cover test (cover/uncover) needs the child to fixate on a target and is the test for older infants and toddlers, roughly from 6 months; a 2 month old cannot cooperate. | C. Referral to ophthalmology is right when the squint is confirmed and constant, persists beyond about 4 months, or the red reflex is abnormal (leukocoria); first you confirm the deviation with the corneal reflex.

q: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 75/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 130 beats per minute. His ECG is shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
k: SVT: stability decides the first step. Unstable (hypotension, shock, altered consciousness, heart failure): synchronized cardioversion Stable: vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine (rapid IV push with flush) Child minimum syst
r: The ECG is a regular narrow complex tachycardia (SVT), and the first decision is stability. A BP of 75/50 in an 8 year old is hypotension (below the lower limit of about 70 + 2 × age = 86 mmHg systolic), so he is haemodynamically unstable even though he is alert. Unstable SVT with a pulse is treated
x: A. Adenosine is the drug for stable SVT after vagal manoeuvres fail (or can be given quickly if IV access is ready), but hypotension calls for cardioversion. | B. Amiodarone is for stable wide complex tachycardia or refractory SVT under expert advice; it is slower and can worsen hypotension. | C. Vagal stimulation (ice to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children) is first line only for a stable child with SVT.

q: A 9 year old girl in contact with her maid who is has confirmed active tuberculosis TB and lives with them at the same house The child is asymptomatic . Doesn't complain from any physical symptoms. After testing, IGRA is +ve and chest x-ray pic is provided What is the most definitive treatment?
o: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid, and rifampin for 4 months
k: Latent TB (positive TST/IGRA, no symptoms, normal CXR): preventive therapy. Preferred: 3 months weekly isoniazid + rifapentine (3HP), 4 months rifampin (4R), 3 months daily isoniazid + rifampin (3HR) Alternative: isoniaz
r: An asymptomatic child with a positive IGRA after household contact and a normal chest X ray has latent TB infection, not active disease, so she needs preventive therapy, not full treatment. Rifamycin based short regimens are preferred because they have higher completion rates and similar efficacy to
x: A. Isoniazid alone for 6 (or 9) months treats latent TB too, but it is the older, longer alternative with poorer completion and more hepatotoxicity; short rifamycin regimens are preferred. | C. A three drug regimen with pyrazinamide is not a latent TB regimen; pyrazinamide belongs to active TB treatment (or old rifampin-pyrazinamide courses abandoned for liver toxicity). | D. Four drugs for 2 months then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months is the standard regimen for active TB, right only if she

q: A 10 years old patient came with mother with eye puffiness for one week and had history of flu like illness No lower limb edema or any remarkable findings in abdomen/chest Protein was low Urine protein was 4+ What's the dx
k: Nephrotic vs nephritic in children: Nephrotic: proteinuria > 3.5 g/day (> 40 mg/m²/h), albumin < 25 g/L, oedema, hyperlipidaemia Child: minimal change disease, steroid responsive, first line prednisolone Nephritic: haema
r: Periorbital puffiness (worse in the morning) in a child, with low protein and urine protein 4+ , is nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, with hyperlipidaemia. The preceding flu like illness is a common trigger, and normal BP without haematuria fits minimal change disea
x: A. Nephritic syndrome gives haematuria (cola urine, RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria and only mild proteinuria, typically 1 to 3 weeks after streptococcal throat or skin infection. | C. Hereditary angioedema causes recurrent non pitting swelling of face, limbs, gut or larynx with low C4, without proteinuria or hypoalbuminaemia. | D. Protein losing enteropathy causes low albumin and oedema through the gut, often with diarrhoea, but urine protein is negative.

q: Parents bring 7 YO to Gp with concerns of not going to school . No other symptoms mentioned. Developmentally and growth are tracking well . Next step in management
k: School refusal: treat with behavioral support and early return, not avoidance or drugs. Rule out organic causes, bullying, learning difficulty first Gradual exposure and gentle separation from parents Coordinate with sch
r: A 7 year old who refuses school with normal growth and development and no other symptoms fits school refusal driven by separation anxiety. First line management is behavioral: reassure the parents, avoid reinforcing avoidance, and promote gradual, gentle separation with an early return to school, wo
kw: Developmentally and growth are tracking well
x: A. Defer school 1 more year: avoidance reinforces the anxiety and harms learning and socialization; deferral is only considered for true developmental unreadiness, which is excluded here. | B. Start home schooling: also rewards avoidance; the goal is the earliest possible return to regular school. | D. Anti anxiety medication: reserved for severe or persistent anxiety disorder that fails behavioral therapy (CBT), not as the first step.

q: A 16-year-old boy came to the Emergency Department complaining of exertional dyspnea and easy fatiguability for the past few weeks. His parents admitted that he used to be a sick child requiring multiple hospital admissions and frequent blood transfusions . His parents are related . He was found to be pale, jaundiced, and have hepatosplenomegaly , with a scar from laparoscopic cholecystectomy (see lab results). Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
k: Hemoglobinopathy workup: Clues: consanguinity, transfusions, hemolysis, gallstones young, hepatosplenomegaly Diagnostic: hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC Screen: solubility test (HbS only) Film: target cells, sickle ce
r: Consanguineous parents , frequent transfusions since childhood, pallor, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and a prior cholecystectomy (pigment stones from chronic hemolysis) indicate an inherited hemoglobinopathy such as thalassemia or sickle cell disease. Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the abnorm
x: A. Peripheral blood film: shows target cells, microcytosis or sickle cells and suggests the diagnosis, but it does not quantify or confirm the hemoglobin type. | B. Sickle cell saturation (the sickling or solubility screen): detects HbS only; it cannot distinguish trait from disease and misses thalassemia, so it is a screen, not the confirmatory test. | C. Bone marrow biopsy: for marrow failure, leukemia or infiltration; not needed for hemoglobinopathies.

q: 3 y/o boy brought to the ER by his mother, he ate unknown number of tablet. His irritable with abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, hematemisis, Melena , admitted for further evaluation, few hour later he seems stable , but after 6 h he become drowsy with high liver enzymes What is the type of tablet?
k: Iron poisoning stages: Stage 1 (0-6 h): GI toxicity, vomiting, hematemesis, melena Stage 2 (6-24 h): latent, apparent improvement Stage 3: shock, metabolic acidosis, lethargy Stage 4 (2-5 days): hepatotoxicity Stage 5 (w
r: Iron poisoning follows a staged course: an early GI phase from direct corrosive injury (abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis and melena ), then a latent phase where the child seems stable , followed by shock, metabolic acidosis, altered consciousness and hepatotoxicity . A toddler with GI
kw: few hour later he seems stable
x: B. Paracetamol: causes delayed hepatotoxicity after 24 to 72 hours, but early symptoms are mild nausea and vomiting, not hematemesis and melena. | C. Digoxin: causes vomiting, arrhythmias, bradycardia, heart block, hyperkalemia and visual changes (yellow vision), not GI bleeding with liver injury. | D. Aspirin: causes vomiting, tinnitus, hyperventilation with mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, and fever; liver failure is not its signature.

q: 6 day preterm baby at 34 weeks of gestation with poor feeding, bilirubin 380 , mainly unconjicated . Instited phototherpay but failed Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: High loading IV fluid or hydration
k: Severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia: Intensive phototherapy first, thresholds lower for preterm babies Rising despite phototherapy or signs of encephalopathy: exchange transfusion IVIG for isoimmune hemolysis
r: A 34 week preterm baby on day 6 with mainly unconjugated bilirubin 380 µmol/L (about 22 mg/dL) and failed phototherapy is at risk of bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus), and preterm babies have lower treatment thresholds. The next step is to remove bilirubin directly by exchange transfusion, whic
x: A. Phenobarbital: induces hepatic glucuronyl transferase but acts too slowly for acute severe hyperbilirubinemia; used in Crigler Najjar type II, not as rescue therapy. | C. High IV fluids: correct dehydration that worsens jaundice, but hydration alone cannot lower dangerous bilirubin levels after phototherapy failure; it is the answer for neonatal polycythemia. | D. Antibiotics: for suspected sepsis (temperature instability, lethargy, raised markers); poor feeding alone does not make it the nex

q: A full-term infant of a diabetic mother has a hematocrit of 71% and appears plethoric . What is the appropriate management?
k: Neonatal polycythemia (venous Hct >65%): Causes: infant of diabetic mother, IUGR, delayed cord clamping, twin to twin transfusion Features: plethora, hypoglycemia, jaundice, lethargy, respiratory distress Asymptomatic or
r: An infant of a diabetic mother is prone to polycythemia (chronic fetal hypoxia drives erythropoietin). A hematocrit of 71% with plethora but no stated symptoms is managed with hydration, enterally or with IV fluids, and close monitoring. Partial exchange transfusion is reserved for very high hematoc
x: A. Reassurance: Hct 71% is above the polycythemia threshold of 65%, so the infant needs hydration and monitoring, not reassurance alone. | B. Partial exchange transfusion if symptomatic: kept for symptomatic infants with Hct ≥70-75% whose symptoms worsen despite IV hydration; benefit is unclear and NEC risk rises, so it is not the appropriate first management. | C. Phototherapy: treats hyperbilirubinemia, which may follow polycythemia, but does nothing for the high hematocrit.

q: 8-year-old girl with an 8-week history of rash, weight loss, and weakness. She has a heliotrope rash over the eyelids , rash over the elbows , and truncal weakness . CK 850 , LDH 650. What is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Juvenile dermatomyositis: Skin: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over knuckles, elbows, knees Symmetrical proximal weakness Raised CK, LDH, AST, aldolase Calcinosis is a later complication in children Treatment: steroids
r: A heliotrope rash on the eyelids, a rash over the elbows (extensor surfaces, like Gottron papules), proximal and truncal weakness and raised muscle enzymes ( CK 850, LDH 650 ) in a child are classic for juvenile dermatomyositis. It is the most common childhood idiopathic inflammatory myopathy and is
x: A. SLE: malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, renal disease; a heliotrope rash and high CK point to myositis. | B. Scleroderma: skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly; not a heliotrope rash with myositis. | C. Muscular dystrophy: progressive weakness with Gower sign and very high CK, but no rash; Duchenne mainly affects boys.

q: A 6 year old presented to the emergency department due to palpitations and being pale for 30 minutes . He was now stable. They didn't mention any interventions. BP: 95/80, HR: 220 , RR: 25. What is the initial step :
k: Pediatric tachycardia approach: Stable: 12 lead ECG first Narrow QRS SVT (infants often >220, children >180, no P waves): vagal maneuvers, then adenosine Unstable (shock, altered consciousness): synchronized cardioversio
r: A 6 year old with sudden palpitations and pallor and a HR of 220 has a tachyarrhythmia, most likely SVT, and he is currently stable . The initial step is a 12 lead ECG (during the tachycardia) to confirm the rhythm and QRS width, which decides treatment: vagal maneuvers then adenosine for narrow com
x: A. Electrolytes: useful later to find triggers (potassium, magnesium), but they do not identify the rhythm or guide immediate treatment. | C. Echo: assesses structural heart disease or cardiomyopathy after the rhythm is managed; not the first step. | D. ABG: for shock, respiratory failure or metabolic derangement; it does not diagnose the arrhythmia.

q: A child presents with signs and symptoms of rheumatic fever and a heart murmur . What is the most appropriate investigation ?
k: Rheumatic fever = Jones criteria + proof of recent strep infection. 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus strep evidence Strep evidence: raised or rising ASO, anti-DNase B, positive throat culture or rapid antigen Echo: de
r: Diagnosing rheumatic fever needs Jones criteria plus evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection . With the clinical signs already present, the ASO titer supplies that evidence and confirms the diagnosis. Echocardiography is not offered here.
x: A. ECG: shows a prolonged PR interval, which is only a minor Jones criterion and is not diagnostic; useful for monitoring, not for confirming rheumatic fever.

q: A child presents with fatigue and weight gain. On examination, the growth velocity is reduced , with delayed growth on the growth chart. Thyroid function tests reveal markedly elevated TSH and low T4 levels. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Short stature with weight gain = endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, Cushing). High TSH, low T4: primary hypothyroidism, give levothyroxine Low or normal TSH, low T4: central cause Short with weight loss or t
r: Markedly elevated TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism, which explains the fatigue, weight gain and reduced growth velocity . Treatment is thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine, which also allows catch-up growth.
kw: markedly elevated TSH and low T4
x: B. Growth hormone therapy: for confirmed growth hormone deficiency or specific syndromes; growth failure here is due to hypothyroidism and corrects with levothyroxine. Hypothyroidism must be treated first.

q: A child with type 1 diabetes experiences recurrent hypoglycemia at night , on basal- bolus insulin regimen:
o: Reduce basal insulin dose at night
Add a meal at 3 at night
k: Match the low to the insulin acting at that time. Night or fasting lows: reduce basal (long-acting) insulin Postprandial lows: reduce mealtime (rapid-acting) bolus Lows with exercise: reduce the pre-exercise bolus Recurr
r: On a basal-bolus regimen, recurrent nocturnal hypoglycemia (overnight and fasting) reflects too much basal insulin acting at night, so the fix is to reduce the night basal dose. Adjust the insulin that is acting at the time of the lows.
x: A. Drink juice at bedtime: a temporary fix that treats the symptom and raises glucose but leaves excess basal insulin in place. | C. Reduce bolus before meal: corrects hypoglycemia occurring a few hours after meals (postprandial), not overnight. | D. Add a meal at 3 at night: disrupts sleep and adds calories instead of correcting the dose; not recommended practice.

q: Newborn in 3rd percentile , family poor was diluting formula milk , what is next most appropriate?
o: Advice family how to make formula
k: Failure to thrive: hospitalize when unsafe at home or severe. Admit: severe malnutrition, dehydration or electrolyte abnormality, failed outpatient management, suspected neglect or unsafe home Diluted formula: risk of hy
r: A newborn at the 3rd percentile whose poor family is diluting formula has failure to thrive from inadequate intake with a risk of hyponatremia and water intoxication from over-dilute feeds. The keyed step is hospitalization to correct the nutritional deficit safely, monitor electrolytes and weight g
x: B. High calorie formula: does not solve the cause (dilution due to poverty) and a poor family may not afford or prepare it correctly; used for children with increased needs (e.g. heart disease). | C. Advise family how to make formula: education is essential and would be enough for mild growth faltering in a family able to comply, but at the 3rd percentile with ongoing dilution and poverty, outpatient advice alone is unsafe.

q: 9-month-old baby mainly breastfed , mother slowly introducing solid foods . Best nutritional advice?
o: Advise mother to introduce solid foods more rapidly
k: Breastfed infants: iron and vitamin D. Vitamin D: from the first days of life for breastfed infants Iron: stores deplete at 4 to 6 months; give iron-rich foods or supplements Complementary foods from about 6 months, one
r: A mainly breastfed 9-month-old whose mother is introducing solids slowly is at risk of iron deficiency: fetal iron stores run out around 4 to 6 months and breast milk is low in iron, so iron must come from foods or supplements. With iron-rich foods not yet established, iron supplementation is the be
x: B. Give vitamin D supplements: breastfed infants should already receive vitamin D from birth; the gap this stem highlights (slow solids at 9 months) is iron. | C. Add formula milk: unnecessary; breastfeeding should continue, and formula does not replace the need for complementary foods. | D. Introduce solid foods more rapidly: complementary foods should progress, but forcing faster introduction does not quickly correct the iron gap, and new foods are still introduced a few days apart.

q: A child presents with signs and symptoms of rheumatic fever and a heart murmur . What is the most appropriate investigation ?
k: Rheumatic fever = evidence of strep + Jones criteria. Major: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules Minor: fever, arthralgia, raised ESR/CRP, prolonged PR Strep evidence: raised or ris
r: Diagnosing acute rheumatic fever by the Jones criteria needs evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection plus 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, criteria. With echocardiography not among the options (the recaller confirmed no ECHO), the ASO titre is the investigation that proves recent str
x: A. ECG: shows a prolonged PR interval, which is only a minor criterion and is not specific; it cannot confirm rheumatic fever.

q: family brought their kid who has a fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested some seed . Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound X ray pictures was shown What is the next thing to do?
o: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
k: Suspected airway foreign body in a child: x-ray first, rigid bronchoscopy for diagnosis and removal. Clues: choking episode, sudden cough, unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds CXR: hyperinflation on the obstructed
r: A choking episode after eating a seed followed by decreased breath sounds on the right is foreign body aspiration (the right main bronchus is wider and more vertical). The fever, cough and runny nose reflect post-obstructive infection. The chest x-ray, the initial test, is already done, so the next
kw: choking after he ingested some seed
x: A. Epinephrine subcutaneous: used in anaphylaxis (urticaria, stridor, hypotension after an allergen); it does not remove an airway foreign body. | C. Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid: right for a simple viral URTI, but the choking history and unilateral reduced air entry make missing a foreign body dangerous. | D. IV: fluids or antibiotics may be supportive for secondary pneumonia, but they do not treat the cause, which is the retained seed.

q: A 1-week-old infant seen in screening clinic (see image). Which of the following is the name of this primitive reflex ?
k: Name the reflex by its stimulus and response. Stepping: upright, feet on surface, walking steps; gone about 2 months Rooting: cheek stroke, turns to stimulus; gone about 4 months Moro: sudden head drop, arms abduct then
r: The image shows a newborn held upright with the soles touching a surface , making alternating walking movements; this is the stepping (walking) reflex, a primitive reflex present at birth.
x: A. Rooting: stroking the cheek or side of the mouth makes the baby turn the head and open the mouth toward the stimulus. | C. Parachute: a postural reflex appearing around 8 to 9 months; when tipped forward the infant extends the arms to break the fall, so it cannot be seen at 1 week. | D. Lateral neck: the asymmetric tonic neck (fencing) reflex: head turned to one side, arm on that side extended and opposite arm flexed.

q: A 2-week-old infant seen in screening clinic (see image). What is expected age (in months) for this reflexto disappear ?
k: Primitive reflexes disappear on a schedule; persistence suggests neurological disease. Stepping: about 2 months Rooting: about 4 months Moro, ATNR: about 4 to 6 months Palmar grasp: about 6 months; plantar grasp about 12
r: The image shows the stepping reflex (infant held upright making walking movements). It is present from birth and disappears early, by about 2 months , which is the earliest age among the options.
kw: age (in months) for this reflexto disappear
x: B. 4: the age at which rooting (and sucking) disappears, not stepping. | C. 6: around when Moro and the asymmetric tonic neck reflex are gone; persistence of these beyond 6 months suggests a CNS problem. | D. 8: around when the parachute reflex appears; it is not a disappearance age for stepping.

q: Pediatric 4 yrs c/o fatigue fever pruritic and changes of sclera on exam splenomegaly . Hb 87, Mcv low, Plt 200, + combs test . He brought a picture close to this picture

q: A baby is observed walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance . At approximately what age is a child typically expected to walk independently this way?

r: A wide-based gait with arms raised for balance (high guard) is how a child walks when independent walking has just been achieved. Independent walking is expected at about 12 months (normal range roughly 9 to 18 months).
x: A. 9 months: the age to pull to stand and cruise holding furniture, not to walk alone. | C. 15 months: by now most children walk well with a narrower gait and arms lowered; the typical age for first independent, wide-based walking is earlier (red flag only if not walking by 18 months).

q: 12 months old Saudi boy and came for vaccination . Which vaccines should be given

Varicella, OPV, MCV, PCV: misses MMR, which is mandatory at 12 months; varicella is given with the 18 month or school entry doses in the current schedule. | D. Hib, MCV, OPV, MMR: Hib is given in the infant series and its booster at 18 months, not at 12 months, and PCV is missing.

q: A child came with his mother to a well-baby clinic for a general check-up. The child can skip , draw a rectangle , count from 1-10 , and knows opposites . How old is he?

q: A neonate with meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) is on maximum oxygenation mechanical ventilation but is still hypoxic . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

Inhaled nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator that reduces the shunt and improves oxygenation; it is
x: A. Increase tidal volume: higher volumes on already maximal settings cause barotrauma, air leak and pneumothorax, a known risk in MAS, so avoiding further lung injury takes priority. | B. Give systemic steroid: steroids are not recommended routinely in MAS and do not reverse pulmonary hypertension.

q: 14 year old child has h-pylori positive doudnal ulcer , started on triple therapy what is the duration of tx ?

r: Triple therapy for H. pylori (PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin or metronidazole) is given for 7 to 14 days , with 14 days preferred in current guidelines because of better eradication. There is a correlation: childhood asthma, especially severe or atopic, increases the risk of adult asthma, and remission can relapse later.

q: A 26-year-old woman presented to the clinic pregnant at 15 weeks. She is known to have epilepsy and is taking Phenytoin. The last convulsion was 6 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

q: A 29-year-old woman presented to the Emergency Room with a very heavy period. She is morbidly obese and diabetic. Her periods are irregular, occurring every 3-4 months. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q: A 79-year-old man is evaluated in follow-up for a 2 mm solitary pulmonary nodule, which was incidentally discovered on imaging for chest pain 4 years ago. q: A 33-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 3 years is evaluated in the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of pain and swelling of the left knee and low-grade fever. q: A 60-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic because of a 6-month history of exertional shortness of breath. q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented to the Emergency Department with 3-hour continuous retrosternal heaviness associated with profuse sweating. Physical examination reveals tachycardia and an S4 gallop on heart auscultation. The patient is commenced on aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin infusion (see reports). q: A 58-year-old man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease. His medications are metformin, sitagliptin, aspirin, lipitor, and lisinopril. He works as a car mechanic. For the last 4 months, he has started to notice exertional shortness of breath that interferes with his job but does not limit him from doing it, provided that at rest, he is fine without any shortness of breath. r: NYHA I: بدون limitation. II: limitation بسيط. III: limitation واضح. IV: أعراض بالراحة.

q: A 38-year-old woman who is not known to have any medical illness is referred to the clinic because of a chest x-ray that showed prominent hilar structures bilaterally. She is having on-and-off cough but denies any history of shortness of breath, sputum production, chest pain, skin lesions, weight loss, fever, or contact with sick people. She is not a smoker. Examination reveals clear chest bilaterally (see lab results and reports). CT chest: Confirmed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, otherwise lung parenchyma was clear. CT-guided biopsy: Showed noncaseating granuloma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

q: A 38-year-old woman known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus just returned from Makkah. She complains of fever, lethargy, and headache. She has no cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or skin rash. Examination reveals a drowsy patient with positive neck stiffness (see report). Lumbar puncture: Low glucose, markedly increased protein, WBC 9000 with predominantly neutrophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to start?
r: لو عمر فوق ٥٠ أو immunocompromised ← أضيفي Ampicillin (Listeria). Bacterial meningitis ← Ceftriaxone + vancomycin.

q: A 50-year-old man known to be an alcoholic presented with progressive abdominal distention and yellow discoloration of the sclera. q: A 60-year-old man known to have systemic hypertension, gout, and dyslipidemia presented to the Emergency Room 5 days ago with signs of heart failure and was diagnosed with congestive heart failure and new-onset diabetes mellitus. q: A 26-year-old woman presented with insomnia, fatigue, and sadness. She delivered her first child 5 days ago. Examination reveals a tearful and depressed appearance. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q: A 50-year-old woman is complaining of hot flashes and insomnia. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?

r: Exudate does not mean strep: conjunctivitis with an exudative throat is adenovirus until proven otherwise.

q: 25-year-old college student came for a routine checkup. He does not have any active complaints. Examination reveals a diastolic murmur increase when the patient leans forward in full expiration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
k: Diastolic murmurs: ARMS on the left (AR, MS) and PaRTS on the right (PR, TS).
r: If only one option is diastolic, the timing alone answers the question.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-153). مكرر من القديم (OCT-6732).

q: A man at a smoking cessation clinic acknowledges the risks of smoking and is willing to quit, but only AFTER he buys nicotine patches (he hasn't bought them yet). Which stage of change is he in?
r: He is aware of the problem and intends to change but hasn't taken a concrete step yet, which is contemplation. (Alhomrani U2924: 'he did NOT buy it → contemplation'.)
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في ياسر (NOV-723). Why not B? preparation requires a step already taken toward quitting (e.g., patches bought). Claude: Alhomrani calls this a linguistic disagreement in a poorly worded ethics recall; this is how the examiner read the stem.

q: A 25-year-old woman is complaining of whitish vaginal discharge and itching for 3 days. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q: 32 years old 20 weaks gestation examination was unremarkable. BMI 24 BP 110/75 Most appropriate?
k: Low-risk pregnancy at 20 weeks: routine care plus supplements; screening tests follow their own calendar.
r: Watch the lead-in: 'now / most appropriate' at 20 weeks = iron; 'at the next visit' (24 weeks) = OGTT.

k: Febrile, toxic looking child + pyuria = pyelonephritis until proven otherwise.
r: Dark urine tempts you toward glomerulonephritis, but high fever, a toxic look and high leukocytes make it pyelonephritis.

q: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing, muscle cramping, and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. A diagnosis of acute kidney injury due to hypovolemia is established. Which of the following is the most expected laboratory abnormality?
o: Blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio is elevated > 20
Presence of dysmorphic red blood cell (RBC) and RBC cast
k: Prerenal vs intrinsic (ATN) AKI indices: BUN/Cr: prerenal >20; ATN <15; FENa: prerenal <1%; ATN >2%; Urine Na: prerenal <20; ATN >40
r: Each wrong option here describes intrinsic renal disease; only the high BUN/Cr ratio fits intact tubules saving volume.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-303). مكرر من القديم (OCT-7478).

q: A 26-year-old man with type I diabetes mellitus on insulin presents to the clinic for regular follow-up. He is asymptomatic (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
k: Diabetes + albuminuria (micro or macro) = ACE inhibitor (ARB if not tolerated).
r: The lab card is hidden in this recall; the clue is "asymptomatic diabetic on follow-up, most appropriate treatment" = proteinuria = ACE inhibitor.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P2-208). مكرر من القديم (OCT-0927).

q: A 45-year-old man diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months ago, started on metformin 500 TDS, comes for his first follow-up. Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, Heart rate 80/min. Glucose fasting 7.4, Creatinine 125 (mildly high), HbA1c 6.8%. Which of the following investigations is recommended to assess his renal function/diabetic kidney disease annually?
k: Diabetic kidney disease screening.
r: If both "urine microalbumin" and "urine albumin/creatinine ratio" are offered, pick the ratio; it corrects for urine concentration.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في سبتمبر/أكتوبر (Medicine) (OCT-2002). Printed answer B. Urine microalbumin; 'annually' in red as the key word. October By Similar update

q: A 32 years old male (not sure of age) who is a construction worker came due to accident during work with a crush injury. ECG shows peaked T waves with shortened QT interval. What's the most immediate management?
k: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes: stabilise, shift, remove.
r: "Most immediate" with ECG changes = calcium; "lowers potassium fastest" = insulin and glucose.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في سبتمبر/أكتوبر (Medicine) (OCT-2251). Printed answer B. Compiler: rhabdomyolysis hyperkalemia; calcium gluconate first to stabilise the myocardium. October By Similar update

q: A mother is worried about her son who has asthma . What is the most appropriate counseling ?
o: He will develop chronic lung disorder
Childhood asthma will disappear by adolescence
He will have asthma for the rest of his life
No correlation between childhood and adulthood asthma
k: Childhood asthma prognosis. Many children outgrow it by adolescence Persistence more likely with atopy, severe disease, parental asthma, female sex in adolescence Remission may relapse in adulthood
r: The reassuring, evidence based counselling is that many children with asthma improve or go into remission by adolescence , especially those with mild disease and episodic viral triggered wheeze. Atopy, severe disease, and parental asthma make persistence more likely.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني (NOV-0960).
kw: worried about her son who has asthma

q: A 60-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension presented to the Emergency Department with 3-hour continuous retrosternal heaviness associated with profuse sweating. Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block. Previous ECG was normal. Cardiac enzymes: Pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Wait for the results of cardiac enzymes
r: STEMI within 12 h and no PCI available: thrombolysis without waiting for enzymes.

o: Start to take the salbutamol regularly

q: Patient in 50s came at follow up clinic k/c of DM on metformin 500 mg PID and gliclazide. HbAlc: 5.8 (normal value 5.6) what to do?
o: Tell him he is at a high risk for cardiovascular disease
k: Follow-up decisions by HbA1c on treatment: Target for most adults: < 7%; At or below target: no change, reassure, continue; Above target: intensify (increase dose or add agent)
r: Same HbA1c 5.8% but BP 149/90 on repeated readings flips the answer to adding an ACE inhibitor.

o: Reassure and tell them about Hand Hygiene
Refer to ENT for possible Tonsillectomy or Adenoidectomy
k: Frequent colds in a thriving young child = normal immune maturation; reassure and advise hand hygiene.
r: The number of colds alone is not a red flag; growth failure or severe, unusual infections are.

q: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with complaints of pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs has low Hemoglobin What is the most likely type of leukemia?
k: Childhood leukemia: ALL: most common childhood leukemia and cancer, peak 2 to 5 years; AML (acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common; CML: rare in children
r: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' = AML; when asked the most common childhood leukemia, pick ALL.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-257). مكرر من القديم (SWR-0379).

q: A 68-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension is admitted with extensive anterior ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). had successful angioplasty and stenting to left anterior descending artery. Aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol and enalapril were started. Cholesterol (HDL) 1.0 > 1.03 mmol/L Cholesterol (LDL) 3.36 <3.36 mmol/L Total Cholesterol 5.0 <5.1 mmol/L Triglycerides 2.2 <2.16 mmol/L Which of the following is recommended?
k: Four statin benefit groups (age over 21).
r: After any MI, ignore the "normal" lipid panel: high-intensity statin is always indicated.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-260). مكرر من القديم (OCT-0411).

q: A 65-year-old man with a known history of cardiovascular disease presents to the emergency department with fever, generalized weakness, and hypotension following a recent infection. On examination, he is febrile and tachycardic, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. Hemodynamic monitoring reveals the following findings: Parameter Finding Central venous pressure (CVP) Decreased Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) Decreased Cardiac output (CO) Decreased Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) Increased Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO) Increased What is the most likely type of shock?
k: Shock type by hemodynamic profile: Hypovolemic: CO low, CVP/PCWP low, SVR high, SvO2 low; Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high, SvO2 low; Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR LOW, SvO2 high
r: The infection history is a distractor: only a HIGH cardiac output with LOW SVR makes it septic.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-270). مكرر من القديم (OCT-3306). Septic Shock = High CO (initially) & Low SVR

q: A 5-year-old child presents with FEVER and dysuria. A urinary tract infection is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
k: Pediatric UTI: route is decided by how sick the child is, not by fever alone.
r: Read for "appears ill" or "vomiting": those words flip the answer from oral amoxicillin to IM/IV ceftriaxone.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في سبتمبر/أكتوبر (Pediatrics) (OCT-2788). Telegram screenshot of another version (no mention of the child appearing ill); answer A. Oral amoxicillin marked CONFIRMED. Contrast with the 'appears ill' version where IM ceftriaxone is endorsed. 20 October update

q: age not recalled male presented to the emergency department with icterus and jaundice. Serology showed: Hepatitis A: + Anti-HAV IgM — positive + Anti-HAV IgG — positive Hepatitis B: + Anti-HBs (surface antibody) — positive + HBsAg (surface antigen) — negative + Anti-HBc (core antibody) — negative + HBeAg (e antigen) — negative What is the diagnosis?
o: Acute hepatitis A with immunization against hepatitis B
Acute hepatitis A with previous hepatitis B infection
r: Anti-HAV IgM + = acute hepatitis A; anti-HBs + alone = immune to hepatitis B (vaccine), not active B.

Increase oxygen to 100% by non-rebreather mask

q: A woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) presents with hirsutism and irregular menstrual cycles. Local cosmetic treatments have not helped. What is the most appropriate management?
r: Combined OCPs are first-line drug treatment for PCOS-related hirsutism: they raise SHBG and suppress ovarian androgens, and they also regulate the cycle. Anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone, finasteride) are added after 6 months if the response is inadequate, with contraception.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في ياسر (NOV-645). Why not C? Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen added after about 6 months of an inadequate response to the COC, not first-line on its own.

q: 50 years old male came c/o painless hematuria (literally written) started 3 day ago. What most appropriate INITIAL investigation?
o: KUB (literally written without mentioning xray nor CT)
k: Hematuria: confirm with urinalysis first, then investigate the cause.
r: "Initial" picks urinalysis; if the question asks for the most appropriate or definitive investigation of painless hematuria in an older man, pick cystoscopy plus CT urography.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-225). مكرر من القديم (SWR-0169).

q: case of febrile seizure. The mother is concerned about future convulsions and already giving antipyrites for fever. What would be the consultation for her?
o: Perform EEG to predict future seizures
Start antipyrites when fever is present
Educate the family about how to deal with future seizure
k: Simple febrile seizure: benign, counsel and educate, no tests or prophylaxis.
r: "Worried about future seizures" = educate on what to do during a seizure; antipyretics and EEG do not change recurrence.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في الحمراني 10-14 (N14-P1-232). مكرر من القديم (OCT-0529).

q: 43y old women attended opd for assessment with weight gain and easly brusing complain for 3-4 months. She also noticed to be having irregular menstruation, truncal obesity and puprble striae Bp: 143/88 ACTH : 15 Cortisol 8am: 870 Cortisol 4pm: 560 Asking about the diagnosis:
k: In confirmed Cushing syndrome, ACTH decides the source.
r: A normal-looking ACTH in a cushingoid patient is NOT suppressed, so it still points to the pituitary, not the adrenal.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في سبتمبر/أكتوبر (Medicine) (SWR-5104). Cushing syndrome with non-suppressed ACTH and loss of diurnal cortisol variation: pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease).

q: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed with a follicular ovarian cyst. She is otherwise healthy and desires reliable contraception. Which method is best suited to help prevent recurrence of functional ovarian cysts?
k: Functional cysts are ovulation-driven, so the method must suppress ovulation: combined OCP.
r: If the same woman had a VTE history, estrogen is out and the answer moves to an estrogen-free method.
n: صورة من سايلنت الأحد 15 – موجود في سبتمبر/أكتوبر (OB/GYN) (SWR-2668). Printed answer C: combined OCPs suppress ovulation and prevent new functional cysts.

q: 9-year-old boy who has nighttime enuresis 3 times a week and has never been dry. His urine CX and analysis are normal, and his PE is unremarkable. What should he do next?
k: Nocturnal enuresis: urinalysis for all, classify, then treat.
r: Never dry plus normal urine and exam = behavioural treatment; imaging only when neuro or spine findings appear.

q: A 31-year-old man presented with a stab wound to the neck in Zone III. Ultrasound showed Avascular injury vessel in Zone III. What is the most appropriate management?
k: Penetrating neck trauma by zone.
r: Zone III vessel injury in a stable patient = endovascular; instability in any zone = operative control.
